conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. You’re here for your planned gastric bypass—how are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, mostly. I’ve tried diets so many times and I’m scared about surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll walk you through each step. The plan is a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and we’ll also do an endoscopy during the operation to check everything from the inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will this help my reflux and sleep apnea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weight loss after bypass often improves reflux symptoms and can improve obstructive sleep apnea over time. We’ll still have you use your CPAP as usual right now, especially while you’re recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I brought my CPAP. Should I use it tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—please do. We’ll also monitor your breathing closely after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take citalopram and Abilify. Do I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we plan to resume your home medications after surgery, but for now and after discharge you’ll need to crush pills so they go down safely while your new connection heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Crush all of them? Even Protonix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—crush all pills. For Protonix specifically, you can crush it and mix it in something like yogurt as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are the biggest risks I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we watch for bleeding, infection, and problems at the new connections like a leak or blockage. After discharge, we’ll review warning signs—fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe belly pain, vomiting, or drainage/redness at the incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And pain—how bad is it usually?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right after surgery we typically use a Dilaudid PCA so you can control pain safely. As you improve, we switch to oral pain medicine like Roxicet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to head to the operating room. Any last questions before we get started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… please tell me if everything goes okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We will. We’ll update you after you’re awake in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in the recovery area now. The laparoscopic gastric bypass and the endoscopy are done, and everything went smoothly. Your blood pressure and heart rate have been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really sleepy. My stomach hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected right after surgery. You have the Dilaudid PCA—press the button when you need it. We’ll keep checking your pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel tight in my belly. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—some tightness and soreness around the small port sites is normal. We also placed a JP drain to collect any fluid; we’ll monitor the output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I drink water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet tonight. Tomorrow we’ll do an upper GI study to confirm there’s no leak, and then we’ll start you on the first stage of the post-bypass diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any nausea or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nauseous, but not throwing up. I used my CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on CPAP at night. Today’s main step is the upper GI imaging study to check the new connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens during that test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll drink contrast while they take X-ray images. We’re looking to make sure contrast goes through the new pathway and that there’s no leak or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your upper GI study looks good—no evidence of obstruction or leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So I can start drinking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start Stage 1 diet today and advance slowly as you tolerate it. Small sips, no straws, and no chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why no straws?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Straws can make you swallow extra air, which can cause painful bloating and discomfort while you’re healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is better but the PCA makes me groggy. Can I switch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—since you’re tolerating liquids and doing well, we can transition from the Dilaudid PCA to oral Roxicet for pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about constipation from pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. We’ll use a stool softener like Colace, and we’ll encourage walking, which also helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been able to get up and walk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I walked in the hallway. It hurts a bit when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal early on. Keep doing short walks—walking helps prevent complications and speeds recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re progressing well. How are you doing with the diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m sipping okay. I’m scared to drink too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That caution is good. Take small, frequent sips. We’ve advanced you gradually, and the goal is to be on Stage III diet by discharge and stay there until your follow-up—don’t self-advance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When does the drain come out? It’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check the output and the sites. If everything looks appropriate, we can remove the JP drain today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your port sites look dry, and the drain output is minimal. We removed the JP drain without difficulty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That was quick. What should I watch for at the incisions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower, but no tub baths or swimming. If there’s clear drainage, cover with clean dry gauze. Call us for increasing pain, swelling, redness, or foul-smelling or colored drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take ibuprofen if I get sore at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, and naproxen. They can cause bleeding and ulcers after this surgery. Use the prescribed pain medication instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medicines am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Roxicet for pain as needed, Colace for constipation, Actigall twice daily to help prevent gallbladder problems, and Protonix twice daily—crushed and mixed as directed. You’ll also resume your home meds like citalopram, lorazepam as needed, and Abilify—also crushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actigall—how long do I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For six months. It helps reduce the risk of gallbladder issues during rapid weight loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard something about vitamins. When do I start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start a chewable complete multivitamin with minerals—no gummy vitamins. That’s important after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about activity? I have kids at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for six weeks. You can do moderate exercise as you feel able, but avoid abdominal exercises. Keep walking daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. __ in about two weeks. Stay on Stage III diet until that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I get a fever, what number is too high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or come to the emergency department for fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by meds, severe nausea or vomiting, bloating, inability to drink, or concerning incision drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still anxious, but I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done very well—walking independently, tolerating the diet, and your pain is controlled on oral medication. We’ll finalize your discharge home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you. I understand you had a gastric bypass a few months ago and now you’re having upper belly pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started yesterday—this burning pain right in the middle, like under my ribs. I felt nauseous and threw up once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Was the vomit bloody or green? And have you been able to pass gas or have bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, not green—just food. I’m still passing gas. I’ve actually had more bowel movements than usual—like three loose ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, or trouble urinating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the pain and nausea. I’m scared something is wrong with the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Your vitals look stable and your belly exam is soft without guarding, which is reassuring. We’re going to check labs and get a CT scan with contrast to look at the bypass connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is a CT safe after surgery? And what are you looking for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—this is a common test. We’re looking for things like a blockage, a leak, or irritation/ulcer near the connection. The contrast helps us see where fluid is traveling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is pretty bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain with IV medication and also give nausea medicine. We’ll keep you from eating or drinking until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do my blood tests show anything serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far your labs are reassuring—your white blood cell count is normal and your kidney function looks fine. Nothing suggests a major infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost about 50 pounds since the bypass. Could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The weight loss itself isn’t the problem, but after bypass some people can develop irritation or ulcers near the gastrojejunal connection, which can cause this kind of pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about a blockage. Wouldn’t I be throwing up more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often with a blockage you’d have persistent vomiting and trouble passing gas. You’re still passing gas, which is a good sign, but we’ll let the imaging guide us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took blood for something called H. pylori. What is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bacteria that can contribute to ulcers. We’re checking a blood test for it. If it’s positive, we treat it with antibiotics; if it’s negative, we focus on acid suppression and other ulcer prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I know the CT results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We should have the read soon. Once we do, we’ll decide if you need an endoscopy to look directly at the connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT is back. It does not show an obstruction. It does show contrast in both the small gastric pouch and the larger gastric remnant, which can suggest a possible communication between them. There’s also some dilation of the proximal efferent limb, but again no clear blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A communication—does that mean a hole? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests there may be a connection between the pouch and the remnant. The CT can’t always confirm exactly what it is. The good news is there’s no free air or fluid and no obstruction. To better understand what’s causing your pain, we’re planning an upper endoscopy today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens during the endoscopy? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable. A flexible camera goes through the mouth into the pouch and down to the connection. We can look for ulcers or narrowing and see if there’s bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be from reflux? I’ve had reflux before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Reflux can contribute to irritation, but after bypass, pain like this is often from an ulcer near the gastrojejunal anastomosis. Either way, acid suppression is a key part of treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the endoscopy. The gastric pouch looked unremarkable, and the connection to the small bowel was widely open. We saw two ulcers on the jejunal side within about 2 cm of the connection—one small superficial clean-based ulcer and one larger deeper cratered ulcer with a pigmented spot. There was no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s ulcers. Is that why it hurts so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ulcers in that area can cause significant epigastric pain and nausea. The reassuring part is there’s no active bleeding and the connection is open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do we do to treat them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a proton pump inhibitor—Protonix—through the IV once daily while you’re here to reduce acid and help healing. We’ll also control pain with IV morphine for now and then switch to oral medication when you’re tolerating intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does this mean my bypass failed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Ulcers can happen after bypass even when the surgery is otherwise intact. Your pouch and the connection looked good on endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink anything yet? My mouth is so dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slowly. Once your nausea is controlled and you’re awake from sedation, we’ll begin with a bariatric diet progression—starting with a Bariatric Stage 2 plan as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine helps, but I don’t want to be on it long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good goal. As soon as you’re taking liquids and your pain is improving, we’ll switch to an oral pain medication like a liquid oxycodone-acetaminophen solution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—pain, nausea, and the loose stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is better than yesterday. I still feel a little queasy. I had another loose stool overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Today we’ll keep you on Bariatric Stage 2 and transition your pain control from IV to oral liquid medication. We’ll keep the acid medicine going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the ulcer bleed? That pigmented spot sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A pigmented spot can be a sign of a recent small bleed, but there was no active bleeding during the procedure. We’ll monitor your symptoms and blood counts, and the PPI helps reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will the H. pylori test come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should be back soon. If it’s negative, we won’t need antibiotics for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your H. pylori blood test is negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused the ulcers then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes ulcers occur from acid exposure at the connection site after bypass. The key is consistent acid suppression. We’ll send you home on a proton pump inhibitor twice a day, and it needs to be crushed so it absorbs properly after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about eating. What if food makes it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance slowly and stick to the bariatric diet stages. Small, frequent, appropriate foods and avoiding irritants will help. If pain spikes with intake, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is much better. I did have some loose stools late last night though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We can adjust your diet to see if that helps. Today we’ll advance you to Bariatric Stage III as long as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stage III is okay so far, but the diarrhea is annoying. Is it from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be from diet changes after bypass, and sometimes lactose can trigger it. If it continues, we can try a lactose-free approach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning, since you’re still having loose stools, we’re switching you to a lactose-free diet. Also, we’ll switch your Protonix from IV to an oral form since you’re tolerating intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m going home, what medicine am I taking for the ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take omeprazole 20 mg twice a day, and you should crush it before taking it. That’s the main ulcer-healing medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain? I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a liquid oxycodone-acetaminophen medication to use only as needed. The goal is to use the smallest amount necessary and taper off as your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious since this started. I keep thinking something will rupture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Based on the CT and endoscopy, we did not see obstruction or active bleeding, and your exam has stayed stable. We can also give you a small dose of alprazolam as needed for anxiety, but we’ll use it carefully, especially with any pain medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about that possible connection the CT mentioned between the pouch and remnant—do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we’re treating what we directly saw causing symptoms—the ulcers. The CT suggested a possible communication, but the immediate plan is medical treatment and close follow-up. If symptoms persist or worsen, your surgical team may recommend additional testing as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go back to work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can return to work as long as your pain is controlled without narcotic medications like oxycodone. If you still need them, it’s safer to wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before discharge: you’re walking independently, tolerating oral intake and meds, and your pain is controlled on oral medication. We’ll send you home on crushed omeprazole twice daily, the liquid pain medication as needed, and alprazolam as needed for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for worsening severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, fever or chills, inability to keep liquids down, or feeling faint. Otherwise, follow up with your surgical team as arranged and stay on the bariatric diet plan, lactose-free if it helps the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I hear you’ve had a hard time keeping anything down. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For about a week I’ve been nauseated all the time. I can’t tolerate liquids or food. I feel weak and barely pee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting? Fever? Severe belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. I’ve had some upper belly pain, not as bad as last time. I’ve thrown up a couple times but mostly it’s just nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were just here recently for ulcers at the connection after your gastric bypass, right? Are you still taking the omeprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been trying, but it’s hard to get pills down. I crush them like they told me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Right now you look dehydrated from not being able to take in enough. We’ll start IV fluids, check labs, and give nausea medicine through the IV so you don’t have to swallow it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need another scope or surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At the moment, no surgery is planned. We’ll focus on rehydration and controlling nausea and stomach irritation. If symptoms don’t improve, we’d reassess, but our first step is supportive care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just scared because I can’t even sip water without gagging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV ondansetron for nausea and restart IV pantoprazole to protect the ulcer area. Once you feel better, we’ll slowly reintroduce your Stage III bariatric diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth feels so dry. How long until the fluids help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually within a few hours you’ll feel less lightheaded and your urine output should pick up. We’ll keep monitoring your vitals and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight we continued IV fluids and nausea medication. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little less dizzy, but still nauseated. The upper stomach area is sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with irritation at the gastrojejunostomy where the ulcers were seen before. We’re continuing IV pantoprazole and ondansetron. We’ll also give vitamins and electrolytes through the IV while you’re not eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my labs okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function and electrolytes look okay right now, which is good, but the story and your symptoms still point to dehydration from low intake. We’ll keep replacing fluids and watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try to drink anything today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—small sips, slowly, and we’ll see how you tolerate it. If nausea spikes, we’ll pause and treat it. No straws or gum, and stay within the Stage III plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How was the night? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. The pain is better, but the nausea is still there. I can sip a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Since the pain is improving but nausea is lingering, we’re going to add sucralfate. It coats the lining and can help ulcers heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that another pill? I’m worried I can’t swallow it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a tablet, but we can work with you on how to take it safely with your bariatric surgery—small amounts, and we’ll make sure it’s given in a way you can tolerate. Keep crushing pills as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starting to have loose stools again. Is that from the new medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from a few things, including your gut being irritated and changes in intake. If it continues or worsens, we’ll send stool tests to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw you’ve had more diarrhea since yesterday. How many times overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A lot—maybe six or seven times. It’s watery. I feel wiped out again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry—this can definitely set you back. We’re going to send stool studies today, and we’ll restart IV fluids to keep you hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it contagious? I don’t want to give it to my family.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some diarrheal infections can spread. While we’re testing, we’ll use contact precautions in the hospital—good handwashing is key. We’ll talk more once results are back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m embarrassed to keep calling the nurse. It won’t stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please don’t feel embarrassed. Frequent diarrhea is a medical issue, and we need to know how often it’s happening so we can treat it and prevent dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool testing came back positive for Clostridium difficile, which is a bacteria that can cause significant diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: C. diff? How did I get that? Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen when the normal gut bacteria get disrupted, often after healthcare exposures. It can be serious if untreated because it can cause dehydration and inflammation, but we caught it and we can treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting oral metronidazole, three times a day. We’ll keep you on fluids and monitor your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oral? I’m still nauseated. What if I can’t keep it down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll time it with your anti-nausea medication and small sips. If you can’t tolerate it, tell us right away so we can adjust the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do the other stool tests show anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cultures did not show salmonella, shigella, or campylobacter, and the ova and parasite exam didn’t show parasites. The main finding is C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are things after starting metronidazole yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still diarrhea, but maybe a little less. The nausea is better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep the metronidazole going and continue sucralfate and the proton pump inhibitor to protect the ulcer area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to stay on the stomach medicine even though it might affect the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You need daily acid suppression right now because of the known ulcerations at the connection. That’s part of why we’re planning a full treatment course for C. diff and watching you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll never be able to eat normally again after the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable to feel that way. The goal is to get you back to tolerating your Stage III bariatric diet reliably—protein, calories, and fluids—without nausea or pain. You’ve already made progress since admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once the diarrhea is clearly improving, you’re staying hydrated by mouth, and you can take your medications reliably. We also want your strength back—walking, urinating normally, and no significant pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How many bowel movements in the last 24 hours?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe three or four. Still loose but not constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. We’ll keep encouraging oral fluids and protein. If you keep this trend, we can start planning discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to be on a special diet because of the C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No special C. diff diet, but because of your bariatric surgery you should stay on Stage III until your follow-up. The key is steady fluids and protein in small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your nausea and epigastric pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea is mostly gone. Pain is gone. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great—those were major barriers. Fatigue is common after dehydration and infection. We’ll keep you moving and eating what you can tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The metronidazole tastes awful. How long do I have to take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll complete a total 14-day course. You’ve already done part of it here, and you’ll finish the remaining days at home. It’s important to take every dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the diarrhea comes back after I finish?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If diarrhea returns, especially watery and frequent, call your surgeon’s office or come back to the emergency department—C. diff can recur and we’d want to evaluate quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today you’re walking on your own and keeping down fluids and protein. Any diarrhea overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just once. It’s much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll continue your medications and start final discharge teaching—diet, pill crushing, and warning signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over the meds again? I’m on so many since the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sure. You’ll continue omeprazole daily for acid suppression and sucralfate four times a day to protect the ulcer area. You’ll finish metronidazole three times a day to complete 14 days total for C. diff. You’ll also continue ursodiol, calcium citrate, vitamin D, and a chewable multivitamin. Trazodone is as needed for sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I still have to crush everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—crush all pills as instructed for your bariatric surgery status, and use chewable vitamins. No gummy vitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about ibuprofen? It helps my shoulder sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, and naproxen. They can cause bleeding and ulcers, especially after gastric bypass and with your known ulcerations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special at home so my family doesn’t catch C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good handwashing with soap and water after using the bathroom is the most important. Clean high-touch bathroom surfaces regularly. If diarrhea is ongoing, be extra careful with shared bathrooms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—this is likely discharge day. Any nausea, belly pain, or trouble drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No nausea. No pain. I’m drinking and eating the Stage III foods okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your vital signs have been stable and you’re afebrile. You’re walking independently and urinating without help. That meets our goals for safe discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your surgeon or return to the ER for fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, severe nausea or vomiting, inability to eat or drink, severe bloating, or if diarrhea becomes severe again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I stay on Stage III even if I feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—stay on Stage III until your follow-up appointment. Don’t self-advance the diet, and avoid straws and chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, any last questions about your reflux, sleep apnea, or other conditions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—should I keep using my CPAP at home like usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea. And keep taking your reflux and ulcer-protection medications as prescribed. We’ll send you home with the plan and follow-up instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain. Can you tell me where it hurts and what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s mostly in the upper middle, but also on both sides up high. It’s been about five days and it feels different than my ulcer pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Different how—more sharp, more constant, or related to eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More constant and kind of gnawing, and I’ve been nauseated. No vomiting though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea or changes in your stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, diarrhea. And my stools have been darker. That’s what scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important to mention. We’ll check for bleeding and monitor your blood counts. Any dizziness, fainting, or racing heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little lightheaded earlier, but I haven’t passed out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll start IV fluids, nausea medicine, and pain control. Given your Roux-en-Y bypass and history of marginal ulcer, we’ll also involve Gastroenterology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s C. diff again. I had that last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern with diarrhea. We’ll send stool tests for C. difficile, and also check for H. pylori because of the ulcer history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, nothing suggests an emergency surgery, but we need to evaluate carefully. We’ll start with labs and imaging to make sure there’s no obstruction or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting an abdominal X-ray now to look for signs of blockage or a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray doesn’t show free air and doesn’t show a high-grade bowel obstruction. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can still come from inflammation or ulcers even when the X-ray is normal. Your bloodwork so far looks stable, and we’ll keep trending it because of the dark stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you checking my blood count for bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll monitor your hematocrit and hemoglobin. We also checked a stool test here that was positive for blood, so we’re taking that seriously.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on pantoprazole and sucralfate already. Is that not enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes ulcers at the gastrojejunal connection need higher-dose acid suppression. We’ll likely increase your pantoprazole to twice daily and continue sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to admit you to the surgical ward for monitoring, IV fluids, and to coordinate an endoscopy with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now we’ll keep you on a cautious plan until GI evaluates you—then we’ll advance as tolerated. The priority is controlling pain and nausea and making sure there’s no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was your night? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain comes in waves. The nausea is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep IV fluids going and adjust your pain and nausea meds. GI is planning an EGD today to look at the anastomosis and check for ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly is an EGD again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a camera test—an endoscope goes through your mouth to look at the esophagus, stomach pouch, and the connection to the small intestine. They can take small biopsies if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous with my bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s commonly done after bypass. There are risks with any procedure, but it’s generally safe and it gives us the best information about ulcers and inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before the EGD, just confirming: you use CPAP at home for sleep apnea, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll make sure anesthesia and recovery staff know, since sedation can affect breathing. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the EGD. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sleepy. My throat is sore. Did they find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw gastritis—irritation of the lining—and at the gastrojejunal connection they saw a new small ulcer. They also saw that your larger known ulcer there looks like it’s improving, and one smaller ulcer they’d seen before is no longer visible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I have another ulcer. Is that why my stool is dark?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: An ulcer can cause bleeding, yes. Your blood counts have been stable, and we’re continuing to monitor them. If you notice black tarry stool or bright red blood, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan to treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing pantoprazole to 40 mg twice a day and continuing sucralfate four times a day. GI also wants an H. pylori stool antigen test to check for active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned something about a biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They took small biopsies during the EGD. If anything important comes back, GI will contact you and we’ll also review it with you while you’re here if it results in time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But you said the findings might not explain how bad the pain is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Because your pain feels out of proportion, GI recommended a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for other causes like obstruction or other complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also sending stool testing for C. difficile given your diarrhea and prior infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. It does not show a bowel obstruction. It also doesn’t show contrast in the gastric remnant, but the oral contrast had already moved through the bowel by the time the images were taken, so it’s not pointing to a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong on the CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing that explains severe pain like an obstruction. There was a small area in the left kidney that could represent a very small infection or an area of decreased blood flow. The radiologist suggested correlating with your urinalysis, and your urine test didn’t show signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need antibiotics for my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At this point, with no urinary symptoms and a reassuring urinalysis, we’re not starting antibiotics just based on that CT finding. We’ll keep an eye on it and on your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I know about the C. diff test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The first C. difficile toxin test came back negative today. We’ll repeat if needed based on symptoms, but so far it doesn’t look like C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today compared with yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the IV morphine helped. I’m nervous about switching to pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We need a plan that works by mouth before you go home. We’ll transition carefully and make sure you’re comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We advanced your diet today. Let us know how you do after eating—sometimes ulcers cause pain after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: After lunch I had worse pain for maybe 45 minutes, then it eased up. I could still keep it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That pattern fits with ulcer irritation. The fact you tolerated the meal overall is a good sign. We’ll keep the pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oral Roxicet isn’t touching the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. If it’s not effective, we’ll switch to a different oral pain medication. We can try oral hydromorphone and see if it controls your pain better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The new pill helped a lot more. I’m less scared now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep it as needed and aim for the lowest dose that keeps you functional—walking, drinking, and eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dark stools? Am I still bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been checking your hematocrit. It dipped slightly with hydration but has stabilized and is back in the normal range. That suggests no ongoing significant bleeding right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the H. pylori test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool H. pylori antigen test is negative, which means we don’t see evidence of an active H. pylori infection contributing to the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I keep getting ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After gastric bypass, ulcers can form at the connection site for several reasons, and sometimes we don’t find a single trigger. The key is strong acid suppression, protecting the lining with sucralfate, and close follow-up with repeat endoscopy to confirm healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My diarrhea is better today. Does that mean it’s not C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It supports that. Also, we repeated the C. difficile toxin test today and it’s negative again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you look more comfortable. Are you able to eat and drink enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m eating regular food, just smaller amounts. Pain is controlled with the Dilaudid pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re also walking and urinating normally, and your vital signs have been stable. We’re planning discharge later today if everything stays steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I go home on? I’m confused about the pantoprazole dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day now—morning and evening. Continue sucralfate 1 gram four times a day, and crush it as you’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need the stronger dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI wants you on the twice-daily dose until your follow-up endoscopy in about six weeks, and then they’ll decide based on healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine—will I get enough? I don’t want to be stuck in pain at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe oral hydromorphone to take as needed for pain. It’s for short-term use. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it, and use the smallest amount that works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back if you have signs of bleeding—black tarry stools, bright red blood in stool or vomit—dizziness, weakness, feeling like you might faint, or a fast heart rate. Also return if you can’t keep down fluids or meds, or if pain worsens or changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything about the kidney spot they saw?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, no specific treatment since your urine test didn’t suggest infection and you don’t have urinary symptoms. If you develop burning with urination, fever, or flank pain, you should call or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Gastroenterology for a repeat EGD in about six weeks. And please call your surgeon’s office to make a follow-up appointment within two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep taking my other meds and vitamins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications unless we specifically changed them. Continue your multivitamin, vitamin D, B12 weekly, ursodiol, and trazodone as prescribed, and crush pills as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still scared this will happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. The repeat endoscopy is important to confirm healing, and staying consistent with the pantoprazole and sucralfate gives you the best chance to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, last check: pain controlled on oral meds, tolerating regular diet, walking independently, and no new bleeding symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I feel ready. I’ll call if I see black stools or get dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll discharge you home now with pantoprazole twice daily, sucralfate, and hydromorphone as needed, and the follow-up plan we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. You were admitted directly today to help with nutrition and ulcer treatment. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly awful. I’m nauseated all the time, and I can barely eat. The pain in the middle of my upper stomach is constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’ve been dealing with that. I see you’ve lost about 20 pounds over the last month and you’ve had more vomiting over the last few weeks. Is that still happening daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Some days I throw up even if I just try a few bites. I’m trying to drink water so I don’t get dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The plan is to place a tunneled central line today so we can start total parenteral nutrition—TPN—through the vein, and also give your ulcer medicine through the IV to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the line the same as a PICC? And is it permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar purpose, but this one is a tunneled catheter that goes into a neck vein and then under the skin to your chest. It’s meant for longer-term use than a regular IV. It’s not permanent—we’ll remove it when you’re able to meet nutrition by mouth again and no longer need IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about infections. I’ve heard central lines can be dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very reasonable concern. There is an infection risk, but we reduce it with sterile placement, careful dressing changes, and teaching you how to keep it clean and dry. Home nursing will also help with dressing changes and lab draws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep for the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get moderate sedation—medication to make you relaxed and sleepy—and numbing medicine at the site. You’ll be breathing on your own, and we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the ulcer—why isn’t it getting better? I’m taking the Protonix and Carafate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your recent endoscopy showed the ulcer is still there but not bleeding. With marginal ulcers after Roux-en-Y, healing can be slow. You’ve been doing the right things—no NSAIDs, no smoking, no alcohol. One thing we can do is keep the acid suppression very consistent by giving Protonix through the IV, and support your nutrition so your body can heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t tolerate my vitamins either. They make me gag.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have Nutrition see you. TPN includes vitamins and minerals, and we can also talk about forms of supplements that are easier to tolerate when you’re ready—like crushed or liquid options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start IV fluids now and a temporary peripheral nutrition while we wait for the tunneled line placement this afternoon. Let us know if your nausea or pain spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for nausea? It’s constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’ll give anti-nausea medication through your IV and keep you comfortable. We’ll also continue your ulcer coating medicine, sucralfate, by mouth as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional Radiology is ready for you soon for the tunneled line. Any last questions before you go down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt afterward? And where exactly will it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll likely be sore at the neck and chest for a few days. The catheter will come out on the upper chest with a dressing over it. We’ll give you pain control and show you how to protect it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the procedure. The tunneled double-lumen catheter was placed without complications, and it’s ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy. My chest feels tight where the dressing is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected right after placement. We’ll check the site frequently. If you notice increasing pain, swelling, drainage, or fever, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do we start the nutrition through it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tonight we’ll transition from the peripheral nutrition to TPN through the new line. We’ll start at a lower rate and increase daily while monitoring your electrolytes and blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night with the new line and the first TPN run?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept some. I’m still nauseated, but I didn’t throw up overnight. The line site is sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign about the vomiting. We’ll keep adjusting nausea meds. Today we’ll increase the TPN a bit and keep you on IV Protonix every 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat at all? Or does that make the ulcer worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can try small amounts as tolerated. The goal is not to force it—TPN is covering your nutrition. We’ll advance your diet slowly and focus on foods that are less irritating. Nutrition will go over a stage-based diet with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition is going to meet with you today. They’ll talk about ways to get calories in without worsening pain—small, frequent, gentle foods—and how TPN will be adjusted to your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll never be able to eat normally again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that. The goal is to use TPN as a bridge—support you while the ulcer heals and nausea improves. We’ll reassess regularly, and you’ll have close follow-up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing today? Any diarrhea or new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No diarrhea. Still nauseated, but I managed a little of the diet yesterday. The pain is still there though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’re increasing the TPN again today toward the goal calories and protein. Your labs look stable, and we’re watching electrolytes closely as we advance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood work—am I malnourished even though my albumin was normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Albumin can stay normal even when intake is poor. We’re looking at the whole picture—your weight loss, how little you’ve been able to eat, and markers like prealbumin. We’re using TPN to reverse the protein-calorie malnutrition and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helps but it wears off fast. I’m scared of taking too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want your pain controlled safely. Because you’ve been needing frequent doses, we’re going to ask the chronic pain team to see you and recommend a regimen that’s effective and safer. We’ll also coordinate with your primary care provider for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Today is hospital day 3, and you’ve reached the goal TPN rate. Next step is to start cycling it—running it over 16 hours instead of continuously—to see how you tolerate the higher hourly rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does cycling do? Is it just for convenience?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Convenience is part of it—especially at home, many people run it overnight. It also gives your body time off the infusion each day. We do it gradually to make sure your blood sugar and fluid balance stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain team came by. They said something about changing how often I can take my medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They felt your pain wasn’t well controlled on the prior schedule, so they recommended increasing the frequency of your as-needed pain medication. We’ll implement that here, and we’ve notified your primary care provider so they can place the order and refer you to the pain clinic for ongoing management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be labeled as drug-seeking. I just want to function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, and your symptoms and history support that this is real pain from the ulcer. Our goal is comfort and safety, with a clear plan and follow-up so you’re not managing this alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the first 16-hour cycle go today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was okay. I felt a little flushed when it started, but it passed. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring your blood sugar and electrolytes. If all stays stable, we can plan for a 12-hour cycle for home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re focusing on discharge planning. You’ve tolerated cycling, and we’re aiming for a 12-hour overnight TPN schedule at home with visiting nurse support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared I’ll mess up the line at home. What if it gets pulled or leaks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get hands-on teaching before you leave—how to keep the dressing clean and dry, how to flush the line, and what to do if the tubing is damaged or the line is pulled. If it’s ever partially or completely pulled out, you should not use it and you should call right away or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How often will someone check on me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home services will provide the TPN supplies, draw labs a few times per week, and change the dressing weekly or sooner if needed. They’ll also be a point of contact for line concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a new dull pain on the right side under my ribs. Is that my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your weight loss and symptoms, it’s reasonable to check. We ordered a right upper quadrant ultrasound to look for gallstones or gallbladder inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound is back—no gallstones and no signs of acute cholecystitis. There wasn’t a sonographic explanation for the right upper abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then? I’m worried something is being missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable to worry. Sometimes pain can be from the ulcer area, muscle strain, or irritation without a clear ultrasound finding. The reassuring part is there’s no evidence of gallbladder infection or stones. If the pain worsens, moves, or you develop fever, vomiting you can’t control, or black/bloody stools, you should seek care immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still going to be on Protonix through the IV at home? Why not pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—IV Protonix every 12 hours for about two months. The goal is to maximize consistent acid suppression while your ulcer heals, especially since you’ve had trouble tolerating oral intake and you’ve improved on IV therapy before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Carafate—do I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue sucralfate four times a day, and crush it as instructed so it’s easier to take after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my vitamins? I haven’t been good about them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending vitamin D in a crushable form, and the TPN will provide vitamins and minerals while you’re on it. As your nausea improves, we’ll work with Nutrition and your outpatient team to get you back on a bariatric-appropriate vitamin routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I manage pain at home? I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have liquid oxycodone as needed, with clear safety instructions—no driving, and don’t take it if your breathing rate is very low. You can also use liquid acetaminophen as needed, staying under 4 grams per day. The chronic pain team recommended changes, and your primary care provider will place the referral to the pain clinic so there’s a structured follow-up plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call right away once I’m home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call or come in for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, redness/swelling/drainage at the line site, chest pain or shortness of breath, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing, or any blood or black material in vomit or stool. Also call if the line is damaged or pulled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still anxious, but I feel better having a plan. I just want the ulcer to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ve tolerated the TPN well, your nutrition markers have started to improve slightly, and you’re stable for discharge. We’ll send you home with services for TPN and line care, and you’ll continue IV Protonix and sucralfate. We’ll also arrange surgical follow-up and the pain clinic referral through your primary care provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you’ve been struggling with nausea and not being able to take in enough by mouth. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseated. I can barely keep anything down, and I’m tired of living on the TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of gastric bypass and the prior ulcer that has healed, our goal this admission is to get you reliable nutrition without needing TPN. We’re planning a laparoscopic gastrostomy tube so we can feed you through the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A G-tube… is that permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Think of it as a bridge—enteral feeding through a tube is safer long-term than TPN through a central line. If your nausea improves and you can meet nutrition goals by mouth later, we can reassess whether you still need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it make the nausea worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t. We start feeds slowly and watch symptoms closely. Many people tolerate tube feeds even when they can’t tolerate eating. We’ll also keep you on acid suppression to protect your stomach and anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of another complication. I’ve already been through so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. The plan is a laparoscopic placement, and we’ll confirm the tube position afterward before using it. We’ll go step by step and keep you informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in before the OR team comes by—any new symptoms overnight? Fever, worsening belly pain, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just the same nausea and I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep you on IV fluids. You’ll be NPO before surgery. After the tube is placed, we’ll manage pain and then confirm placement with a contrast study before starting feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my Hickman line? I hate having it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our goal is to stop TPN once you’re tolerating tube feeds. When we’re confident you’re meeting nutrition through the G-tube, we can have Interventional Radiology remove the tunneled catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the OR. The laparoscopic gastrostomy tube placement went smoothly—no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts around the site. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—some soreness around the tube site is expected for the first few days. We’ll treat your pain, and we’ll keep an eye out for anything concerning like worsening severe pain, redness spreading, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I use it? I’m worried it’s in the wrong place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll confirm placement with a post-op contrast study before starting feeds. Once that shows it’s in the stomach, we’ll begin tube feeds slowly with Nutrition’s guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your nausea since surgery—about the same, better, or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About the same. The incision pain is more noticeable than the nausea right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with what we expect. Tonight we’ll focus on recovery. Tomorrow we’ll do the contrast study and, if it looks good, start feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’ll confirm the G-tube position with a gastrografin study. After that, we can start tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be on TPN today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes, until we’re safely feeding through the tube. Once feeds are started and you’re tolerating them, we’ll stop TPN—often by the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray thing—what exactly are they looking for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They inject contrast through the G-tube and take images to make sure the tube is in the stomach and the contrast fills the stomach appropriately. It’s a safety check before feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastrografin study is back—it confirms the G-tube is in the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we can start feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start tube feeds with Fibersource HN at a low rate and advance as tolerated. We’ll also monitor for bloating, worsening nausea, or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I feel too full or sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tell the nurse right away. We can pause feeds, adjust the rate, and check residuals by aspirating the tube with a syringe. If there’s a large residual—more than 50 mL—we stop and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check: how did you do overnight with the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surprisingly okay. My nausea didn’t get worse. I’m still not hungry, but I didn’t throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. Since you’re tolerating feeds, we can discontinue TPN today and focus on advancing tube feeds toward goal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the central line can come out soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—once we’re confident you’re at goal tube feeds and stable, we’ll arrange removal of the tunneled catheter with Interventional Radiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat anything at all, or is it only tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can continue a stage V diet in small amounts as tolerated. The tube feeds will cover your nutrition while your oral intake is limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition is recommending we work toward a nocturnal cycle—feeding overnight for 12 hours—so you’re free from the pump during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Overnight sounds better. What rate would that be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The goal plan is 80 mL per hour over a 12-hour cycle at night, if you tolerate it. We’ll ramp up gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site looks a little wet. Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A small amount of drainage early on can be normal. We’ll examine it—what we worry about is increasing redness, pus-like drainage, worsening pain, or fever. For now, keep it clean with mild soap and water, and we can use a dry dressing if there’s drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re at goal tube feeds on the 12-hour nocturnal cycle, and you’ve been stable off TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it. Does that mean the Hickman comes out today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Interventional Radiology is scheduled to remove the right internal jugular tunneled catheter this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? Do I need anesthesia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They use local anesthetic—numbing medicine—then remove it under sterile conditions. You may feel pressure, but it’s usually quick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter removal is done and went uncomplicated. There’s a dressing in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. What do I watch for at that site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you notice bleeding that won’t stop with pressure, increasing swelling, redness, drainage, or fever, call us. Otherwise keep the dressing clean and dry as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about doing the tube feeds at home. What if I mess it up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re comfortable before discharge. Home services will also help with supplies and teaching. The key steps are: check residuals by aspirating with a 60 mL syringe before feeding, and if you pull back more than 50 mL, stop the feeding and call the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to do bolus feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—you’re going home on cycled continuous feeds over 12 hours at night using a pump. Bolus is an option in some cases, but it’s not your plan right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nausea meds and the ulcer medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue an oral proton pump inhibitor to reduce acid and protect healing. For nausea, you’ll use the medications as prescribed if symptoms flare. The goal is that steady nutrition through the tube helps your overall symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You can wash around the tube with mild soap and water. If there’s drainage, you can apply antibiotic ointment and a dry dressing until the incision closes. Once there’s no drainage, you can leave it open to air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What symptoms mean I should call right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call for fever over 101.5, severe or worsening abdominal pain, persistent nausea or vomiting, increasing redness or drainage at the tube site, or if the tube dislodges. Also call if you have high residuals—more than 50 mL—when you check before feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat at all when I’m home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue the stage V diet in small amounts as tolerated. The tube feeds are your main nutrition for now, and oral intake is supplemental.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
