conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ as scheduled after discharge. At that visit we’ll review your tolerance of tube feeds, your weight and nutrition, and whether we can adjust the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still anxious, but I feel better knowing there’s a plan and I’m off TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re tolerating goal nocturnal tube feeds, your nausea hasn’t worsened with feeds, and the central line is out. We’ll discharge you home with services today, and you can call us anytime with concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I hear you’ve been having worsening dry heaves and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been nonstop. I’m dry heaving many times a day now. I’m scared I’m not getting any nutrition in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Since your G-tube was removed, have you been able to keep down any liquids or soft foods at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Very little. I try, but then the pain and heaving start. I’m not really vomiting food—just retching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood when you vomit or in your stool? Any black, tarry stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. My bowel movements have been normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea, fevers, or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and prior anastomotic ulcers, we want to make sure there isn’t a new ulcer or narrowing at the connection. We’ll start with IV fluids tonight to treat dehydration and help your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this is happening because I had the tube removed. Did I mess things up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You didn’t do anything wrong. Sometimes symptoms return after changes in how nutrition is supported, and sometimes irritation or reflux can flare. Our job now is to stabilize you and look for a treatable cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me in the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fluids, and we’re also planning a vitamin-containing infusion—often called a banana bag—because people with poor intake can get depleted. We’ll also check labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. First we’ll see if we can get you comfortable and tolerating a bariatric diet again. We’ll also plan an upper endoscopy to look at the pouch and connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was started on Carafate in clinic. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—sucralfate, or Carafate, coats irritated areas. We’ll continue it here, and we’ll also increase acid suppression while you’re inpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My reflux has been awful too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with what you’re describing. We’ll give pantoprazole through the IV twice a day for now, which is stronger and faster than pills when you’re not keeping things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still having waves of pain. Can I have something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll treat pain, but we’ll do it carefully because stronger pain meds can worsen nausea. We’ll aim for the lowest effective dose and reassess often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after the fluids and medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still dry heaving, but not as constant. I’m exhausted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it eased some. Your vital signs have been stable. We’re going to start you on a stage 4 bariatric diet today—very gentle, small amounts—and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does stage 4 mean again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a soft, more advanced bariatric diet than clear liquids, but still easy to digest. The key is tiny portions, slow sips, and stopping before you feel full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start heaving again, does that mean something is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not automatically. Dry heaving can come from irritation, reflux, or sensitivity after bypass. The endoscopy will help us rule out a narrowing or ulcer at the connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down a little of the diet, but I’m scared to push it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach—don’t push. The goal today is tolerance without triggering symptoms. You’re also urinating well, which tells us hydration is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When is the scope happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning it for tomorrow. You’ll need to be NPO—nothing by mouth—for a period beforehand. The team will give you exact timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. What are you looking for exactly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll look at the gastric pouch and the small intestine limbs created by the bypass, including the connections. We’re checking for ulcers, erosions, inflammation, or narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Today is the endoscopy day. How are your symptoms right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some pain, but less. The dry heaves are less frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the IV pantoprazole going. After the procedure, we’ll decide whether to switch back to pills and advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable and usually don’t remember much. It’s done through the mouth with a camera; no incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the endoscopy. It went smoothly. Want to hear what we found?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. Is there an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The good news is the bypass anatomy looked as expected. The blind limb looked unremarkable, and the alimentary limb and the jejuno-jejunal connection looked unremarkable. We did see a small erosion in the cardia area of the gastric remnant/pouch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a big ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—this was described as a small erosion, not a large ulcer, and there was no mention of a blockage. That fits with irritation and reflux-type symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What causes an erosion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often acid exposure and irritation. After bariatric surgery, the anatomy changes and the lining can be more sensitive. That’s why we’re focusing on strong acid suppression and sucralfate to protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart with your bariatric diet and advance as tolerated. Start slow. If you can keep it down without worsening symptoms, that’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the dry heaves will come back when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid worry. We’ll send you home on pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day. We’ll also give you metoclopramide to use as needed for nausea, and a short course of pain medication for the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pantoprazole twice a day—wasn’t I on it once a day before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given the erosion and your symptoms, we’re increasing it to twice daily to better control acid and help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you do overnight with eating and drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had small amounts and didn’t dry heave as much. Pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re tolerating a stage 5 bariatric diet now, you’re walking around, and you’re urinating without trouble. Those are the main discharge goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What is stage 5 compared to stage 4?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stage 5 is a step up—more regular textured bariatric foods, still focusing on small portions and avoiding anything that triggers reflux or discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My labs—are they okay? I’m always worried about being malnourished again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this stay were overall reassuring—kidney function and electrolytes looked stable, and your blood counts were acceptable though on the lower side earlier. The bigger issue is making sure you can maintain intake at home, and we’ll give you clear return precautions if you can’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking all my other meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications unless we specifically changed them. The key changes are pantoprazole now twice daily and continuing sucralfate. Metoclopramide is as needed for nausea, and lorazepam is as needed for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back if you can’t keep down fluids or medications, if you feel dehydrated—dry mouth, fast heartbeat, dizziness when standing—if you vomit blood or see black stools, if you have worsening pain, chest symptoms, shortness of breath, or fever over 101.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drive myself home if I’m taking pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—don’t drive or operate machinery while taking pain medication. Arrange a ride today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to avoid lifting or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—avoid heavy lifting until you follow up with your surgeon. Also rest, walk several times a day, and focus on hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the plan is just meds and diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Since the endoscopy didn’t show a blockage and only a small erosion, the treatment is medical: acid suppression with pantoprazole twice daily, mucosal protection with sucralfate, and careful bariatric diet progression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel better knowing it wasn’t something severe. I’ll follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork now and make sure you understand the medication schedule and follow-up instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you. I understand you came in from clinic for nausea, epigastric pain, dry heaves, and trouble keeping enough nutrition down. Can you tell me what the last week and a half has been like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been awful. Constant pain right here in the upper middle, and I keep dry heaving. I can sip water but I feel full fast and I can’t get enough calories in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting with blood, black stools, fevers, chills, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, no black stools. No fevers. Bowel movements are basically the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and prior ulcer issues, we want to control stomach acid, treat nausea and pain, and make sure you don’t get dehydrated or malnourished. We’ll start IV fluids, a vitamin-containing infusion, IV pantoprazole, and nausea and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this is the ulcer again. Last time they said there was an erosion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. We’ll check labs today and trend them, and we’ll likely repeat an upper endoscopy during this stay to look for ulcers or inflammation. For now, we treat symptoms and protect your stomach lining with pantoprazole and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also scared I’m not getting any nutrition. I can’t hit anything close to what I’m supposed to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s one of our main goals. We’ll involve Nutrition early. If you can’t meet needs by mouth, we may use IV nutrition temporarily—called TPN—through a special IV line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be allowed to drink anything at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—small sips as tolerated, but we’ll be cautious. The priority tonight is hydration and symptom control. We’ll reassess in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork looks reassuring for infection—white count is normal. Your hemoglobin is a bit low but stable. Electrolytes look okay so far. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing suggests an infection right now. This seems more like inflammation/acid-related symptoms and poor intake. We’ll keep an eye on you and adjust as we learn more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting or dry heaves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still dry heaving on and off. The pain is still there. I’m tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Nutrition reviewed your intake history and we’re concerned you’re at risk for malnutrition. Our plan today is to place a PICC line—a longer IV in the arm—and start TPN so you can get calories and protein while your stomach settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is a PICC safe? I’ve had lines before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s commonly used and generally safe. Risks include bleeding, infection, or a clot, but we use sterile technique and monitor closely. After it’s placed, we confirm position with a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will TPN make me sick? I’ve heard people can have problems with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people feel fine; some can have blood sugar or electrolyte shifts. Because you’ve had low intake, we’ll start slowly and increase stepwise while checking labs to prevent something called refeeding syndrome. We’ll also watch your liver tests and triglycerides over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC is in good position on the chest X-ray—tip is where we want it near the central circulation, and your lungs look clear. We can start TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Does that mean I can stop trying to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking small sips and tiny amounts as tolerated, but don’t force it. TPN will cover your nutrition while we work on the cause of symptoms and slowly advance your bariatric diet when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning with the TPN running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little less weak. Still some nausea, but fewer dry heaves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your electrolytes—like potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus—are staying in a safe range, which is what we watch closely when starting TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you checking for that bacteria… H. pylori? Someone mentioned it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we sent an H. pylori antibody test. It came back negative, which makes that less likely as a driver of gastritis or ulcer symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will you do the scope? I just want to know what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re coordinating with Gastroenterology. The plan is for an upper endoscopy during this admission once you’re stable and we’ve supported your nutrition—likely later in the stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re increasing your TPN toward the goal calories and protein. We’ll keep checking labs daily while we advance it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home on TPN. Is that really necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can’t meet enough nutrition by mouth safely, TPN at home can be a bridge while we treat the stomach inflammation and you rebuild intake. We’ll only discharge you on it if you’re stable and trained, with home services to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long would I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It varies. The goal is to use it temporarily until you can reliably tolerate enough of the bariatric diet. Your surgeon and GI team will reassess based on symptoms and your nutrition labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is still there, but it’s not as sharp. Is that a good sign?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Improvement suggests the acid suppression and rest are helping. We’ll keep you on pantoprazole and sucralfate, and we’ll use nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your endoscopy is scheduled for today. You’ll be NPO—nothing by mouth—before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you looking for exactly? Another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking for ulcers at the connection sites, inflammation like gastritis, any narrowing, and anything that would explain the nausea and pain. They may take small biopsies during the EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about being sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The GI team will review sedation with you and monitor you closely throughout. It’s a common procedure and usually quick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the EGD. The findings were mild gastritis and a small hiatal hernia. No bleeding was seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an ulcer this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on today’s scope, the main finding is gastritis—irritation of the stomach lining—and the small hiatal hernia. GI recommended increasing your pantoprazole dose to 80 mg twice a day, and we’ve made that change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Eighty twice a day sounds like a lot. Why so high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your symptoms have been severe and persistent, and you have a history of ulcer-type problems after bypass. Higher-dose acid suppression can help the lining heal and reduce nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the dry heaves? They feel like they come in waves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI also raised the possibility of cyclic vomiting syndrome contributing—episodes of nausea and retching that can come in cycles. That’s something they’ll evaluate further as an outpatient, since it’s a diagnosis made after ruling out structural causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now that the scope is done, we’re transitioning you to oral medications as much as possible and advancing your bariatric diet to stage 5 in small amounts, as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stage 5 is like soft foods, right? I’m scared it’ll trigger the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—soft, higher-protein options in very small portions. We’ll go slowly. If you feel worsening pain or nausea, stop and let us know. TPN will still cover you while we test what you can tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing today—any nausea or dry heaves overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, no dry heaves. Nausea is much better. The pain is still there but more manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re also walking on your own and your vitals have been stable. Since you’re tolerating small amounts of stage 5 diet, we can plan discharge with home TPN and IV pantoprazole at the higher dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How does TPN work at home? Do I have to run it all day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve transitioned you to a nocturnal cycle—running it overnight—so you can be off the pump during the day. Home nursing will help with supplies, line care, and teaching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about infections with the PICC? That scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the biggest risk. You’ll be taught sterile technique, how to keep the dressing clean and dry, and when to call for help—like fever, chills, redness, drainage, or pain at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also ordering outpatient lab work while you’re on TPN—electrolytes and kidney function, magnesium and phosphorus, albumin, liver enzymes like ALT/AST, and triglycerides—to make sure the formula is safe for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking my vitamins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep your B12 weekly and your iron daily. For the multivitamin with minerals, we want you to hold it while you’re on TPN, since the TPN contains vitamins and we don’t want you doubling up unless Nutrition tells you otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stomach meds—what exactly am I taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue sucralfate four times a day by mouth, and pantoprazole will be IV at 80 mg twice daily at home as recommended by GI. You’ll also have ondansetron dissolving tablets as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start vomiting again at home, what should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can’t keep down fluids or meds, or you feel dehydrated—dry mouth, fast heartbeat, dizziness—call us or come to the ER. Also come in for black stools, blood in vomit, fever over 101.5, chest pain, or worsening abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who do I follow up with? I don’t want to bounce back again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Gastroenterology to evaluate the nausea pattern and the possibility of cyclic vomiting syndrome, and you’ll follow up with your surgeon, Dr. ___, to monitor nutrition, symptoms, and the plan to wean off TPN as you tolerate more by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re stable, walking independently, urinating well, and your nausea and dry heaves have resolved. We’ll discharge you home with services for TPN and IV pantoprazole. Do you have any last questions or concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I just want to keep improving. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. You’re back from Interventional Radiology after the gastrostomy tube placement. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little groggy. My belly hurts where the tube is. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—some soreness around the tube site is expected for the first few days. We’ll keep an eye on it and treat the pain with oral medication as you’re able to take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did everything go okay with the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It went smoothly. The report says it was an uncomplicated, fluoroscopy-guided placement, and the tube is positioned in the gastric remnant where we want it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this is to get me off the TPN, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The goal is to transition from parenteral nutrition through the PICC to enteral nutrition through the G-tube, since feeding the gut is generally safer and better long-term when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous because eating has been so hard. The nausea and dry heaves are still happening most days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The tube feeds let us give nutrition in a controlled way even when solid food is difficult. We’ll start gently—first clear liquids by mouth today if you feel up to it, and we’ll start tube feeds after the first 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why do we have to wait 24 hours to use it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right after placement, we give the tract time to settle and we monitor for any early issues like bleeding, worsening pain, or signs of infection. If everything stays stable, we begin feeds and advance stepwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I drink water now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—clear liquids are fine. Start slow. If you feel nausea, let us know and we can adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels tight when I move. Am I allowed to get up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we want you to. We’ll help you the first time. Walking reduces the risk of blood clots and helps your lungs. You’ll also have compression boots and you’ll get heparin shots to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed the PICC line is still there. Are we keeping it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll keep it while we’re transitioning. Once you’re tolerating tube feeds at goal, we can remove the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is not terrible right now, but I’m scared it’ll come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll monitor closely. You’re continuing your nortriptyline at bedtime, and we’ll keep your acid suppression as well. The hope is that steady nutrition through the tube will also help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what the nortriptyline is for? GI mentioned something about cyclic vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI raised concern for possible cyclical vomiting syndrome, and nortriptyline is sometimes used to reduce the frequency and severity of those nausea/vomiting cycles. You mentioned you’ve had some improvement since starting it, even though symptoms aren’t fully gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site stings. How will I know if it’s infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. Mild soreness is normal. Concerning signs are increasing redness, swelling, warmth, foul odor, yellow or bloody drainage, fever, or worsening pain instead of gradual improvement. We’ll teach you how to check it daily at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. I had some nausea but no throwing up. The pain is mostly at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Your vitals have been stable. Today we’ll start tube feeds and advance as tolerated. We’ll also keep tracking your labs and hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of tube feeding is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The plan is a formula called Replete with Fiber. We’ll work up to a goal rate and then cycle it over 12 hours, so it can run overnight at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to eat normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—tube feeds don’t prevent you from eating by mouth. We’ll advance your oral diet as you tolerate it. The tube is there to make sure you get enough nutrition even if your intake is limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the feeds will make me nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea increases, we can slow the rate, pause, or adjust the schedule. We’ll start gradually and see how your body responds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the tube feeds. How are you feeling so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surprisingly okay. A little full, but not like the dry heaves I get with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep advancing toward the goal rate as long as you’re comfortable and your abdomen stays soft without worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with this tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower, but avoid soaking it—no baths, hot tubs, or swimming. Clean the area gently with warm soapy water and keep it dry otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the cap? Do I keep it capped when it’s not running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When it’s not in use, you can cap the outside opening and secure the tube to your abdomen with tape so it doesn’t tug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is dry. Do I need extra water with the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your home plan includes free-water flushes—150 mL three times a day through the tube. You can also drink fluids by mouth as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re at the goal tube feed rate now. How did you do overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually slept. I had less nausea than usual. The site is still sore but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your pain control sounds appropriate, and it’s encouraging that nausea is improving. We can also advance you to a regular diet by mouth today, as tolerated, while continuing the tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Regular diet? Even with my bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As tolerated—small amounts, slow, and stop if you feel symptoms. The tube feeds are the main nutrition right now; the oral diet is to see what you can comfortably take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do you take out the PICC? I’m worried about infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now that you’re tolerating tube feeds at goal, we can remove the PICC today. That reduces infection risk and means you won’t need IV nutrition at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home with the pump?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go home with services and a Zevex Infinity pump. The feeds will run at 110 mL per hour for 12 hours, and you’ll do the water flushes three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I get constipated from the pain medicine or the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending docusate liquid to use as needed for constipation. Also keep walking and stay hydrated—both help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared I’ll mess up the tube at home. What if it gets pulled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common worry. Keep it secured to your abdomen, avoid tugging, and be careful with clothing and seatbelts. If it dislodges or you have sudden severe pain, fever, or vomiting you can’t control, call us or come to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking all my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your home medications unless we specifically told you otherwise. You’ll continue aripiprazole, citalopram, lamotrigine, lorazepam, nortriptyline at bedtime, and temazepam as needed. Your pantoprazole will be a 40 mg tablet once daily now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain, just the liquid oxycodone-acetaminophen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—use it as needed. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it, and let us know if pain is worsening instead of improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call for fever over 101.5, severe or worsening abdominal pain, increasing redness or drainage at the tube site, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing, or any blood or black material in vomit or stool. Otherwise, keep the site clean and dry, walk several times a day, and follow up as arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you came in with left upper abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s this sharp pain on the left, kind of under my ribs, and it shoots to my back near my shoulder blade. It’s been about a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does anything make it worse or better—like eating, drinking, or your tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Eating makes it way worse. Tube feeds also bring it on, but it doesn’t last as long as when I eat by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fevers, chills, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting lately. No fevers or chills. My stools have been normal, just haven’t gone in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also see you’ve had a Roux-en-Y bypass and prior marginal ulcers. Have you taken any NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I avoid them. I’m on my PPI every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re going to start with bowel rest—no food by mouth for now—IV fluids, pain control, and stronger acid suppression with IV pantoprazole. We’ll also check imaging to make sure there’s no perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s something like a leak. Wouldn’t I be really sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often people are much sicker with a leak—fever, fast heart rate, severe belly rigidity—but we don’t rely on that alone. That’s why we’re doing X-rays and checking how contrast moves through your tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial chest and abdominal X-rays don’t show free air, which is reassuring—no sign of a perforation on those tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much when I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, an ulcer at the connection between the stomach pouch and small intestine is high on the list. We’ll likely confirm with an endoscopy—an EGD—so we can look directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There’s also been some drainage around my G-tube site. It’s not a lot, but it’s annoying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll examine it closely each day. If there’s redness, pus, or worsening pain at the site, we may need to culture it, but right now the bigger issue is the pain with feeds and eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave contrast through the G-tube to check the tube position and flow. It moved through the small bowel without leaking outside the intestines, which supports that the tube is in place and there’s no extravasation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean the tube isn’t causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the tube isn’t blocked and we don’t see a leak from it. It still could be that feeds irritate an ulcer or trigger pain, but it’s not malpositioned based on this study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How was your pain overnight with no feeds and IV medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better when I’m not eating. Still there, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That pattern fits with an ulcer. We’re planning the EGD for tomorrow to confirm and guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had EGDs before. Are you going to fix it during the scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s an ulcer, the main treatment is medication—high-dose acid suppression and sucralfate to coat the ulcer. We use the scope to diagnose and make sure there’s no bleeding or narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you for the EGD. You’ll be sedated, and we’ll look at the gastrojejunal connection and the small bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to know what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re back from the EGD. We found a single ulcer—about 10 millimeters—right at the gastrojejunal anastomosis. The rest looked normal, including the jejuno-jejunal connection and the limb down to the duodenal bulb.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is an ulcer again. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be painful and can bleed if it worsens, but right now we didn’t see active bleeding or a perforation. The plan is aggressive ulcer therapy: IV pantoprazole and sucralfate, both by mouth and through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long until it stops hurting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain often improves over days, but healing takes longer—weeks. We’ll also adjust your nutrition so you can get calories without triggering severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted tube feeds. You were previously cycling at a higher rate. How did it feel at the cycled rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At the higher rate it was awful—cramping and that same left-sided pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch from cycling to continuous feeds at a lower rate—55 mL per hour—to reduce the stress on the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better at the slower rate, but I still feel pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. If it persists, we can try a more concentrated formula at an even lower rate so the volume is smaller.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We changed to a concentrated formula at 30 mL per hour. Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurts. Not as intense as eating, but it’s there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the ulcer meds going and also advance your oral diet carefully to a bariatric stage 5 diet—small, soft meals—only as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a little food and it flared up again. I’m scared to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. For now, don’t push through severe pain. We’ll prioritize healing and nutrition, and we’ll keep portions very small and bland when you do try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs look stable—white count is normal, kidney function is normal. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but not dropping, which argues against active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could the pain be from constipation? I haven’t gone much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Constipation can add discomfort. We’ll start stool softener and a stimulant laxative as needed. But the meal-related sharp pain pattern still points to the ulcer as the main driver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We obtained a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast. It shows no bowel obstruction and no gastrogastric fistula. It does show a large stool burden in the rectum, so constipation is definitely part of the picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After bypass, a fistula would be an abnormal connection between the small stomach pouch and the larger remnant stomach. It can cause ulcers and symptoms. Your CT did not show that, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There’s a little bump above my belly button that’s tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see a small pustule there. We’re going to open it at the bedside to drain it and send a culture, to make sure there’s no spreading skin infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That drainage was gross. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was small and localized. You’re afebrile and your vitals are stable, which is reassuring. We’ll keep it clean and watch for redness spreading. The culture will tell us what bacteria it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you’re still having significant pain with tube feeds and you need reliable nutrition, we’re going to start TPN—nutrition through the vein. That requires a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a PICC before. Are there risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—clot, infection, and line malposition. We place it with sterile technique and confirm position with a chest X-ray. We’ll remove it as soon as we can get you back to tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first chest X-ray shows the PICC tip was bent back a bit in the upper central vein. The PICC nurse is going to adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Repeat X-ray looks good now—the PICC tip is in the low SVC where we want it. We can safely use it for TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no tube feeds at all right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re stopping tube feeds for now to let the ulcer calm down and to avoid triggering pain. You’ll get calories, protein, vitamins, and fluids through TPN while we continue the ulcer medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain today compared to when feeds were running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better. Still sore, but I’m not getting those spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep you on IV pantoprazole and sucralfate. The goal is to transition back to enteral feeds once you can tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do we need to move the G-tube? It feels like it’s part of the problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed it with Interventional Radiology. Because your gastric remnant is small, they don’t think repositioning is feasible. Another option is converting to a GJ tube that feeds into the jejunum, but that’s a different tube and procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another tube procedure if I can avoid it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll keep it as a backup option if we can’t find a feeding plan you can tolerate through the current tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your skin culture from the pustule grew Staph aureus that is resistant to oxacillin, which means MRSA. The good news is it’s localized and you’ve had no fevers or spreading redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA sounds scary. Am I contagious? Is it in my blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common skin bacteria that can be resistant to some antibiotics. Right now it’s from the abscess drainage, not your blood. We’ll focus on local wound care and monitoring. If you develop fever, worsening redness, or new drainage, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home? I hate being on TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want you home too, but only once we have a nutrition plan that doesn’t cause severe pain. The plan is to retrial tube feeds once the ulcer pain is more controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re going to retrial tube feeds. We’ll stop TPN once we see you can tolerate feeds again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous it’ll hurt like before, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start cautiously and adjust the regimen based on your symptoms. If pain increases, we can change the formula or rate rather than pushing through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s worse at night again. During the day it’s tolerable, but now it’s really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling us. We’re going to switch to a more easily absorbed, ‘pre-digested’ bariatric formula—Peptamen Bariatric—to improve tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight after switching to Peptamen Bariatric?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I still feel some discomfort, but it’s not that stabbing pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to trial cycling it at 60 mL per hour for 12 hours, with water flushes every 4 hours and before/after meds. If you tolerate that, we can stop TPN and remove the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I go home on this, what meds do I need to keep taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key ulcer meds: liquid pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and sucralfate four times a day—both by mouth and through the G-tube as instructed. And absolutely no NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with docusate twice daily and senna as needed. Keep up fluids and walking. If you go several days without a bowel movement or have worsening pain, call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard pain service changed my nortriptyline. I’m confused—do I take 25 or 50?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should take 50 mg at bedtime now and stop the 25 mg tablets. Please notify your prescribing doctor and therapist about the change as soon as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped TPN and removed the PICC today since you’re tolerating the tube feeds. Your vital signs are stable and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, signs of dehydration like dizziness, any black or bloody stools or vomit, fever or chills, worsening or changing abdominal pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube site—can I shower? What if it drains?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can wash around it with mild soap and water. If there’s no drainage, you don’t need a dressing. If you see increasing redness, pus, foul smell, or worsening pain, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to check anything before I start feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—aspirate the tube with a 60 mL syringe before feeding to check residual. If you pull back more than 50 mL, stop the feeding and notify the clinician managing your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your surgeon in about a week, and with Gastroenterology in about three weeks. We’ll also arrange home services to help with tube feeding supplies and support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go—any last questions about the ulcer treatment or the feeding plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… will this ulcer keep coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people do get recurrent marginal ulcers after bypass. Staying on the PPI as prescribed, taking sucralfate, avoiding NSAIDs, and following the bariatric diet guidance lowers the risk. If pain returns, call early so we can address it before it escalates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m relieved we found an answer. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you’ve had about a week of epigastric and left upper abdominal pain that feels similar to your prior marginal ulcer pain. Can you tell me what it feels like right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s that sharp pain under my left ribs and it goes through to my mid back. It comes and goes, but last night it got bad again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, black stools, or blood in the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No black stools or blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about reflux, pain with swallowing, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the stomach pain and my usual nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you taking any NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen? Any smoking or alcohol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No NSAIDs. I don’t smoke or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your G-tube feeds—are you still running them at 60 mL an hour for about 12 hours a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 60 an hour. They’ve been going okay. I’m also eating by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam your belly is soft, and I’m seeing some granulation tissue around the tube site—kind of a small raised area—but no signs of an acute abdomen. Given your history, we’re worried about a recurrent marginal ulcer, even though you’ve been on high-dose Protonix and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily during this short stay. First we’ll stabilize symptoms and make sure there’s nothing dangerous like a perforation or obstruction. We’re going to start IV Protonix twice a day and continue sucralfate, and we’ll keep you NPO at first to rest the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: NPO again… I’m worried the pain will get worse if I don’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The goal is to calm the irritation down. We’ll give IV fluids and a daily vitamin infusion—what we call a banana bag—with thiamine and folate while you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain control? I’m scared it’ll spike overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can start a PCA so you can control small doses for pain. We’ll watch closely for nausea, because opioids can worsen it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get nauseated easily. Can I still have Zofran?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ondansetron as needed. We’ll also check labs, including nutrition labs, since absorption can be tricky after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said I’m going for an X-ray. What are you looking for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A plain abdominal X-ray—often called a KUB—to look for free air that could suggest a perforation, and to see the bowel gas pattern for obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your KUB is reassuring: normal bowel gas pattern, no free air, no obstruction. It does show a moderate amount of stool in the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may contribute to discomfort, but given your history and the way the pain feels, we’re still treating this like possible recurrent ulcer pain. The X-ray mainly helps us rule out emergencies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bloodwork looks stable overall—white count is normal, kidney and liver tests look okay, and lipase is normal. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, and your iron and ferritin are low, which fits iron deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from bleeding from an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we don’t see signs of active bleeding—no black stools, no drop in blood counts during this evaluation. After gastric bypass, iron deficiency can happen from absorption issues. We’re going to adjust your iron supplementation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Iron pills upset my stomach. Is there another way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to a liquid iron formulation and dosing it twice a day. We’ll also keep you on your bariatric vitamins—chewable multivitamin, calcium with vitamin D, and weekly B12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The PCA is helping the pain, but I feel queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common side effect. If you’re getting nausea or dry heaving, we may need to back off narcotics and use other strategies. I’m going to ask the chronic pain service to see you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had dry heaves. The pain is a little better, but the nausea was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the dry heaving, we’re going to stop the narcotics and hold the PCA. We’ll keep the IV Protonix twice daily and sucralfate. The pain team will help adjust your non-opioid regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop the pain meds, won’t the pain come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll still treat pain—just in a way that doesn’t trigger the nausea cycle. One change we expect is increasing your nortriptyline at bedtime, which can help with chronic abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain team mentioned changing my antidepressants. What’s happening with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They recommended increasing nortriptyline to 100 mg at bedtime from 50 mg. They also recommended stopping Effexor. We’ll communicate their recommendations to your psychiatrist, Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about stopping meds. Will I feel withdrawal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a fair concern. We’re following the pain service plan and coordinating with your outpatient psychiatrist. If you notice mood changes, anxiety spikes, or other symptoms, tell us right away and we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more result: we checked H. pylori antibody testing, and it’s negative. That makes an H. pylori-driven ulcer less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I keep getting these ulcer symptoms if I’m doing everything right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After Roux-en-Y, the connection between the stomach pouch and small bowel can be prone to irritation in some people even without NSAIDs or smoking. The best-proven steps are exactly what you’re doing: high-dose PPI, sucralfate, and avoiding NSAIDs and tobacco.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually hungry now. Can I try something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Let’s start with bariatric Stage 3 diet. If you tolerate it without worsening pain or nausea, we’ll keep advancing slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept the Stage 3 down. No vomiting. Mild nausea but way better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll continue Stage 3 for now and keep your tube feeds cycled as you’ve been doing—60 mL per hour for a total of about 760 mL over 12 hours daily—along with your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site has that little bump. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like granulation tissue—overgrowth of healing tissue—rather than an infection. There’s no fever and your labs don’t suggest infection. If you notice spreading redness, foul drainage, or worsening pain at the site, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are your symptoms today—pain, nausea, and how you’re doing with the diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is much better. I’m not nauseated now. I’m walking around fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Since you’re stable and tolerating Stage 3, we can plan for discharge later today. You’ll continue pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and sucralfate 1 gram four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I take the sucralfate by mouth or through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take it by mouth as prescribed. At home you’ve also used it via the G-tube—continue following the instructions you’ve been given for your regimen. The key is four times a day, spaced out from other meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nortriptyline—100 at night now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 100 mg at bedtime. We’re also stopping Effexor per the pain service plan, and we’ll make sure your psychiatrist receives the note so your outpatient team can follow you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What diet do I go home on? I don’t want to trigger the pain again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go home on bariatric Stage 3 and advance to Stage 4 and then Stage 5 as tolerated. Continue your cycled tube feeds at 60 mL/hour for 12 hours daily as supplementation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to crush all my pills again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—crush all pills unless you’ve been specifically told not to. It helps with absorption and reduces the risk of irritation after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for that means I need to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by your plan, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or concerning drainage or redness around the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the iron make me constipated? The X-ray said I had a lot of stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. If you get constipation, you can use a stool softener like Colace twice daily as needed until your bowel pattern is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved it’s better, but I’m still worried it’ll come back as soon as I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That worry makes sense given your history. The plan at home is the same ulcer-protection strategy that helped here: pantoprazole twice daily, sucralfate four times daily, strict avoidance of NSAIDs, and gradual diet advancement. We’ll have you follow up with Dr. ___ to monitor symptoms and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review your discharge meds: pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, sucralfate 1 gram four times daily, ondansetron as needed for nausea, nortriptyline 100 mg at bedtime, liquid iron 300 mg twice daily, calcium with vitamin D, weekly B12, and a chewable multivitamin with minerals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. No NSAIDs, crush pills, Stage 3 diet and advance slowly, and keep the tube feeds cycled. I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re stable, walking, and tolerating intake, so we’ll discharge you home now. If anything worsens, don’t wait—call or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you came in with left upper abdominal pain near your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started about two days ago. It’s this sharp pain on the left side, right around the tube. I’ve been able to do my tube feeds and eat a little, but today I just don’t want to eat because it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills? Any diarrhea or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. No diarrhea. I don’t think I’m constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about vomiting—has your cyclic vomiting been acting up more than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nausea and some vomiting like I usually do, but the pain is what’s different. I’m worried the tube moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. On exam your belly is soft, but you’re tender right near the tube site. We’ll check labs and have Interventional Radiology evaluate the tube position and likely exchange it if it’s not sitting right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Like could it be leaking inside?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If a tube is out of position it can cause pain and irritation, and rarely leakage. Right now you look stable—no fever, your abdomen isn’t rigid, and your vitals are okay. The safest next step is imaging with contrast through the tube in IR and replacing it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: While we’re getting things arranged, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and give you medication for nausea and pain. We’ll also continue your stomach-protecting medicines like pantoprazole and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I still use the tube tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, let’s hold tube feeds until IR checks it. Small sips by mouth are okay if you can tolerate them, but we’ll prioritize keeping you comfortable and not worsening nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your morning labs are back—your electrolytes and kidney function look normal, and your white blood cell count is not elevated, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing in the labs suggests infection right now. The pain seems localized to the tube area, so tube position and local irritation are still the top concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will they fix the tube? It really hurts when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: IR is planning to take you today. They’ll inject contrast through the tube under X-ray to see where it sits, and then exchange it over a wire through the same tract if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be put to sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually it’s moderate sedation—medication through the IV to make you sleepy and comfortable, plus numbing medicine at the skin. You’ll be monitored the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go down, any new symptoms—worsening vomiting, chest pain, shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the same nausea and the pain at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: IR is ready for you. After the exchange, we’ll reassess your pain and decide when to restart your home meds and oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from IR. They exchanged the gastrostomy tube through the same tract and confirmed it’s positioned in the gastric pouch area. They also treated some irritated tissue at the skin entry site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember them saying something about burning the tissue. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—when there’s overgrowth of granulation tissue at the skin, they can apply silver nitrate to reduce it. It can sting briefly, but it helps with irritation and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is better than before, but it’s still sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness is expected for a few days after an exchange. We’ll use oral pain medicine as needed, and we can add a lidocaine patch near the site to help with localized pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go back to tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk about that. The tube is currently in the gastric pouch, which is connected up to your esophagus. Feeding into that area may not help the way feeding into the excluded stomach would, especially with cyclic vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube isn’t doing what it’s supposed to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may not be providing the benefit we want for nutrition if it’s effectively feeding the same pathway that triggers nausea and vomiting. That’s why we want to follow up with an endoscopy to better map your anatomy and make a longer-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you saying I should have it removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that option because if it’s not useful, keeping it can mean ongoing site discomfort and care needs. But it’s your decision. If you’re not ready to remove it now, we can leave it in place and reassess after the endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want it removed today. I’m scared I’ll end up unable to eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll defer removal. For now, we’ll focus on controlling pain and nausea and making sure you can take nutrition by mouth safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with sips of liquids or small amounts by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve kept down some liquids. I’m still nauseated but not throwing up right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll restart your home medications tonight—pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate four times daily are important given your history of ulcers. We’ll also continue ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My antidepressant and anxiety meds—will I get those too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your citalopram, lorazepam, and quetiapine as you take them at home. We also have nortriptyline on your list; we’ll keep it at the dose you’ve been using.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in. How was the night? Any vomiting? How’s the tube site pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. The site is sore but not like yesterday. I can walk around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your repeat labs remain stable. Since you’re tolerating oral intake, we can plan for discharge later today if pain stays controlled on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do with the tube at home if I’m not using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s not in use, you can cap the outside opening and secure the tube to your abdomen with tape so it doesn’t tug. Check the site daily for redness, swelling, warmth, bad odor, or yellow/bloody drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—wash gently with warm soapy water and keep it clean and dry afterward. Avoid baths, swimming, or hot tubs—don’t submerge the site in water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about malnutrition. That’s what they keep telling me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The concern is that with persistent vomiting and limited intake after bariatric surgery, it’s easy to fall behind on calories and protein. Right now you’re able to take some nutrition by mouth, and we’re keeping you on vitamins and iron. The endoscopy follow-up will help us decide the best long-term way to support nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s review your discharge medications. You’ll continue pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day and sucralfate 1 gram four times a day. You’ll also continue your multivitamin, vitamin D, and iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For the tube site pain, you’ll have a lidocaine patch to place near the site daily, and an oxycodone-acetaminophen liquid to use only as needed. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m afraid the pain meds will make me nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen. Use the smallest amount you need, and rely on the lidocaine patch and non-medication measures when possible. If you do need the liquid pain medicine, take it with what you can tolerate by mouth and use ondansetron as prescribed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call if you have severe or worsening pain, fever over 101.5, increasing redness or drainage at the site, or if you’re vomiting and can’t keep down fluids or medications. Also come in for signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing, very dry mouth, or a fast heartbeat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the plan is an endoscopy soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—follow up with the bariatric surgery team in early follow-up for an endoscopy to better delineate your anatomy and decide what to do about the gastrostomy tube and nutrition plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’re walking independently, your pain is controlled with oral meds, and you’re tolerating oral nutrition. Are you comfortable going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still nervous, but I feel better than when I came in. I’ll watch the site and follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the bariatric surgery team. I hear you were admitted after your G-tube was removed today, and you had some low blood sugars on the way over. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shaky. And my stomach is crampy. I’m scared because they said my sugar was really low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We saw a very low fingerstick earlier—around 35—and you improved after juice and then some IV dextrose. We’re going to keep checking your blood sugar frequently and treat it right away if it drops again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why would it drop like that? I’m not diabetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In your case it’s most likely related to not eating much today plus how your body handles sugar after gastric bypass. Sometimes after bypass, people can have big swings—especially if they go a while without food, or if they take in something sugary and then ‘crash’ afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That happened after the apple juice. I felt better, then I got diarrhea and cramps right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with dumping-type symptoms—rapid movement of sugar into the small intestine causing cramping and diarrhea. We’ll try to avoid large sugary drinks and instead use small, frequent snacks that you can tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My fingers and lips were tingling earlier. Is that from low sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
