conversation_lines.text: It can be. Low blood sugar can cause tingling, sweating, nausea, lightheadedness, and shakiness. If you feel any of those, tell us immediately so we can check a fingerstick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tube site? It hurts where they pulled it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some tenderness is expected right after removal. I examined your abdomen—soft, and the tenderness is localized near the old G-tube site. We’ll manage pain carefully; we can use IV medication initially if needed and then transition off as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be in agony, but I also don’t want to be knocked out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and reassess often. The goal is to keep you comfortable enough to move around and drink small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat anything tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’ll start slowly on a bariatric stage 1 diet and advance stepwise as you tolerate it. The key for the low sugars is frequent small snacks—especially when you wake up, between meals, and before bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been really anxious. The trip and everything… I barely ate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stress can absolutely affect appetite and your gut. We’ll continue your home psychiatric medications while you’re here, and we’ll keep the plan simple and predictable so you feel more in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starting to feel sweaty again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We just checked—your blood sugar is trending down again. We’re giving a dose of dextrose now and then we’ll have you take a small snack as soon as you can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous? Like, could I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it gets very low, yes, it can cause confusion or fainting. That’s why we’re monitoring closely in the hospital and treating early. You’re in the right place for this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick evening check-in: how’s the pain at the tube site and any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is better after the medicine. I’m a little nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you ondansetron as needed for nausea. Also, we’re keeping you on a proton pump inhibitor through the IV while you’re here to protect your stomach and anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I keep burping a lot too. It’s weird.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noticed that—persistent burping can happen after procedures and with changes in how you’re eating. As long as you’re not having severe belly distension, vomiting that won’t stop, or worsening pain, we’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight your vitals were stable. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Less shaky. Still nervous it’ll drop again. And I’m still burping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sugars have been more stable with the dextrose and the small, frequent intake. We’ll keep checking. For the burping, we’ll continue to monitor and make sure there’s no sign of obstruction or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly feels crampy again. Do you think something’s wrong from the tube removal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your symptoms, we’re going to get a plain abdominal X-ray to be safe. It helps us look for things like obstruction or free air. Most of the time after tube removal it’s just local soreness and GI upset, but we don’t want to miss anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a normal bowel gas pattern—no obstruction and no free air. There’s a small amount of retained contrast in the left upper quadrant from a prior study, which isn’t concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is leaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no signs of a leak or perforation on that imaging, and your exam is reassuring. We’ll keep focusing on symptom control and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m afraid to eat because I don’t want diarrhea again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. The strategy is small portions, more protein-focused options within the bariatric stages, and avoiding big sugar loads. Eating a little bit regularly actually helps prevent the low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I can’t keep up with snacks at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set you up with a clear plan: snacks right when you wake up, between meals, and before bed. And you’ll check your blood sugar at specific times and anytime you feel symptoms. If it’s low, you treat it and recheck in 15 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to keep getting IV sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. The IV dextrose is a bridge while you’re not reliably eating. As you tolerate more by mouth and your sugars stay stable, we’ll stop the IV and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning update: you’ve been stable overnight without severe lows. We’re going to advance your diet another step today, aiming toward stage 4 by discharge if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does stage 4 mean again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stage 4 is a more advanced bariatric diet compared with clear liquids—still small portions and careful choices, but more variety and more substance. We don’t want you to self-advance beyond that until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube site looks okay, but it’s a little wet on the gauze. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A small amount of clear drainage can be normal as the tract closes. Keep it covered with clean, dry gauze. Call us if you see foul-smelling drainage, pus, increasing redness, swelling, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this hypoglycemia means something is wrong with my pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After gastric bypass, some people have changes in how insulin is released after meals. We’re consulting the clinic team that focuses on this, and we’ll arrange outpatient follow-up to evaluate further. The immediate safety steps are the snack schedule and glucose monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my sugar drops at home, should I drink juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s below 70, take a small snack and recheck in 15 minutes. Juice can raise it quickly, but it can also trigger dumping and then another drop. If you do use something sugary, keep it small and follow it with something you tolerate that has more staying power.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re planning for discharge if your sugars stay stable on oral intake. How are you feeling about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Relieved, but nervous I’ll mess up the diet or miss a low sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with very specific instructions. You’ll stay on stage 4 diet until follow-up, no straws or gum, and you’ll do scheduled blood sugar checks: on waking, two hours after each meal, before bed, whenever you feel symptoms, and anytime you’ve fasted four hours or more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What symptoms should make me check it right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nausea, sweating, shakiness, lightheadedness, tingling, or feeling suddenly weak or confused—check immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medicines am I leaving with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home nortriptyline, quetiapine, and temazepam as needed for insomnia. We’re also prescribing pantoprazole twice daily and promethazine as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t expect you’ll need prescription pain medication. If you have mild pain, you can use liquid acetaminophen. And avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen because they can cause ulcers and bleeding after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anything else I should take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start a chewable complete multivitamin with minerals—no gummy vitamins. And you can use a stool softener like Colace twice daily as needed if constipation comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with the site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you may shower. No tub baths or swimming for now. If there’s clear drainage, cover it with clean, dry gauze afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by what you’re taking, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or any foul-smelling or colored drainage, redness, or swelling at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have lifting restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—no heavy lifting for six weeks, and avoid abdominal exercises. You can do moderate exercise as you feel up to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your blood sugars have stayed in a safe range with snacks, you’re tolerating stage 4, and your exam is stable. We’re discharging you home today with follow-up arranged, including outpatient evaluation for the hypoglycemia after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still anxious, but I feel better having a plan. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I want to review the plan for today—placing a gastrostomy tube to help with your hard-to-control low blood sugars after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Why do I need a tube again? I thought we were trying to avoid more surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The reason is your hypoglycemia has been medically refractory—despite diet changes and medications. Feeding into the stomach through a G-tube can sometimes stabilize sugars, and it also helps us see whether stomach feeding improves things enough to guide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this the same as reversing my bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—this is not a bypass reversal. This is a way to “temporize,” meaning help control symptoms now, and it can act like a test: if feeding through the stomach improves your blood sugars, it supports the idea that changing the bypass anatomy might help in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are the risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Risks include bleeding, infection, injury to nearby organs, and problems with the tube like leakage or blockage. We do everything we can to minimize those. Anesthesia will also review their risks with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start you on a bariatric stage 5 diet when it’s safe, and we’ll add tube feeds when your bowels are ready. The tube feeds will be continuous at first to keep sugars steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared of getting those shaky low sugar episodes again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood sugars closely here—before and after meals, at bedtime, and anytime you feel symptoms. If you feel shaky, sweaty, confused, or weak, call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to head to the operating room. Any last questions before we go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… please tell me you’ll keep me comfortable after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll start with a pain pump right after surgery and then transition you to oral pain medicine as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi—surgery is done and you’re in recovery. We placed the gastrostomy tube. We also had to convert from laparoscopic to open surgery, and we repaired a small injury to the colon during the operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A colon injury? That sounds really bad. Am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know that’s scary to hear. It was recognized right away and repaired during the same operation. We’ll watch you closely—your belly exam, your vital signs, and your labs—for any sign of a problem, but right now you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why it became an open surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Converting to open gives better exposure and lets us repair things safely. It’s not uncommon when anatomy is complex after prior surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach hurts a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a hydromorphone PCA—press the button when you need it. We’ll keep checking your pain and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any nausea or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Some nausea, and the incision feels tight. I’m afraid to move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That tightness is common after an open incision. Moving is important to prevent lung issues and blood clots. We’ll help you get up, use the incentive spirometer, and we’ll keep your pain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I stop the pain pump?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll start transitioning—oral oxycodone for baseline pain, and IV hydromorphone only if you need breakthrough relief. The goal is to get you comfortable on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood sugars? Are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far they’ve been stable with close monitoring. We’ll keep checking frequently, especially as we adjust diet and start tube feeds later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m checking in because your abdomen looks more distended today. Have you passed gas or had a bowel movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I feel bloated and uncomfortable. Is something wrong with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This can happen after abdominal surgery—your intestines can temporarily “go to sleep,” called an ileus. We’re going to get an abdominal x-ray to look for ileus and to make sure there’s no free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The x-ray tech said they couldn’t see the tube tip well. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The x-ray shows an ileus—gas in the bowel consistent with things being slow—and no free air. The tube is seen over the left abdomen, but the exact tip isn’t well visualized on this type of film. Clinically the tube site looks fine, and we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do we do for the ileus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mainly supportive care: walking, minimizing narcotics as we can, and time. We can try a suppository to help stimulate things, but sometimes it takes a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We repeated the abdominal x-ray this afternoon. It still looks like a post-operative ileus, and the contrast hasn’t moved much yet. Importantly, there’s still no sign of free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a leak from the colon repair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s nothing suggesting a leak—your exam and imaging don’t show free air, and we’re watching your temperature and labs closely. If you develop worsening pain, fever, or new tenderness, we’d reassess immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning? Any flatus yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still no. I’m frustrated. And my heart feels like it’s racing sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some intermittent tachycardia—faster heart rate—but you’ve been stable and not having chest pain or shortness of breath. Pain, dehydration, and the stress of surgery can contribute. We’ll keep monitoring and make sure you’re well hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink more? My mouth is so dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll balance sips with your belly distention. We’ll also keep IV fluids going as needed while the ileus improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your abdomen looks less distended today. Have you passed gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, yes. And I had a tiny bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign the ileus is resolving. Today we can start tube feedings slowly and advance as you tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of formula is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A high-protein, moderate-carbohydrate formula—about 45% carbohydrate. The goal is steady delivery to help prevent big swings in blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel sick when it starts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might feel some fullness. We’ll start at a low rate, check for nausea, distention, diarrhea, and we’ll check residuals as instructed. If you feel worse, we slow down or pause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The feeding is running. I’m worried it will make my sugars drop like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching your glucose closely. Continuous feeding tends to smooth out the peaks and dips. If you feel symptoms—shaky, sweaty, lightheaded—tell us immediately and we’ll check a fingerstick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight with the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than I expected. No vomiting. Some cramping but not too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll continue to advance toward the goal rate as long as your belly stays soft and you’re not getting distended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my incision and the tube site—how do I take care of it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll teach you. For the tube site: wash gently with mild soap and water. Keep a dressing if there’s drainage; once it’s dry, you can leave it open. For the incision, keep it clean and watch for redness, swelling, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the tube clogs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll flush it with water on schedule—at home it will be 100 mL free water every 8 hours. If you can’t flush or the feeding won’t run, stop and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you’re at the goal tube feed rate and tolerating it. Your blood sugars have been stable on this regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean the hypoglycemia is fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we’ve found a way to control it right now. The underlying issue—what we’ve been calling nesidioblastosis—can still cause episodes, so you’ll continue frequent glucose checks and follow up closely after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still taking my acarbose and pramlintide, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll resume your regular home medications unless we specifically tell you otherwise. Your discharge list includes acarbose with meals and pramlintide with meals, along with your other medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about constipation with the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good concern. You’ll have docusate twice daily, and bisacodyl as needed. Also walking and fluids help. We’ll aim to keep the oxycodone only as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I shower? And do I need to keep a dressing on the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can wash around the tube with mild soap and water. If there’s no drainage, you can omit the dressing. If you notice new drainage, redness, or worsening pain, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge planning day. You’re afebrile, walking independently, tolerating bariatric stage 5 diet plus continuous tube feeds, and your pain is controlled on oral medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going home with the feeding pump running all day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continuous 24 hours per day for now: Replete with Fiber at 55 mL per hour. You’ll flush with 100 mL water every 8 hours. Home services will help with supplies and teaching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What symptoms mean I should stop the feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop significant abdominal distention, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, worsening abdominal pain, or high residuals when you aspirate the tube—especially more than 50 mL—stop the feeding and call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I check residuals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use a 60 mL syringe to aspirate from the tube before feeding. If you pull back more than 50 mL, hold the feeding and notify the physician who ordered the formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar checks—how often at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Routinely before and after meals, at bedtime, and any time you feel symptoms. If you have trouble tolerating feeds or tube issues, check even more closely and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about fever? I’m scared of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have shaking chills or a fever over 101.5°F, or if the incision or tube site becomes red, swollen, draining, or increasingly painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special because of the colon repair?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main thing is to watch for concerning symptoms—worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fever, or inability to pass gas or stool again. You’ve been doing well, and we didn’t see signs of infection during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. This tube feeding plan is meant to keep you stable while you follow up with the specialists who’ve been evaluating your hypoglycemia. We’ll make sure you leave with clear instructions and contacts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’ll continue your home meds, plus omeprazole twice daily, liquid oxycodone as needed, and the bowel regimen. You’re set up for home services for the tube feeding. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No—just please make sure I have the number to call if the tube leaks or my sugars drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. You’re just arriving from the recovery area after we reopened and cleaned out the top part of your abdominal incision and removed a piece of suture that was acting like a foreign body. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sore and kind of worried. Why wouldn’t it heal? It kept draining even though the skin looked closed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common pattern when there’s a small cavity underneath the skin—sometimes it tracks deeper and keeps producing drainage. In your case we were concerned there might be retained suture material irritating the tissue, so we reopened the area, debrided the unhealthy tissue, and removed the suture we found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t like the G-tube itself causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This was in the upper part of your midline incision rather than the tube site itself. The tube is still in place, and we’ll resume your tube feeds once you’re fully awake and comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need another big surgery if it doesn’t close?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our goal is to avoid that. By removing the foreign body and cleaning the wound, we’re giving it the best chance to heal from the inside out. The key part at home will be packing the wound with dressing twice a day so it doesn’t seal over too early on top.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts. What are you giving me for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use oral pain medicine as needed—an oxycodone-acetaminophen liquid is ordered for breakthrough pain. We’ll also keep an eye on nausea and make sure you can drink fluids and take your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have an infection? They mentioned cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was concern for infection around the wound given the persistent drainage and irritation. After cleaning it out, we’re treating you with antibiotics to cover skin bacteria—at discharge you’ll take amoxicillin-clavulanate for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I eat? And can I restart my tube feeds today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll advance your diet as you tolerate it, and we’ll resume your tube feeds as well. We’ll also check your blood sugars while you’re here since your feeding plan is part of keeping them stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been okay lately with the tube feeds. Will this wound thing mess that up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t. Today you’ve tolerated restarting feeds, and your blood sugars have stayed stable. We’ll keep your usual regimen and home medications unless we tell you otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you show me what the dressing is supposed to look like? I’m nervous I’ll do it wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. The nurse will do the next change with you watching, and we’ll have you practice. The idea is to gently pack the wound so it fills the space, then cover it with a clean dry dressing. You’ll do that twice daily at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call you or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or return right away for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, worsening redness or swelling, increasing or foul-smelling drainage, worsening pain, vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, chest pain, or new shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight you stayed afebrile and your vital signs were stable. How’s your pain this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than yesterday. Still tender when I move. The tube feeds didn’t bother me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we want to hear. Your heart and lungs look good, your abdomen is soft, and the dressing is clean and dry. Since you’re tolerating diet and tube feeds and your pain is controlled with oral medication, we’re planning discharge today with home services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on any special restrictions? I have kids at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest and walk several times a day, but avoid heavy lifting until you see your surgeon in follow-up. Also don’t drive or operate machinery while you’re taking the narcotic pain medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I leaving with? I don’t want to mess up my usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your regular home medications. New or changed items: amoxicillin-clavulanate by mouth every 12 hours for 7 days, oxycodone-acetaminophen liquid as needed for pain, and mupirocin nasal ointment twice daily for 30 days. Everything else stays the same unless your outpatient doctors adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up is with Dr. __, right? If the drainage comes back, I call sooner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—follow up with Dr. __ in clinic as scheduled, and call sooner if you notice increasing drainage, redness, swelling, fever, or worsening pain. You’re doing well to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor seeing you tonight. I understand you’ve had abdominal pain around your G-tube site—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three days ago I stepped on the tube at home and it yanked hard. I’ve had pain since, and it’s been leaking more. The skin looks red too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea? Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting or diarrhea. I don’t think I’ve had a fever. I’m mostly worried I pulled it out of place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. On exam your belly is soft and only minimally tender right around the tube, and I don’t feel signs of a severe abdominal infection. The redness is in a very square shape where the bandage sits, which can happen from irritation and moisture under the dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The drainage is yellow and kind of cloudy. Is that pus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it doesn’t smell bad and the skin isn’t hot or hard, which is reassuring. Sometimes tube feed can leak around the site and look yellow and cloudy. But because you had a strong tug and ongoing pain, we want to make sure the tube is still in the stomach and there’s no leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do you check that? I’ve had so many tube problems before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a G-tube contrast study—radiology injects a small amount of water-soluble contrast through the tube and takes X-rays to confirm it goes into the stomach and small bowel without leaking outside. While we’re waiting, we’ll keep you NPO—no tube feeds—and give IV fluids and pain medicine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no feeds tonight? I’m worried I’ll get low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep a close eye on you. The IV fluids help, and we’ll restart feeds as soon as the study shows it’s safe. If you feel symptoms of low blood sugar, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is really right at the tube. It stings when anything touches it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see some granulation tissue at the site—that extra healing tissue can be very tender and can ooze. We’ll do more frequent dressing changes to keep it clean and dry, and we can give you medication for pain while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do my labs show infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work looks reassuring—your white blood cell count is normal, and your kidney function is normal. Your urine test is negative as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When is the X-ray study happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been completed. The images show the tube tip is in the stomach. When they put in about 20 mL of contrast, it filled the stomach and moved into the small bowel, and there was no contrast leaking outside. That means no evidence of a perforation or leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it didn’t get pulled out of place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—the tube appears well positioned and patent. The pain is most likely from the tugging injury and the irritated tissue at the skin level, plus the leakage causing skin irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I restart my tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll restart your tube feeds and watch for any nausea, vomiting, worsening pain, or abdominal distension. If you tolerate feeds, that’s another reassuring sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeds are going in okay. The drainage is still there though. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some drainage can persist, especially if there’s leakage around the tube. What we’re watching is whether it becomes foul-smelling, the redness spreads, or you develop fever. With frequent dressing changes, the skin irritation often improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The redness looks better this morning, but it still hurts when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I agree—the redness has nearly resolved compared with last night. The site is still tender where the granulation tissue is. We’ll transition you to oral pain medication as needed and keep focusing on good dressing care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need antibiotics? I’m worried because I’ve had MRSA before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s no sign of a deep infection—no fever, no elevated white count, and the skin findings look like irritation from the dressing and leakage rather than cellulitis. If anything changes—spreading redness, warmth, worsening pain, or fever—you should call right away or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan when I go home? I’m scared it’ll get yanked again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re safe to go home today. Keep doing frequent dressing changes to keep the area clean and dry. Continue your tube feeds as you’ve been doing since you’re tolerating them. We’re sending you with oxycodone for pain as needed and docusate to prevent constipation. And you’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in about two weeks—if the tube keeps bothering you, it may need repositioning in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call urgently if you develop fever, worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, a hard or distended belly, rapidly spreading redness, foul-smelling drainage, or if the tube stops working or gets pulled out. Otherwise, keep up the dressing care and we’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery/bariatric team. I hear you came in because your blood sugar dropped low today. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: This morning I felt jittery and kind of hazy, and my hypoglycemia alarm went off. It said 43. I took sugar pills and it came up, but it scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That is scary. Any passing out, seizures, or confusion that didn’t get better after the sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No passing out. I was shaky and not thinking clearly, but it improved after the pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you had episodes like this since you started tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, this is the first time since I started the feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you mentioned more drainage around the G-tube site. What are you noticing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The gauze gets soaked, so I’ve been changing it twice a day. It’s more painful too. I don’t think it’s red, and I don’t have fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any new belly pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the tube site hurting and the drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You also had a question about whether the feeds are going into you or refluxing back into the bag by the pump. Tell me what you’re seeing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it looks like the formula is backing up. I’m worried it’s not actually going in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Tonight we’ll check your blood sugars closely and we’ll do a contrast study through the tube to confirm it’s in the stomach and not leaking. We’ll also examine the skin and tissue around the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous? Like could the tube be in the wrong place again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The concern is exactly that—position and leakage—but we can evaluate it quickly with imaging. Right now your exam is reassuring and you don’t have fever or severe abdominal pain, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the low sugar—why would it happen if I’m on feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After gastric bypass, some people can have hypoglycemia related to how the body handles nutrients and hormones. We’ll make sure you’re safe tonight, and we may involve Endocrinology to guide a more detailed work-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to do the G-tube contrast check now. You’ll feel some fluid go through the tube while we take X-ray images.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can feel a little uncomfortable or full, but it shouldn’t be painful. Let us know if you feel sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tube study is back: the G-tube is located in the stomach and there’s no sign of contrast leaking outside the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—proper location and no leak. That makes a major complication much less likely. We’ll continue your tube feeds here and keep checking fingerstick sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why is there so much drainage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often it’s irritation at the skin opening and sometimes overgrowth of granulation tissue—extra healing tissue that can ooze and be tender. We’ll look closely and treat it if that’s what it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I examined the site—there is some granulation tissue around the tube. The surrounding skin doesn’t look significantly red or infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is granulation tissue bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common and not dangerous by itself, but it can bleed a little, drain, and hurt. We can treat it with silver nitrate to shrink it and use an antibiotic ointment called mupirocin on the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Silver nitrate sounds intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a topical treatment—brief stinging sometimes, but it’s quick. We’ll do it carefully and protect the surrounding skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any more shakiness overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept some. No big low sugar episode like yesterday, but I’m still worried it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick sugars have been stable so far while on the tube feeds. That’s reassuring. We’re also reviewing possible contributors, including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been treated for that before. Are you going to restart antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re restarting metronidazole—Flagyl—500 mg every 8 hours, since bacterial overgrowth may be contributing to the hypoglycemia pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that upset my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause nausea or a metallic taste. We can give ondansetron as needed for nausea. Let us know if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site still hurts when I move. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With granulation tissue, tenderness is common. After the silver nitrate treatment and ointment, it should gradually improve. We’ll also keep the dressing clean and dry and change it when saturated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got another abdominal X-ray today to make sure contrast has moved through. It shows the contrast has passed into the colon and rectum, and there’s no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my intestines aren’t blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no ileus or obstruction seen. It also notes a lot of stool in the colon, which can happen, but the key point is there’s passage through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my sugars are okay today, why do I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you had multiple low readings with symptoms before coming in, and your outpatient endocrinologist asked for a fasting hypoglycemia work-up. That requires close monitoring and timed blood tests while we temporarily stop tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fasting sounds like it could make me crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we do it in the hospital. Nursing will check fingersticks every hour, and we’ll draw labs at specific times. If your sugar drops, we’ll treat it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology reviewed your case and recommends we proceed with the supervised fasting study today. Are you okay moving forward with that plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but yes. What exactly are you testing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When your glucose gets low, we’ll draw blood for glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin, and we’ll also check ammonia. Those results help your endocrinologist understand the cause and guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to stop the tube feeds completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, temporarily, so we can see what your body does without continuous nutrition. We’ll stop them and monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starting to feel a little shaky. Is my sugar dropping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just checked—your fingerstick is still in a safe range right now. Keep telling us about symptoms; we’ll keep the hourly checks going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube site looks less wet today. Is that from the ointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes—between the silver nitrate shrinking the granulation tissue and the mupirocin plus better dressing care, drainage often improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off tube feeds for many hours now. We’re continuing the hourly fingersticks overnight. If you feel sweaty, confused, very shaky, or weak, call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky and kind of foggy again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick is 55. This is the threshold we were watching for. We’re drawing the final set of labs now, then we’ll treat the low sugar immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Please don’t let it get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t. Labs are being drawn now, and we’re giving glucose to bring your level back up. We’ll recheck frequently until you feel normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your sugars have been stable, and you’re alert and feeling better. The fasting work-up is complete, and the results will be visible to your outpatient endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re stable, and we want you to make your outpatient appointments. Before you go, we’ll review your medications and tube site care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep the tube feeds the same at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated tube feeds here, and the tube is in the right place. Continue your prescribed tube feeding plan at home, and follow your endocrinologist’s guidance based on the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do if my sugar drops again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use glucose tablets as prescribed for symptoms or low readings. If you have severe symptoms—confusion, inability to take tablets, or you don’t improve—seek emergency care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube site—just keep changing the dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes: keep it clean and dry, change gauze when saturated, and apply mupirocin ointment to the granulation tissue twice daily as prescribed. Call if you develop spreading redness, fever, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking the Flagyl?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—metronidazole 500 mg by mouth every 8 hours, as prescribed, for bacterial overgrowth treatment. If you get significant side effects, contact your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Anything new besides those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: New from this stay are the Flagyl and the mupirocin ointment for the tube site. You’ll also have glucose tablets available for hypoglycemia. The rest of your regimen continues as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home after that 55 overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The drop happened during a supervised fast, which we did on purpose to capture labs. With your usual tube feeds and your rescue glucose tablets, you have a plan. And your endocrinologist will review the results quickly at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any last questions before discharge paperwork?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No—just please make sure my endocrinologist can see the lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The insulin, glucose, C-peptide, proinsulin, ammonia labs from the fasting study are in the system for your outpatient endocrinology team to review. We’ll discharge you home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you were admitted for low blood sugars and confusion. Can you tell me what’s been happening at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been almost every day. I get shaky and dizzy, then I can’t think straight. Sometimes I don’t remember things I did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds frightening. When you check your glucose during those episodes, what numbers do you see?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes in the 40s or 50s. But then other times it says like 70 and I still feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll check your glucose here with our fingerstick checks and compare to your home meter, because meter accuracy can be an issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also sent an email to my doctor that was… not like me. I don’t even remember writing it. That’s what scared me the most.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. Confusion and short-term memory problems can happen when glucose drops. We’re also asking Neurology to weigh in to make sure there’s nothing else we’re missing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m worried it’s something in my brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very reasonable worry. We’ll do a careful neurologic exam and review your story with Neurology. If they think imaging is needed, we’ll do it, but often with this pattern it tracks with hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also see you have a G-tube for continuous feeds. How have you been tolerating feeds and the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeds are okay, but I’ve been nauseated and dry heaving. The tube site has that extra tissue again and a little drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll examine the site daily. Right now I don’t see spreading redness, but there is hypergranulation tissue and a small amount of drainage. We’ll keep it clean and monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’m so constipated. I can only go if I use an enema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Constipation can definitely worsen nausea and make you feel unwell. We’ll address that while we’re also working on the glucose issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s our plan today: frequent bedside glucose checks, continue tube feeds but cycle them—lower rate during the day and higher overnight—and we’ll consult Endocrinology and GI. We’ll also send labs to look at nutrition and other contributors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on octreotide before, but they stopped it and started diazoxide. Is that why this is happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to pin it on one change, but Endocrinology will help us evaluate whether your current diazoxide dosing and feeding schedule are the best combination for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to stop my feeds to see what happens? That sounds risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We may do a supervised fasting trial, but only in the hospital with close monitoring. The Endocrine team typically asks for specific blood tests if your glucose drops below a certain threshold, and we treat immediately if it does.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your initial bloodwork looks reassuring—no signs of infection, kidney function is normal, and your glucose on the lab draw was in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I feel so foggy then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fogginess can come and go with glucose swings, nausea, poor sleep, and constipation. We’re going to track your glucose closely here to see if we can capture what’s happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My fingerstick just now was 82. That’s not low, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—82 is not hypoglycemia. It’s helpful information, because it suggests your symptoms aren’t always tied to a dangerously low number, or that your home meter may be reading differently than our checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still taking Flagyl three times a day for bacterial overgrowth. Could that be making me nauseated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can contribute to nausea in some people. GI will review whether it’s still helping you and whether it’s worth continuing right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight your glucose checks stayed in a safe range. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but I’m scared it’ll drop again. And my stomach still hurts up high, like my old ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of that epigastric pain and your history of gastrojejunal ulcers, we asked GI to evaluate you for an endoscopy to look for any active ulcer or irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re working on scheduling. If it’s not today, it may be tomorrow, but we’ll keep you updated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Neurology came by. They asked me questions and had me follow their finger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—Neurology reviewed your symptoms and exam. Their impression is that additional brain imaging isn’t needed right now and that the confusion is most likely related to hypoglycemia episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief, but also… I hate that it’s still happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to reduce the frequency of those episodes and make your monitoring more reliable so you can feel safer at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology’s plan is to do a supervised trial off daytime tube feeds starting early afternoon, with frequent fingersticks. If your glucose drops below 55, we’ll draw special labs—glucose, C-peptide, cortisol, and proinsulin—then treat the low sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do those labs tell you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They help determine what your body is doing at the moment of hypoglycemia—whether insulin is inappropriately high, and whether stress hormones like cortisol are responding appropriately. That can guide medication and feeding strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about stopping the feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll be checking your glucose frequently, and if you feel symptoms—shaky, sweaty, confused—tell the nurse immediately even if the number isn’t low yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So far it’s been like 80s and 90s. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign. It means during this monitored period you’re not dropping into the dangerous range, so we may not trigger those special lab draws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My home meter says 68 but the nurse got 84. Which one is right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That difference is exactly why we’re comparing. If your home meter is reading lower than our fingersticks, it could be misleading you into thinking you’re hypoglycemic when you’re not. We’re going to replace your meter and strips to improve accuracy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your lowest fingerstick overnight was still safely above the threshold. How’s the nausea and constipation today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea is still there. Constipation is a little better but not great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI recommended we switch your nausea medicine from ondansetron to prochlorperazine as needed, since ondansetron can worsen constipation for some people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can in some people. We’ll start with the prescribed dose and you can tell us how you feel. We’ll also keep working on bowel regularity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another update: GI also recommends stopping metronidazole for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stopping it? I thought it was for bacterial overgrowth and my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on it for a while, and it may be contributing to nausea. Given your current course and the lack of clear benefit during this admission, they feel it’s reasonable to stop and reassess with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is the day for your endoscopy. It will let us look at the esophagus, stomach pouch, and the connection from your bypass to see if there’s an ulcer or other cause of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried they’ll find another ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If they do, we’ll treat it. And if they don’t, that’s also helpful—it means we can focus more on motility, reflux, and feeding/medication adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the endoscopy. The GI doctor looked carefully: the bypass anatomy and the gastrojejunal connection were intact, and they did not see an ulcer at the anastomosis. They noted abnormal-appearing mucosa in the esophagus and stomach, but no acute process requiring surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain isn’t an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what they saw today, there isn’t an active ulcer at the connection. We’ll continue your pantoprazole twice daily for reflux and irritation, and we’ll keep managing nausea and constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the hypoglycemia? I didn’t have a big low here, but I swear it happens at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. In the hospital, with the feeding schedule and close monitoring, your fingersticks never dropped below the level where Endocrinology wanted the special labs, and the lowest we saw was still in a safe range. That’s reassuring, but it doesn’t erase what you’ve experienced at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what changes when I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key changes: first, we’re sending you home with a new glucose meter and strips so you can trust the readings more. Second, we’re simplifying your feeding plan—tube feeds overnight only, from 11 pm to 7 am at a rate of 40, plus a complex-carbohydrate diet during the day as the dietitian reviewed with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No daytime tube feeds at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—based on how you did here, the plan is nocturnal feeds only. If you start having recurrent low sugars again, you should contact your endocrinologist right away, and treat any true low glucose per your usual plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I eat during the day? I’m scared to eat the wrong thing and crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Focus on complex carbohydrates paired with protein and avoid large simple-sugar loads. The nutrition team gave you specific examples and a schedule—small, steady intake tends to prevent spikes and drops after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nausea medicine—what am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have prochlorperazine to take every 6 hours as needed for nausea. We stopped ondansetron and stopped metronidazole during this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My memory… will it come back? I feel embarrassed about that email.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Many people have memory gaps around hypoglycemia episodes. The best way to prevent that is preventing the lows. Your mental status today is clear, and we’ll have you follow up with Dr. ___ in about three weeks to review how you’re doing on the new plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tube site tissue? It keeps coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You still have hypergranulation tissue but no signs of spreading infection. Keep the site clean and dry, and continue the care plan you’ve been using. If you notice increasing redness, warmth, worsening drainage, fever, or severe pain, call right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I safe to go home tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your vitals are stable, you’re walking independently, your glucose checks have been stable here, and we have a clear feeding and medication plan. We’ll make sure you have the new meter, your prescriptions, and your follow-up appointment before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you came in because of diarrhea and feeling dehydrated. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had diarrhea for a few days and today I just felt dried out—dry mouth, chills, sweaty, really tired. I tried drinking and flushing my G-tube with saline but it didn’t feel like enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How many days of diarrhea, and was there any blood in it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About three days. No blood. It comes with cramping low in my belly before I go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, vomiting, or severe belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No vomiting. No real pain—just cramps before the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When was your last bowel movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Around 4 this morning. Then it kind of stopped, but I still feel wiped out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and prior C. diff, we’ll take this seriously. We’re going to start IV fluids now and give your gut a rest—nothing by mouth for the moment—while we evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s C. diff again. Last time was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. If you have a bowel movement here, we’ll send a stool test for C. difficile. Right now you haven’t had one since early morning, so we may need to wait for a sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Am I going to need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing suggests that right now. Your belly exam is soft and not tender, and your vital signs look stable. This looks most consistent with dehydration from diarrhea, but we’ll keep checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my tube feeds? I’m scared to stop them because of my low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. For now we’re holding feeds while we rehydrate and let your intestines settle. We’ll monitor your blood sugar and restart tube feeds as soon as it’s safe and you’re tolerating things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also get reflux if I don’t take my stomach medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your pantoprazole. We can give nausea medicine if you need it too—either ondansetron or prochlorperazine, depending on what works best for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: we reviewed your abdominal X-ray from earlier today. It shows some air in small bowel loops but no signs of obstruction and no free air. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no evidence of a blockage on that imaging, and your symptoms don’t fit an obstruction either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel really thirsty and kind of shaky. Is that from dehydration?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. The IV fluids should help. We’ll also check your electrolytes and keep an eye on your potassium since diarrhea can lower it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I don’t have a bowel movement, how will you test for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can only test if we have a stool sample. If the diarrhea has stopped, that’s actually a good sign. If it returns, we’ll collect a sample right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today—any more diarrhea overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No diarrhea overnight. I’m less dizzy, but I’m nervous to start eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Your labs this morning look reassuring—your kidney function is normal and your white blood cell count isn’t elevated. Your potassium is at the low end of normal, so we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean it wasn’t an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It makes a serious infection less likely, but it doesn’t completely rule it out. Clinically, you’re improving with fluids and bowel rest, which is encouraging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something to drink? My mouth is still dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start with small sips of clear liquids and see how you do. If there’s no nausea or diarrhea, we’ll advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not nauseated, but I’m scared it’ll trigger dumping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slowly and avoid sugary liquids. The goal is gentle hydration and then a diet you can tolerate without triggering symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to resume your enteral nutrition through the G-tube today, starting carefully. Let us know right away if you feel cramping, nausea, or diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m relieved we’re restarting it. Will it make the diarrhea come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might not. Since your diarrhea has resolved, restarting feeds slowly is reasonable. If symptoms return, we’ll reassess and consider sending stool studies if we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been able to drink and the tube feeding seems okay so far. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep the IV fluids going a bit longer and then transition to oral and tube hydration as long as you keep tolerating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home too soon. What if I get dehydrated again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t send you home until you’re taking in enough and your symptoms are controlled. Before discharge, we’ll review a plan for hydration, tube flushes, and what warning signs should bring you back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it is C. diff, would I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If testing showed C. diff, yes, we’d treat it. Right now we don’t have a stool sample yet, and your diarrhea has stopped, which makes active C. diff less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any bowel movement since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I finally went this morning. It was loose but not like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect timing—we sent that stool sample for C. difficile testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still having some mild cramping. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild cramping can happen as your intestines recover and as we restart intake. The key is that you’re not having severe pain, fever, or persistent watery diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile test came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh thank goodness. So what caused it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it’s a short-lived irritation or viral-type gastroenteritis, or diet-related changes, especially with your altered anatomy after bypass. The important part is you became dehydrated, and that has resolved with fluids and bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I okay to go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I think so. You’re tolerating oral intake without nausea or vomiting, your tube feeds are resumed and tolerated, your pain is controlled, and you’re walking around independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I do if the diarrhea comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Focus on hydration early—small frequent sips, and use your G-tube flushes as instructed. If you have persistent diarrhea, can’t keep up with fluids, feel lightheaded, have fever, blood in stool, or worsening abdominal pain, you should call your doctors or come back to the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking my usual medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your pantoprazole for reflux and your other home medications as directed. Use prochlorperazine as needed for nausea. For anxiety, your lorazepam is prescribed as needed. We’ll also make sure you have your nighttime sleep medication as listed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up is with my bariatric doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—follow up with Drs. ___ and ___ as previously scheduled. They know your history with dumping and hypoglycemia and can adjust your feeding plan if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a lot better now. I just don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you’re improved. The big prevention steps are early hydration, monitoring symptoms, and reaching out quickly if diarrhea returns. We’ll get your discharge paperwork together now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Smith from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you came in with bloating and a change in your G-tube output. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. I’ve been really bloated and uncomfortable, and the stuff coming out of my tube looks brown—almost like stool. Sometimes it’s greenish-yellow too, and there’s more of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds very distressing. Any fevers, chills, shortness of breath, vomiting, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. No vomiting. No diarrhea either. Just pressure and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When was your last tube feed, and what’s your usual regimen at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last feed was this morning. I do Replete with Fiber at 30 mL an hour for 12 hours. I also eat small amounts by mouth during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I also see you’ve been taking antibiotics through the tube—Flagyl and Noroxin. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve been doing them like I was told, but the output still changed and I feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history after Roux-en-Y—dumping, hypoglycemia episodes, and prior small intestinal bacterial overgrowth—we want to make sure there’s no blockage and that the tube is in the right place. We’ll start with bowel rest—nothing by mouth for now—IV fluids, and IV antibiotics while we evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you worried it’s C. diff again? I’ve had that before and it was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it in mind because of your history, but right now you’re not having diarrhea. We’ll still send stool testing to be safe if we can get a sample, and we’ll watch your labs and symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the brown output—does that mean something is really wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Brown output can happen for a few reasons, including slowed movement and backup of intestinal contents, or irritation/infection. It doesn’t automatically mean an emergency, but it’s a reason to check for obstruction and confirm the tube position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just scared because I’ve had so many surgeries and complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll take this step by step and keep you updated. First, we’ll get an abdominal X-ray tonight to look at the gas pattern and any signs of obstruction or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
