conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we don’t have evidence you need surgery. Most of our plan is supportive care and treating possible bacterial overgrowth. Imaging will help guide us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting IV fluids now and an IV antibiotic called Zosyn to cover a broad range of bacteria while we sort this out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interact with my other meds? I take fluoxetine, nortriptyline, lorazepam, and quetiapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your home medications. We’ll continue them unless there’s a specific reason to hold something, and we’ll monitor you. If you feel overly sleepy or different than usual, tell us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly feels tight. Is there anything to relieve the bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We can start soap-suds enemas every six hours to help move stool and gas through and reduce distention. We’ll also keep checking your abdominal exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a nonobstructive bowel gas pattern—so no clear blockage—and no large amount of free air on this limited view. The G-tube is seen in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not blocked? Then why do I feel so bloated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can still feel very bloated from slowed bowel movement, constipation, or bacterial overgrowth even without a mechanical obstruction. The enema plan and antibiotics should help, and we’ll also do a contrast study through the tube tomorrow to confirm it’s positioned correctly and functioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any nausea, vomiting, or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. The enemas are not fun, but I do feel a little less pressure. The tube output is still weird though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad the pressure is easing. We’re going to proceed with the G-tube contrast check this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube check is reassuring: the tube is patent, the tip is in the stomach, and there’s no leak of contrast outside the GI tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. They mentioned a lot of stool on the scan—does that mean I’m constipated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests there’s a large amount of fecal material in the colon, which can contribute to bloating. We’ll continue the enemas for now and keep your bowel regimen in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you still thinking bacterial overgrowth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s still high on our list given your history and symptoms. Since you’re stable—no fever, no concerning labs—we can narrow antibiotics. Today we’ll transition from Zosyn to ceftriaxone plus Flagyl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to restart feeds? I’m worried about getting low blood sugar if I don’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important point with your post-bypass hypoglycemia history. Since you’re improving and the tube study looks good, we’ll restart your tube feeds carefully and monitor how you feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And eating by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance you to a bariatric Stage 5 diet today. Go slowly, small portions, and let us know if you get nausea, discomfort, or worsening bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tolerated the tube feed restart so far. No nausea. Still some bloating but less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep the plan steady: ceftriaxone and Flagyl IV, enemas as ordered, and we’ll keep an eye on your vitals and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took blood cultures earlier—what are those for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you came in with concerning GI symptoms and we started IV antibiotics, we check blood cultures to look for bacteria in the bloodstream. So far, they’re showing no growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about being on antibiotics again. Could it trigger C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics can increase that risk, so we’re being cautious. We’ll test your stool for C. difficile, and we’re using the narrowest regimen that still treats what we think is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight you stayed afebrile and your exam is improved. We also have stool results: C. difficile PCR is negative, and stool cultures did not show Salmonella, Shigella, or Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. So what’s the plan now—do I keep taking Flagyl?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since you were already on Flagyl and you’ve improved with treatment, you’ll continue metronidazole 500 mg by mouth every 8 hours after discharge. We’ll stop the IV antibiotics once you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Noroxin I was using at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For today, the discharge plan is to continue Flagyl as discussed and resume your other home medications unless we specifically tell you otherwise. For your tube feed regimen and any additional antibiotics, we want you to confirm with your bariatric clinic team rather than changing things on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m eating the Stage 5 foods okay. When can I go back to my normal diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on Stage V until your follow-up appointment. Don’t self-advance the diet. Also avoid drinking through a straw and avoid chewing gum, since both can worsen gas and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I restart tube feeds at home the same way as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume tube feeds in consultation with your bariatric provider. Please call the clinic in the morning to verify the tube feed regimen with the nurse, so it’s clear and safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take ibuprofen when I get aches. Is that okay after all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—please avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, and naproxen. After gastric bypass they can cause ulcers and bleeding. Use only what your bariatric team recommends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call us if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by your meds, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or any concerning drainage or redness around any sites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling much better—less bloated, and the tube output looks more normal. I’m still nervous it’ll come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s normal to worry, especially with your history. The reassuring parts are: imaging didn’t show obstruction, the tube is in the right place without leak, you stayed stable without fever, and the stool testing for C. diff was negative. We’ll send you home with clear instructions and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you review my meds one more time so I don’t mess it up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sure. Continue your home meds: fluoxetine, nortriptyline, lactulose, lorazepam, quetiapine, pantoprazole, and use ondansetron or prochlorperazine as needed for nausea. Keep taking Flagyl 500 mg by mouth every 8 hours; we’re giving you a refill prescription. And remember: no NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and bloating, plus some low blood sugars. Can you tell me what’s been going on over the last few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been about four days of belly pain and feeling really swollen. I’m nauseated but not throwing up. And my sugars have been dropping a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Where is the pain—more on the right side, left, or all over? And is it constant or crampy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mostly lower belly and sometimes on the right. It comes and goes, like cramps, but it’s been more constant tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fevers, chills, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No vomiting. Just nausea and I feel shaky when my sugar drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still using your G-tube feeds? Any change in the tube site or output?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tube feeds are going in okay. The site looks fine. I’ve been trying not to eat much by mouth like nutrition told me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still taking metronidazole—Flagyl—for the bacterial overgrowth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking it. And my lactulose dose was increased last week, so I’ve been going to the bathroom more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any burning when you pee, urgency, or back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually yes—burning and I feel like I have to go a lot, but not much comes out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that’s helpful. We’ll check labs and urine testing. We also got an abdominal X-ray to look for obstruction or free air, and we’ll likely do an ultrasound of the gallbladder since you have some right-sided pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s another blockage. With my bypass history, it always feels like something is wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. The good news is your exam right now doesn’t suggest an emergency, and we’re checking imaging to be safe. We’ll also keep a close eye on your blood sugars while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a normal bowel gas pattern—no obstruction and no free air. It does show moderate stool in the right side of the colon, which can contribute to bloating and crampy pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation? But I’ve been having more bowel movements with the lactulose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can still happen—sometimes you can have frequent stools but still have stool sitting higher up. We’ll keep your bowel regimen going and make sure you’re hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sugars? My monitor keeps going off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a blood sugar here and it’s okay at the moment. We’ll do frequent checks and we’re going to involve endocrinology to help with the hypoglycemia plan and your continuous glucose monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your morning labs are reassuring overall. One of the tests we sent, cortisol, is elevated, but that can happen with stress and illness. Nothing here suggests an acute surgical problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean my adrenal glands are okay? I’ve worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what we have, there’s no sign of adrenal insufficiency. Endocrinology can also weigh in when they see you, especially since the main issue is the low sugars after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your right upper quadrant ultrasound is back—no gallstones and no signs of gallbladder infection. Liver and bile ducts look normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Then why does it hurt on the right sometimes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can come from bowel distention, stool burden, or chronic abdominal pain related to your prior surgeries. The key is we’re not seeing anything dangerous like obstruction or gallbladder disease today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to continue your tube feeds as directed. Nutrition is documenting the enteral feeding plan, and we’ll keep your oral intake limited to liquids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Liquids only again? I’m worried I’ll crash if I don’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll balance that. The tube feeds provide steady nutrition, and for the hypoglycemia we’ll focus on responding earlier when your glucose starts trending down, rather than waiting until it alarms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine testing is consistent with a urinary tract infection, which can also make you feel unwell and worsen appetite and glucose swings. We’re starting an antibiotic called Bactrim by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. How long do I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a total of five days of treatment. Since you’ll start it here, you’ll go home with the remaining doses—twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly still hurts. Tylenol isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you stronger pain medication as needed, but we’ll use the lowest effective dose and keep it short-term. Opioids can worsen constipation, so we’ll be careful and keep your bowel meds going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology reviewed your glucose monitor data with you. Their main concern is that you’ve been waiting for the alarm before taking sugar, which means you’re treating late.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought the alarm meant it was time to fix it. I didn’t want to overdo sugar and then dump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Their recommendation is to act earlier—when you see the number trending down—so you can take a smaller amount of sugar and prevent a bigger crash. That can actually reduce dumping-type swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it’s dropping, what should I take? I’m mostly on tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll give you a specific plan, but the principle is quick sugar when it’s falling—don’t wait for the alarm. Since you’re on tube feeds, we’ll also make sure your feeding schedule is consistent and you have a way to take sugar safely if you’re symptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting, worsening pain, or very low sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is better with the meds. My sugar dipped once but I treated it earlier like they said and it didn’t get as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want. Any urinary symptoms today—burning or urgency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little burning still, but it’s less than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great—Bactrim often starts helping within a day or two. We’ll keep you on it and make sure you can tolerate everything by mouth or tube before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need surgery for any of this? I keep ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not based on what we’re seeing this admission. Imaging doesn’t show obstruction or gallbladder disease, and your abdomen is soft without signs of an acute surgical issue. The focus is treating the UTI, managing chronic abdominal pain, and tightening the hypoglycemia plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about being on Flagyl so long. Do I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue the Flagyl as you’ve been prescribed for the small bowel bacterial overgrowth. We’re not changing that plan during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting to plan for discharge tomorrow if things stay stable: pain controlled with oral meds, sugars manageable with the new approach, and UTI improving on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home with pain meds? I don’t want to be stuck in pain, but I also don’t want to get constipated again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give a short course of an oral pain medication to use only as needed. Keep taking lactulose and bisacodyl as directed, drink the liquids you’re allowed, and call if constipation or pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—your vitals look good and your abdominal exam is improved: soft, only mild tenderness, not distended. Are you comfortable going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. I’m still nervous about the low sugars at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. The key instructions are: keep trending your glucose, and when you see it dropping, take in sugar then—don’t wait for the alarm. Endocrinology also wants you to follow up with your outpatient doctor who manages your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the UTI—just finish the Bactrim?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll take Bactrim DS one tablet twice daily to complete five total days of treatment. If you develop fever, flank pain, or worsening urinary symptoms, you should call your primary care provider or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about eating? Can I have solids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, no solid food by mouth—continue liquids only, and continue tube feeds as directed. That’s to keep things steady while your symptoms settle and to help with glucose stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been struggling mentally with all of this. I missed my therapy appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you told me. Please reschedule with your psychologist/therapist as soon as you can, and follow up with your primary care provider too. We’ll include that in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: you’re going home with Bactrim to finish the UTI treatment, a short supply of pain medication as needed, and you’ll continue Flagyl and your usual meds. Any last questions about the glucose monitor plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to be clear—if I see it trending down, I treat it even if it hasn’t alarmed yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Treat early when it’s dropping, so you can prevent a severe low. And keep your tube feeds consistent. If you have repeated lows despite that, call your endocrinology doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining it in a way I can follow. I’ll finish the antibiotics and set up my follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in because of episodes of confusion and low blood sugar—can you tell me what’s been happening at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For weeks I’ve been exhausted and sweaty, and sometimes I get confused, especially after I eat. I’m scared I’m not absorbing my meds or my antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to worry about, especially after a Roux-en-Y bypass. When you feel confused, do you notice shaking, slurred speech, or trouble remembering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—shaky and my speech gets weird. And later I don’t remember parts of it. It’s embarrassing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone—those symptoms can happen with post-bypass changes, including dumping syndrome and post-bypass hypoglycemia. We’ll monitor your glucose closely and also check labs to look for causes of confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two weeks ago another hospital told me my ammonia was high. Could this be liver failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take that seriously. Right now your exam doesn’t show signs of advanced liver disease, and we’ll trend your ammonia and liver tests here. We’re also going to involve the liver specialists to help interpret everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I finished a 10-day course of rifaximin recently, but I’m worried I’m not absorbing it. I’ve had bacterial overgrowth after the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll continue rifaximin while you’re here, and we’ll focus on what’s driving the confusion and the low sugars. We’ll also keep your tube feeds running for now and start with clear liquids by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m dry heaving more than usual. Is that from the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from several things—your baseline nausea, reflux, or how your stomach empties after bypass. We’ll keep ondansetron available and watch how you do with feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork looks reassuring: blood counts and electrolytes are okay, and your liver tests are normal right now. Your ammonia level is actually very low at the moment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I feel like I’m losing my mind after I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One possibility is that after bypass, your body can release too much insulin after meals, which can drop your sugar and cause confusion, tremor, and sweating. Another possibility is a metabolic issue that only shows up under certain conditions. We’ll try to capture an episode safely while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was your night? Any confusion or low sugar symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept a little. No big episode, but I’m anxious. I keep thinking I’m not absorbing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t measure absorption of every medication directly, but we can look for consequences—like whether your glucose is stable, whether your labs suggest malnutrition, and how you respond clinically. We also checked vitamin levels; your B12 and folate are high, which suggests you’re getting those in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology is coming, right? I’ve had scary lows at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Their plan is to do a supervised fast: we’ll hold tube feeds and any calories by mouth overnight, and if your sugar drops we’ll draw specific labs to see whether insulin is inappropriately high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds dangerous. What if I crash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it with frequent fingersticks and nursing checks. If your glucose drops, we’ll treat it immediately and still get the labs we need. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm the plan: tonight you’ll be NPO except water, and we’ll stop tube feeds for the fast. We’ll restart feeds after the morning labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m worried because at home it’s after meals that I get weird, not when I’m fasting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great point. The fast helps us rule in or out certain causes like insulin overproduction at baseline. If the fast is normal, we may still be dealing with a post-meal insulin surge—common after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the overnight fast now. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hungry and nervous. But okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning update: you did not become significantly hypoglycemic overnight. We’re drawing the endocrine labs now—glucose, insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and a few others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean it’s not real? Because it’s real at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s real. It may mean the trigger is different—like after eating, or with your usual routine at home. Hospital conditions don’t always reproduce it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your tube feeds now that the labs are drawn. We’ll keep monitoring your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat anything by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to be careful. Endocrinology’s recommendation is to rely on continuous tube feeds and avoid taking calories by mouth, except water, because oral intake can provoke dumping and hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some of the endocrine results are back: insulin, C-peptide, and beta-hydroxybutyrate from the fast are within normal limits. One test—proinsulin—is still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If those are normal, why did they say hyperinsulinism?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your history fits a hyperinsulinemic pattern after meals, which can happen after bypass—sometimes related to islet cell changes. The fasting labs being normal doesn’t rule out a post-meal surge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do I do at home? I can’t keep having these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The safest plan right now is continuous tube feeds and no calories by mouth. That reduces the rapid swings that can trigger symptoms. We’ll also make sure you have close endocrine follow-up to adjust the long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver team will see you today or tomorrow. Your ammonia levels here have been variable but not consistently high, and your exam doesn’t show signs of cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved, but then what explains the confusion and the memory gaps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a metabolic explanation that can be triggered by protein intake—something like a urea cycle issue. It’s uncommon, but given your symptoms and the outside report of high ammonia, it’s worth checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hepatology evaluated you. Their impression is that your episodes are not typical for hepatic encephalopathy, and they do not think you have cirrhosis based on what we’re seeing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see evidence of advanced liver disease right now. They suggested checking B12 and folate—which we did—and they also suggested a two-week trial of lactulose could help if constipation is contributing to symptoms and ammonia buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactulose makes you poop a lot, right? I’m already dealing with so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can increase bowel movements, yes. The goal would be to relieve constipation, which can sometimes worsen gut bacterial overgrowth and ammonia handling. We can talk through whether it’s right for you and how to use it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to try to observe one of your post-meal episodes in a controlled way. If you agree, we can give you a high-protein meal and then check labs over time—ammonia and liver tests—and watch your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared, but I also want you to see what happens. Will you stop it if it gets bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll do it with you on the unit, frequent checks, and we’ll stop if you feel unsafe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after the meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s starting. My hands are shaky and my words feel thick. I have a headache and I’m nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’re checking your vitals and glucose now, and we’re drawing the labs we discussed. Stay seated; we’ll keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s easing up a little, but I feel foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what you described at home. We’ll keep monitoring until you’re fully back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you told the nurse you don’t remember much from last evening after the episode. That’s consistent with what you’ve been experiencing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… it’s like a blank spot. Did the labs show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that your AST and ALT and your albumin rose after the high-protein meal compared with your baseline, and your ammonia levels were trended. This pattern makes us think about a metabolic pathway issue rather than cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what? Is it genetic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. One category is a urea cycle disorder—an inherited problem with processing nitrogen from protein. We sent a urea cycle panel after a 12-hour fast. Those results won’t be back before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be seizures? Sometimes it feels like I’m not in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for that. Your EEG monitoring was normal—no seizures seen. And we also did an MRI of your brain today to look for any structural cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brain MRI is normal—no mass, no stroke, no abnormal enhancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s really my metabolism and the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading thought: post-gastric surgery physiology causing dumping and hypoglycemia, with a possible metabolic contribution that we’re testing for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site hurts. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your home Percocet for pain and can use oxycodone for breakthrough if needed. We’ll also check the site—right now it looks clean and intact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge planning: your heart rate has been low here, so we held your atenolol during the stay. We’ll have you discuss restarting or adjusting it with your outpatient clinician.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my feeds? I’m confused about the formula changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At home, the plan is to switch to NutriHep at 50 mL per hour continuously, with 200 mL water flushes four times per day. Until NutriHep arrives, continue your prior Nutren with Fiber at 65 mL per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no food by mouth at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no calories by mouth for now, only water. That’s to reduce dumping and prevent post-meal hypoglycemia and confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking rifaximin? I’m not sure it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you on rifaximin, and we want you to follow up with endocrinology to discuss whether you still need it long-term, since we don’t think bacterial overgrowth is the main driver of these episodes right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What results are still pending?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key items: the urea cycle panel and the proinsulin level from the endocrine workup. Those will be reviewed with your outpatient doctors as soon as they result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it is a urea cycle problem, what happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your specialists will guide that. It may involve dietary adjustments and sometimes additional testing. Hepatology also mentioned that a liver biopsy could be considered as an outpatient if needed for more definitive evaluation, depending on the rest of the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll have another episode at home and not know what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel confusion, tremor, or sweating, check your glucose if you can and seek urgent care if symptoms are severe or you can’t keep yourself safe. The best prevention right now is sticking to continuous tube feeds and avoiding oral calories until you’re reassessed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay to go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re alert, walking independently, and your exam is stable. We’ll send you home with clear instructions, your medication list, and follow-up appointments with your primary care doctor and your surgical and specialty teams.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the medicine team. I understand you came in with nausea, dry heaving, diarrhea, and now constant epigastric pain. Can you tell me what’s bothering you most right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain. It’s right in the middle, like my old ulcer pain. And I can’t stop gagging even when there’s nothing to throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Is it different from the chronic pain you get around the G-tube site on the left?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The tube site always aches, but this is deeper and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the diarrhea? Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fever. The diarrhea is actually slowing down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER your labs were mostly reassuring—white count normal, liver tests normal. Your lipase was elevated, which can suggest pancreatitis, and your potassium was high at first but came down. They started IV fluids and pain and nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it pancreatitis again? Or is it another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we’re keeping both on the table. With your Roux-en-Y anatomy and history of marginal ulcers, ulcer disease is definitely possible. The lipase elevation could be mild pancreatitis, but we also want to make sure there isn’t a biliary issue or something else driving the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s an obstruction. I’ve had so many surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very reasonable worry. The abdominal x-ray didn’t show free air, and surgery has already evaluated you and doesn’t think this looks like a surgical abdomen or a clear obstruction right now. We’ll keep checking your exam closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned my bladder was huge on the x-ray. What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The x-ray noted a severely distended bladder, which can happen if you’re retaining urine. We’ll ask you about urination and check a bladder scan if needed—sometimes pain meds and dehydration can contribute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been peeing less because I haven’t been drinking. But I can go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. For now, we’re going to rest your gut—no tube feeds temporarily—give IV fluids, treat nausea, and control pain while we sort out the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop my feeds, won’t my sugar crash? That happened before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that closely. In the ER your fingerstick was 74, so they switched fluids to include dextrose. We’ll keep checking your blood sugars and adjust fluids so you don’t become hypoglycemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to get confused again like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. If you feel shaky, sweaty, lightheaded, or notice confusion, tell us right away. We’ll also keep your home meds that help your baseline GI issues, like rifaximin, unless there’s a reason to hold them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is a little better with the zofran, but the pain keeps coming back. What’s the plan for tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tonight we’ll continue IV fluids and bowel rest. We’ll trend labs, including lipase, and keep an eye on your abdominal exam. Given your history, we’re also planning more detailed imaging of the biliary tree and pancreas with an MRCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like an MRI? Do I have to drink contrast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s an MRI focused on the bile ducts and pancreas. In your case, they can give oral contrast through the gastrostomy tube. It helps us see anatomy without radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s an ulcer, how do you prove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The best test is an upper endoscopy—an EGD—where GI looks directly at the gastrojejunal connection and can treat an ulcer if they see one. We’re discussing that with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My diarrhea stopped. Does that mean it’s not C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It makes active C. diff less likely, especially since you’re not having ongoing watery stools here. If diarrhea returns, we can test, but right now it’s not the main concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or new diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No diarrhea. Still dry heaving sometimes. Pain is still there but maybe a little less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs remain stable, and your lipase has been coming down from where it started. That supports either a mild pancreatitis picture or a non-pancreatic cause with a transient lipase bump. We’re still going ahead with MRCP tonight to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could my antidepressant be causing pancreatitis? Someone mentioned that once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are rare reports of pancreatitis with fluoxetine. It’s uncommon, and we don’t have proof that’s what’s happening here, but it’s something we keep in mind while we evaluate other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to stop it suddenly. I get really anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not planning to stop it abruptly during this admission. We’ll focus on treating what’s in front of us and coordinate with your outpatient clinicians if medication changes ever become necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I restart my tube feeds? I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your pain and nausea are controlled and we’re confident there’s no acute obstruction or severe pancreatitis, we can restart feeds slowly. We’ll likely use your usual continuous NutriHep and monitor symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from MRCP. How are you feeling after the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. My stomach hurts from lying still. Did it show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Preliminary read is reassuring: the biliary tree and gallbladder look normal, and the pancreas looks normal without signs of acute inflammation. It also shows fast transit of contrast, which fits with your dumping syndrome history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It argues against significant acute pancreatitis or a biliary blockage. Given your symptoms and history, an ulcer at the anastomosis is moving higher on the list, and GI is planning an EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If they find an ulcer, can they fix it right then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often they can treat bleeding or high-risk spots during the procedure—like cauterizing a lesion—plus we treat with strong acid suppression and a coating medication to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. GI plans to do the EGD today. You’ll need to stay NPO—nothing by mouth—and we’ll keep tube feeds off until after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the scope. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable and typically don’t remember it. GI will review the risks and benefits with you beforehand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you worried about—bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking for a marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal connection, and if there’s a spot that looks like it could bleed, they can treat it. Your blood counts have been okay, and you haven’t reported black stools or vomiting blood, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from endoscopy. GI found a marginal ulcer with a pigmented lesion, and they cauterized it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was an ulcer. Is the cauterizing enough? Am I going to bleed later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Treating the lesion reduces the risk of bleeding. The bigger piece is healing the ulcer: we’re increasing acid suppression to pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and starting sucralfate four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I put the sucralfate through my tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI specifically wants it as a slurry by mouth, not through the tube, so it coats the area better. We’ll go over exactly how to take it before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not supposed to eat because of the hypoglycemia and confusion stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—your calories should still come from continuous tube feeds as you’ve been doing. The sucralfate is medication, not nutrition, and it’s a small volume. We’ll keep your feeding plan otherwise the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I restart NutriHep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can restart continuous tube feeds today at a low, steady rate and see how you tolerate it. We’ll keep it low protein as you’ve been doing given your chronic issues and prior episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds—can I stop the IV stuff? It makes me foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll transition from IV to oral pain medication as soon as you can tolerate it. The goal is to use the lowest effective dose and avoid constipation and sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with feeds back on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So far okay. No diarrhea. Pain is better, but still there when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep monitoring overnight. If things stay stable, we’ll plan discharge tomorrow with the new ulcer medications and a short course of oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement here. GI wanted some stool test, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’d like an H. pylori stool antigen test, but since you haven’t had a bowel movement in the hospital, we can’t send it now. We’ll make sure it’s on the plan to follow up in GI clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my hypoglycemia? Do I need endocrine again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your prior endocrine workup suggested a hyperinsulinemic state after gastric bypass, possibly from islet cell hyperplasia. During this admission, we focused on the ulcer, and your sugars have been stable with continuous feeds. We’ll keep your feeding strategy the same at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the confusion after meals—any new answers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new results came back during this stay. The prior workup didn’t show cirrhosis, and there’s still concern a urea cycle issue could contribute, especially with higher protein intake. That urea cycle panel from the prior admission is still pending, and you’ll review it with hepatology/GI outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep avoiding eating real food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the plan you were discharged with previously—continuous tube feeds and avoid oral caloric intake unless your outpatient team changes it. For this ulcer, the key additions are pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I take the pantoprazole twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until you see GI. They want a repeat EGD in about 8 weeks to check healing, and you should stay on pantoprazole 40 mg every 12 hours until then unless GI advises otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the sucralfate—any timing with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can interfere with absorption of some medications. We’ll give you a schedule, but in general take it as directed four times daily and try to separate it from other meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home with pain meds. I get constipated fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing a short course of oxycodone for ulcer pain—about five days’ worth—and we’re also prescribing a bowel regimen: docusate twice daily and senna twice daily while you’re taking oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back like this, do I come straight to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe worsening pain, vomiting blood, black stools, fainting, fever, or you can’t keep feeds going, you should seek urgent care. For milder symptoms, call your GI team promptly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what exactly happened in the scope? The nurse said something about a pigmented spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw a marginal ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with a pigmented lesion—an area that can indicate recent bleeding risk—and they cauterized it to reduce the chance of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my tube site—there’s always that granulation tissue and oozing. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw granulation tissue around the G-tube site, similar to before. We didn’t see signs of an acute infection. Keep your usual site care, and if you notice increasing redness, pus, fever, or worsening pain at the site, let your outpatient team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review the discharge plan: home today, continue continuous NutriHep tube feeds, start pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, take sucralfate slurry by mouth four times daily, and follow up with GI in 8 weeks for repeat EGD. You’ll have oxycodone as needed for a few days plus stool softeners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds—rifaximin, ursodiol, fluoxetine, lorazepam, zolpidem, aripiprazole, atenolol—those stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your home regimen, and adding the ulcer medications. Use ondansetron as needed for nausea. If any medication causes new symptoms, call your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m relieved it wasn’t something surgical. I’ll set up the GI appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll send you with written instructions and the prescriptions. Please come back if you have any warning signs, and we’ll see you through GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you. I understand you’re here with epigastric abdominal pain and nausea/vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started again about four days ago. It feels like the ulcer pain I had last time—burning right in the middle. I’ve been nauseated and threw up dark yellow stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever or chills? Any blood in vomit, black stools, or new diarrhea or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No blood. No black stools. I’m passing gas and had a bowel movement today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Are you taking your ulcer medications—acid suppression and sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve been taking pantoprazole and sucralfate like I’m supposed to. They switched me to liquid omeprazole because they thought I wasn’t absorbing the pantoprazole. I started that yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your bypass and absorption issues. We’ll treat this like a flare of the marginal ulcer, but we also want to make sure there’s no perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think it could be a hole again? I’m scared of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now your vitals are stable and your labs don’t show a high white blood cell count, which is reassuring. We’re getting X-rays to look for free air, which would suggest a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also noticed more drainage around my G-tube this morning. It’s not red, but it’s wet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We’ll examine the site and keep an eye on it. If there’s no redness, increasing pain, or fever, it’s often irritation or leakage, but we’ll make sure it looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I staying NPO again? I can’t really eat anyway because of the low sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—nothing by mouth for now. We’ll continue your continuous tube feeds once we’ve ruled out anything dangerous on imaging. We’ll also give IV fluids and IV acid suppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is pretty bad. What can I get for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give IV pain medication and anti-nausea medication now, and start IV pantoprazole to calm the ulcer irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back—no free air under the diaphragm and no acute lung issues. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This makes a perforation much less likely. We’re also doing abdominal X-rays to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is a little better after the meds, but I still feel that burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common early on. The IV pantoprazole can take some time to fully help. We’ll keep you comfortable and reassess frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I checked your labs: white blood cell count is normal, kidney function looks good, electrolytes are okay, and your lactate is normal. Those are all reassuring signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean it’s definitely the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It points toward an ulcer flare being the most likely cause, especially with your history and similar symptoms. Imaging helps us rule out emergencies like perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep my tube feeds running? I’m worried about my blood sugar dropping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once the abdominal X-ray confirms no free air, we’ll resume your continuous tube feeds. We’ll also monitor your blood sugars while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back—no obstruction and no free air. It does show a mild to moderate stool burden, but nothing surgical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can restart the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll restart your continuous tube feeds and keep you NPO by mouth. We’ll continue IV pantoprazole and your sucralfate through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the drainage around the tube—could it be infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now the skin doesn’t look red or swollen, and you don’t have fever. We’ll keep it clean and dry and watch for changes. If it becomes painful, red, or foul-smelling, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting or dry heaving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. I still feel queasy sometimes, but it’s better. The pain is less sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your tube feeds are running okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m tolerating them. No cramping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep the IV pantoprazole today and continue pain control as needed. We’ll also keep checking your blood sugars—so far they’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why do I keep getting these ulcers? I’m doing what I’m told.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Marginal ulcers can recur after Roux-en-Y because the connection between the stomach pouch and small intestine is sensitive to acid and irritation. Even with good medication use, some people are prone to them, and absorption can be tricky after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the liquid medicine is better for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often, yes—liquid or dissolvable forms can be absorbed more reliably in some patients after bypass. We’ll make sure your discharge plan uses a form you can take consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about taking too much pain medicine. I don’t want to be constipated or out of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good concern. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and pair it with a bowel regimen like docusate and senna if needed. We’ll also avoid anything that could worsen the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This evening, since you’re stable and not vomiting, we’ll start planning to transition you off IV medications when appropriate. For now, we’ll keep the IV pantoprazole going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I might go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your pain stays controlled, you tolerate tube feeds, and there’s no vomiting, discharge in the next day or two is possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your abdominal pain today compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. It’s still there, but not constant. I haven’t thrown up since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s what we hoped to see with IV acid suppression. We’ll keep you on continuous tube feeds and NPO by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least sip water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to stick with nothing by mouth because that’s been safest for your hypoglycemia management and to avoid irritating the ulcer. You’ll continue water flushes through the tube every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site is still leaking a little. Is that going to keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A small amount of drainage can happen. As long as the skin stays healthy—no spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain, or fever—we manage it with local care. If it worsens at home, you should call the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’ve been stable—no low blood sugars, tube feeds tolerated, and pain improved. Today we’ll focus on getting you ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will I be taking at home for the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue sucralfate four times a day through the tube, and we’ll send you home on an acid-suppressing medicine that’s easier to absorb—lansoprazole in an orally disintegrating form.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not the pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we used IV pantoprazole because it works well and bypasses absorption issues. For home, we’re choosing a formulation that should work better for you without needing an IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scope like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not during this admission. Since you improved with medication and there were no signs of bleeding or perforation, we’re treating it medically and having you follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also sending a bowel regimen home—docusate, and senna or bisacodyl as needed—because pain medication can cause constipation and your X-ray showed some stool burden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What pain medicine am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe hydromorphone to use only as needed for pain, with instructions not to drive or drink alcohol while taking it. The goal is to taper off as your ulcer pain settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Any nausea or vomiting since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I feel a lot better. I’m just nervous it’ll come right back when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The key is staying consistent with the acid suppression and sucralfate, keeping tube feeds continuous as prescribed, and staying NPO by mouth as you’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for severe or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, fever, or if the tube site becomes very red, painful, or starts draining pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to discharge you today. You’re stable, walking independently, tolerating continuous tube feeds, and your symptoms improved with IV antacid therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over the plan one more time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sure: continue continuous tube feeds and remain nothing by mouth; take lansoprazole daily and sucralfate four times daily; use hydromorphone only as needed for pain; use docusate and senna/bisacodyl as needed for constipation; and follow up with your surgeons in clinic as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you. I’ll keep an eye on the tube site and stick to the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you came in for worsening left upper abdominal pain near your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same pain I’ve had for months, but the last two weeks it’s been getting worse. Tonight it got unbearable. It’s right here by the tube and it shoots to my left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it tied to your tube feeds—like it flares when the feeds are running? Any vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, or blood in stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It gets worse when the feeds are going in. I’ve been dry heaving sometimes, but no real vomiting. No fever, no diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. In the emergency department your vitals were stable, and your bloodwork—CBC, electrolytes, and lipase—looked normal. We also got a chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm, and it did not show any free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—based on your exam and that X-ray, we don’t see signs of a perforation. Your belly exam is reassuring too—no guarding or rebound, and the tube site doesn’t look infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much? I’m scared something is wrong with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, the bariatric surgery team thinks this is most likely pain from your known marginal ulcer, and possibly irritation around the tube site—especially if it’s been manipulated a lot. They don’t recommend more imaging or any surgical intervention tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’re not going to do anything? I can’t live like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are going to treat your pain and keep you safe. You got IV Dilaudid in the ED and it helped. Our plan is to control pain here, keep your ulcer medicines going—lansoprazole dissolvable and sucralfate through the tube—and restart your continuous tube feeds as you can tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My feeds were off because it hurt too much. I’m worried my sugar will crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real concern with your post-bypass hypoglycemia. In the ED you were supported with dextrose fluids while feeds were off. Now that you’re here, we’ll restart your continuous tube feeds and monitor your glucose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But what if the tube is infected? It feels sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam there’s no redness, warmth, drainage that looks infected, or swelling around the tube. Your white blood cell count is normal as well. We’ll keep checking it, but right now there’s no evidence of infection causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how is your pain after the medication? Any new nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better than when I came in. Still there, but not as sharp. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your morning labs look stable—blood counts and electrolytes are in a good range, and your glucose this morning was normal. How did you do overnight with the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They restarted them and I didn’t have a low sugar episode. The pain still flares when it runs, but it’s manageable with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we’re seeing. Since there’s no sign of obstruction or infection and surgery doesn’t think more testing is needed right now, the focus is symptom control and continuing ulcer treatment. You still have the plan for an EGD at the end of the month, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled. Will that actually help figure this out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. The scope lets your team directly look at the gastrojejunal area and assess the marginal ulcer. In the meantime, staying consistent with lansoprazole and sucralfate is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What am I going home with for pain? The pills don’t always absorb right with my bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you with liquid oxycodone to use as needed for pain, which can be given through the G-tube. We also want you to follow up with a pain management clinic to talk about longer-term strategies, since this has been going on for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about taking opioids. And I’m already on lorazepam and Ambien.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important point. Use the oxycodone only as prescribed and only when you need it. Because sedating medicines can add up, avoid extra doses of lorazepam or Ambien beyond what you normally take, and don’t drive or do anything risky while you’re using the oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review: continue your continuous tube feeds to prevent hypoglycemia, keep taking lansoprazole and sucralfate for the marginal ulcer, and watch the tube site for redness, swelling, pus-like drainage, fever, or worsening pain. If any of those happen, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep the feeds running and take the ulcer meds. I’ll follow up with pain clinic and keep my scope appointment. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the doctor on the medicine team. I hear you came in with severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same deep pain right under the tube and in the middle of my upper belly, but it got way worse after they changed the tube in clinic yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it mostly at the skin, or does it feel deeper—like inside the abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Deeper. The skin is sore, but the worst is deep. I feel nauseated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, chills, or sweats?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just nausea. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How have your tube feeds been going—any trouble running them, or does the pain change when feeds are going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need them constantly or my sugar drops. The pain is just there all the time, but it’s worse since the exchange.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I also see you were recently discharged for similar pain and were supposed to use liquid oxycodone. Were you able to get it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I couldn’t find the liquid anywhere, so I’ve been crushing pills and putting them through the tube. I don’t think it’s working right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense—crushing can change how it absorbs and can irritate the tube. In the ED your labs looked okay, and the chest X-ray didn’t show free air, which is reassuring. Surgery saw some irritation at the site and recommended admission for pain control and to make sure there’s no deeper problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s in the wrong place again. That happened before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, that’s a very reasonable concern. The next step is a CT scan of your abdomen with contrast to confirm the tube position and look for bleeding, a collection, or an abscess around the tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT hurt? And can I keep my feeds running? I don’t want my sugar to crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT itself shouldn’t be painful—just lying still. We may pause feeds briefly for the scan, but we’ll monitor your fingerstick glucose and keep you safe. We’ll check sugars every six hours while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is really bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain. We’ll use liquid oxycodone here so it’s easier on the tube, and we’ll also use acetaminophen as a baseline. We’ll avoid NSAIDs because of your marginal ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this from the ulcer again? It feels like it’s right at the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be a mix. The tenderness is at the tube site, but you also describe epigastric pain, and you have a known chronic marginal ulcer. Frequent manipulation of the tube can also irritate the tract and the abdominal wall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to examine the site now. I see a small amount of whitish drainage and some focal redness, but no spreading redness or warmth. Your vitals are stable and your white blood cell count is normal, which makes a serious infection less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So do I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, without fever, spreading redness, or a high white count, we’re not seeing signs of a deeper infection. We’ll keep the area clean and continue the topical ointment you use, and the CT will help us confirm there’s no abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is still there. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we can give medication for nausea as needed. Also, we’ll continue your ulcer medicines—lansoprazole and sucralfate—through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: surgery reviewed you again this morning. We’re proceeding with the CT abdomen with contrast today to check tube position and look for any complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the CT is normal, what then? I can’t keep coming back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s normal, we focus on symptom control and preventing hypoglycemia, and we coordinate follow-up with your primary doctor and your surgeons. We also want to be careful with opioids—sometimes with chronic use, pain can actually become more sensitive, so we’ll aim for the lowest effective dose and a plan for outpatient management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They restarted my tube feeds, right? I feel shaky when they stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your continuous tube feeds are running. We’ll keep checking fingersticks and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT is back. The G-tube balloon is in the stomach where it should be. There are some inflammatory changes in the abdominal wall muscle where the tube goes in, but there’s no hematoma, no abscess, and no discrete fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not misplaced and it’s not an abscess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no misplacement and no abscess seen. That supports the idea that this is irritation/inflammation at the tract plus your chronic ulcer-related pain, rather than a dangerous complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can be severe even without a collection—especially when the abdominal wall is inflamed and when there’s chronic pain in the background. The recent tube exchange can flare things up. Our goal is to get you comfortable enough to go home safely while keeping your sugars stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helps some, but I’m worried I’ll run out again or not find the liquid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe tablets you can take by mouth as directed, and we’ll make sure you have a clear plan for refills through bariatric surgery and pain management rather than the emergency room. We’ll also add acetaminophen to reduce how much opioid you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is still there but not as sharp as yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your sugars have been stable on the continuous feeds. We’ll keep your ulcer medications going and continue to avoid NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little lightheaded when I stand up. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the pain meds, but your blood pressure has also been running low. I see you’re on atenolol at home. Did you take it recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took it like I always do. Sometimes my pressure is low and I skip it, but I didn’t this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
