conversation_lines.text: We think the atenolol is contributing to the low blood pressure, especially if you’re a bit dry from not feeling well. You’re not having chest pain or shortness of breath, and your heart rhythm looks like normal sinus rhythm. We’re going to stop the atenolol here and give you IV fluids to bring the pressure up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to just stop it? I thought you can’t stop those suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In your case, given the low pressures, it’s safer to hold it. We’ll monitor you closely. Also, beta blockers like atenolol can mask symptoms of low blood sugar, which is a concern for you since you’re at risk of hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pressure feels better after the fluids. Does that mean I shouldn’t take atenolol anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend not restarting it for now. We’ll document that clearly and ask you to follow up with your primary care doctor to reassess your blood pressure plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site still looks a little red. Should I be worried about MRSA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your history of MRSA is important, but right now we’re not seeing signs of a spreading infection—no fever, no worsening redness, and the CT didn’t show an abscess. Keep using the mupirocin as prescribed and watch for warning signs like increasing redness, warmth, pus, fever, or feeling ill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your pain seems improved compared with admission. If you feel comfortable with the plan, we can discharge you today with medications and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home and the pain coming back. What do I do if it spikes again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as prescribed for breakthrough pain and acetaminophen as directed. Keep your ulcer medications—lansoprazole and sucralfate—consistent. Avoid NSAIDs. If you develop fever, vomiting that won’t stop, worsening redness around the tube, or severe worsening pain that feels different, you should seek urgent care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still supposed to get that scope for the ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—there’s a plan for an EGD at the end of the month per prior notes. That’s important to reassess the marginal ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tube feeds—no changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes today. Continue your continuous tube feeds as you’ve been doing to prevent hypoglycemia, and keep checking your sugars as you normally do. We monitored fingersticks here and they stayed stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How much oxycodone are you sending me with? I don’t want to be stuck without it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re providing a two-week supply: oxycodone 10 mg, one tablet every 4 hours as needed, total 84 tablets. After that, ongoing prescriptions should come from bariatric surgery and/or pain management, not the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And just to confirm—no more atenolol at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—do not restart atenolol. Your blood pressures were low here, and it can also hide low blood sugar symptoms. Please follow up with your primary care doctor soon after discharge to review blood pressure management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re stable, walking independently, and your pain is improved. You’ll go home on your home meds, continue tube feeds, continue lansoprazole and sucralfate, and use oxycodone and acetaminophen for pain. Follow up with your PCP and your surgeon. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that covers it. I just hope it settles down. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the bariatric surgery team. I hear you’re back because of severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been happening since you went home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It never really got better. The pain around the tube keeps getting worse, and today it was so bad I couldn’t make it to clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Any fevers or chills? Any change in how the skin looks around the tube—more redness, swelling, or drainage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. It looks the same to me. It just hurts a lot, like deep and sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still tolerating your tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been running them continuously—about 40 an hour. I’m always nauseated, but that’s not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You were seen in the pain clinic yesterday, and they thought the pain might be from inflammation or a reaction around the tube, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They said maybe it needs to be removed or replaced. But they didn’t change my meds, and the oxycodone isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’re going to focus on two things tonight: making sure there’s no infection or collection around the tube, and getting your pain under control. Your last CT showed inflammation around the tube but no abscess or hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected? Why does it hurt this much then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even without infection, the tissue and muscle around the tube can get inflamed and very sensitive—especially if it’s been irritated repeatedly. That can cause severe pain. We’ll examine the site closely and monitor you for any signs of infection while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the ED we can try a steroid medication through the G-tube to see if it calms the inflammation locally. It doesn’t always work, but it’s a reasonable first step. Are you okay with us trying that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll try anything. I just can’t go home like this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the steroid trial through the tube. How does the pain feel now—any change at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a tiny bit, but honestly it still really hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given that minimal response, we’re going to admit you overnight to manage the pain and nutrition safely. We’ll start with oral pain medication and adjust to what works best for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean surgery? Are you taking the tube out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgery is planned during this admission. Tonight the goal is symptom control and making sure your feeds and blood sugars are stable. Decisions about removing or replacing the tube are best made with your surgeon in follow-up, unless something urgent comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: we gave you oxycodone, but you’re still uncomfortable. We’d like to switch to oral hydromorphone—Dilaudid—because some patients get better relief with it. Does that sound okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m nervous about strong meds, but I need something that works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely reasonable. We’ll use the lowest effective dose, keep it as-needed, and also keep you on your bowel regimen to prevent constipation. And no driving or operating machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after switching to Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. It’s not gone, but it’s finally manageable. I slept a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it helped. From our exams, the tube site looks stable—tender, but no signs of spreading redness or drainage, and you’ve had no fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tried changing your feeding schedule to bolus feeds to see if that would be easier at home. Unfortunately, your blood sugar dropped after each bolus, which fits with your post-bypass hypoglycemia history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I was afraid of. I felt shaky and sweaty. So I can’t do bolus at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. For safety, we’re switching you back to continuous tube feeds. We’ll send you home on NutriHep at 50 cc per hour, and you should keep checking your blood sugars like you’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home? I’m worried I’ll miss something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call right away for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, worsening redness or drainage at the tube site, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, black or bloody stools or vomit, chest pain, shortness of breath, or if the pain is getting worse or changing location.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid—how long will I have it? I don’t want to run out and end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you with a short course: hydromorphone 2 mg tablets to take by mouth every 4 hours as needed for pain, with a limited quantity. The plan is for you to follow up with your surgeon and your pain team to decide next steps for the tube and longer-term pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep all my other meds the same? The anxiety meds and everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications as before, including your fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and lorazepam, plus your ulcer protection meds like lansoprazole and sucralfate. Just be careful because lorazepam and Dilaudid together can make you extra sleepy—take them only as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re afebrile, your vitals are stable, you’re walking independently, and your pain is controlled on the oral regimen. We’ll discharge you home on continuous tube feeds at 50 cc/hr and the as-needed Dilaudid. Do you feel comfortable with the plan and the return precautions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still worried about the tube pain coming back, but I understand the plan and I’ll follow up with my surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you came in with sharp pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me when it started getting worse today and what it feels like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It got really bad this morning. It’s a sharp, stabbing pain right around the tube. I ran out of my oxycodone, and Tylenol isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea or vomiting? Fevers or chills? Any trouble running your tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting, no fever or chills. Feeds are running fine. It just hurts so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I examined the site—it's clean and dry, and I don’t see redness, swelling, or drainage. Your vital signs look stable. We’ll check labs and urine to make sure there’s no infection or bleeding, but right now this looks like pain without signs of an acute complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it keep happening if everything looks normal? I feel like no one can tell me what’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. You’ve had similar episodes before, and prior imaging showed nonspecific inflammation but no abscess or hematoma, and even exchanging the tube didn’t relieve it. Sometimes the tissues around the tract can stay irritated or sensitive even when there’s no infection. Tonight our goal is to get your pain controlled safely and make sure nothing new is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need another CT scan or another tube change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not automatically. Since you don’t have fever, vomiting, or changes at the site, and your exam is reassuring, we’ll start with labs and close monitoring. If anything changes—worsening pain, new tenderness, fever—then we’d reconsider imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now we’re going to admit you overnight for pain control. We’ll start with oral oxycodone, and if you need it, we can give a small amount of IV hydromorphone for breakthrough pain, then taper off the IV as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about my blood sugars if I’m here. I get low if my feeds stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll keep you NPO by mouth but continue your continuous tube feeds, and we’ll monitor your blood sugars while you’re here. When you go home, you’ll go back to your usual continuous regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain medicine helps, but it comes back fast. Is it okay to take this much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use the lowest dose that keeps you comfortable and safe. We’re also watching your breathing and blood pressure. As soon as we can, we’ll rely on oral medication only so you can go home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning update: your labs look okay—white count and blood counts are normal, kidney function is normal, and your urine test doesn’t show infection. No fevers overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected. Why does it still hurt this badly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can still be real and severe even without infection—especially with a long-standing tube tract and prior surgeries. The good news is we’re not seeing warning signs like infection or bleeding. The plan today is to keep feeds running, get you walking a bit, and transition off IV pain medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat anything? Or do I have to stay completely NPO?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now we’re keeping you NPO by mouth while we focus on tube feeds and symptom control. We’ll reassess later today, but the priority is maintaining steady nutrition and avoiding anything that might worsen symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your enteral nutrition through the tube as planned. How are your blood sugars and pain right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sugars have been okay. Pain is better than last night, but I’m nervous it’ll spike again when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Before discharge, we want your pain manageable on oral meds alone. We’ll stop the IV hydromorphone and make sure you can control symptoms with oral oxycodone as needed, plus your usual home medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it gets worse at home, how do I know when it’s serious enough to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call right away if you get fever over 101.5, shaking chills, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, new redness or drainage at the tube site, black or bloody stools or vomit, chest pain or shortness of breath, or if the pain is getting worse or changing location. Also come in if you feel dizzy or dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable, walking, and your pain is controlled on oral medication. We’re planning discharge home today. You’ll resume your home continuous tube feeds—NutriHep at 50 cc per hour—and keep checking your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What am I going home with for pain? I don’t want to run out again and end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with oxycodone 10 mg to take every 4 hours as needed for pain, and you’ll also continue your home hydromorphone as prescribed for breakthrough if that’s part of your regimen. Don’t drive or drink alcohol while taking these. Keep using your bowel regimen medicines as needed for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll follow up with my surgeon. I just hope this stops happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you’re here for severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same pain again, but worse. I ran out of my oxycodone at home and Tylenol isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this again. Any fever or chills? Any redness, drainage, or swelling around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. The site looks the same to me—no pus or anything. It just hurts so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea or vomiting? Are you able to keep down water? And are you still tolerating your tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I can drink water. The feeds go in, but they irritate the area and make it ache more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you passing gas and having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m going to examine the tube site now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The site looks clean—no redness or induration—and your belly is soft. It’s tender right at the tube, like you said. Your vital signs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt this bad if it looks normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the frustrating part—pain can be severe even without an obvious infection or abscess. In the past, your CT scans showed nonspecific inflammation around the tube but no collection, and the tube exchange didn’t fix it. Tonight we’ll focus on getting your pain controlled safely and watching closely for any signs of infection or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried Naproxen because it actually helped, but then I was told to stop. Is it really that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—because of your gastric bypass history and prior marginal ulcer, NSAIDs like naproxen and aspirin can greatly increase the risk of another ulcer and bleeding. I want you to avoid them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what am I supposed to do when the oxycodone runs out? I can’t live like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. For tonight, we’ll restart oral oxycodone and, if needed, use a small amount of IV hydromorphone for breakthrough pain while you’re here. The goal is to get you comfortable and then transition back to oral-only before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do another CT scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, since you don’t have fever, vomiting, or a change in the appearance of the site, and your exam is reassuring, we may not need repeat imaging tonight. We’ll check labs and keep reassessing—if anything changes, we’ll escalate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want anyone to think I’m making it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you’re in real pain. Our job is to treat it and also keep you safe—especially with your history of ulcers and the tube dependence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs are back and look reassuring—blood counts and chemistries are stable, and there’s nothing suggesting infection or pancreatitis. We’ll continue to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s no sign of infection right now—no fever, no redness, and your labs don’t show a concerning pattern. We’ll keep watching your temperature and the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep my tube feeds running? I’m scared my sugar will drop if I stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your home continuous tube feeds and monitor your intake and output. And keep checking your blood sugars like you do at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The feeds make the area sting. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some irritation can happen, especially if the area is already inflamed or sensitive. Since the skin looks okay, we’ll focus on pain control and make sure the tube isn’t causing skin breakdown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helped some, but it’s still breaking through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We can give a dose of IV hydromorphone for breakthrough pain now, but we’ll keep it limited and work toward stopping IV meds by later today so you can go home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be stuck here, I just need it controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our plan—short stay for symptom control, then discharge once you’re stable on oral medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the rest of the night after the breakthrough dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept a little. The pain is still there, but it’s not as unbearable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Today we’ll continue oral oxycodone as needed and stop the IV hydromorphone so we can make sure the oral regimen is enough for you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’ll spike again once the IV is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it spikes, tell us right away—we’ll reassess. But we want to avoid IV opioids unless absolutely necessary, because they make discharge harder and can cause side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can drink water like you’ve been doing. Your nutrition is primarily through the continuous tube feeds, and we’ll keep that running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to review safety steps while you’re here: we’ll use the leg compression devices and give you heparin shots to prevent blood clots, and we’ll encourage you to walk in the hallway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heparin shots again? Do I really need them for just a short stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—any hospitalization increases clot risk, even short ones. The dose is preventive and we’ll also get you up walking as much as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure is always low. Is that a problem with the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Your pressures have been in your usual range and you’re alert, breathing well, and not dizzy. We’ll keep monitoring, especially with opioids on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain this afternoon on oral medication only?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. Still sore at the tube, but I can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any new symptoms—fever, nausea, vomiting, or change at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. It looks the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the long-term plan? I keep ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already in the middle of a longer work-up to find a solution. You have upcoming appointments for a second opinion with a bariatric surgeon, follow-up with Dr. ___, and a visit at the Pancreas and Liver Institute to discuss options including pancreatectomy for the hypoglycemia issues. Our role this admission is symptom control and making sure nothing dangerous is developing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreatectomy sounds extreme. Is that really on the table?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a specialized discussion and not a decision made during this short admission. The institute visit is to review your case and talk through risks, benefits, and alternatives. For now, we’re keeping your tube feeds steady and your sugars monitored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been afebrile and stable overnight. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but controlled with the oxycodone. I’m nervous about going home and running out again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you with a prescription for oxycodone 10 mg to take every four hours as needed for pain, with no refills. We’ll also review how to take it safely and when to call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No refills—so what if the pain comes back before my appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your pain isn’t improving, is getting worse, or changes in character or location, you should call your surgeon’s office or come back to the ED—especially if there are red flags like fever, vomiting, black stools, or blood. We also want to avoid you using NSAIDs because of ulcer risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what to watch for with ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—vomiting blood or dark material, black or tarry stools, worsening abdominal pain, dizziness or fainting, or feeling very weak. If any of those happen, come in right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about infection at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Look for new redness spreading around the tube, warmth, swelling, pus-like drainage, worsening tenderness, or fever over 101.5°F. If you notice those, call or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your feeds, resume your home continuous regimen—NutriHep at 45 cc per hour—and keep monitoring your blood sugars at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I can do that. Can I drive myself home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not if you’ve taken oxycodone today. Avoid driving or operating machinery while on it. Please arrange a ride.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also continue your usual medications—like lansoprazole and sucralfate for ulcer protection, and your other home meds. Any questions about your medication list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—no naproxen, no aspirin, no NSAIDs at all, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless a doctor specifically tells you otherwise, because of your marginal ulcer risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, I want to make sure you’re walking okay, urinating normally, and tolerating your tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been up walking, I’m peeing fine, and the feeds are running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll discharge you home today. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ as scheduled. If anything changes—fever, vomiting, dehydration, bleeding, chest pain, or worsening pain—call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m still scared this will keep happening, but I understand the plan and the warning signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain. Can you tell me where it hurts most right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started around my G-tube like usual, but now it’s more up here—epigastric and right upper side. It feels like when I had an ulcer before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any vomiting, black stools, or blood when you spit up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No vomiting. I’m just nauseated and it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been able to keep your tube feeds running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continuous at about 40 mL an hour. No diarrhea. But it’s leaking around the tube a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Any fevers, chills, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: What have you taken for pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tylenol, but it barely touched it. I ran out of oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of marginal ulcers after the Roux-en-Y, we want to be careful and avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen, and aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’m allergic anyway, and I’m scared to take anything that could make an ulcer worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. On exam your belly is soft, but you’re tender where you describe. Your G-tube site doesn’t look infected—no redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much? And why the right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right upper pain can come from the gallbladder, liver area, or stomach/ulcer pain that radiates. In the ED you had a right upper quadrant ultrasound, and it did not show gallstones or gallbladder infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no evidence of cholecystitis or stones on the ultrasound. Your labs also don’t suggest pancreatitis; the lipase was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then you think it’s the ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading concern—recurrence of a marginal ulcer. The plan is bowel rest for now, IV fluids, and strong acid suppression with IV pantoprazole. We’ll watch your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can’t have anything by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight, we’ll keep you on bowel rest except small sips of water if you’re not nauseated. We’ll continue your tube feeds as tolerated since you rely on them, and we’ll monitor your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about hypoglycemia if feeds stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep the feeds running and adjust if needed. If you can’t tolerate them, we’ll support you with IV fluids and close glucose checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the leaking around the tube? It’s messy and burns my skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have nursing help with dressing changes and skin protection. Since you already have revisional G-tube surgery scheduled, we’ll focus on keeping the site clean and watching for increased redness, pain, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you move the surgery up? I’m so tired of coming back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I can’t promise we can move it sooner, but we’ll communicate with your surgeon’s office and make sure the plan is on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also really anxious. Every time it hurts like this I think something is tearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Right now your vital signs are stable, you’re not having bleeding symptoms, and your exam doesn’t show signs of a surgical emergency like guarding or rebound. We’ll keep reassessing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get pain medicine? Tylenol isn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll use acetaminophen and can use opioid pain medication as needed while we treat the underlying irritation. We’ll aim to keep it safe and transition to oral-only as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your blood work is overall reassuring. Your white count was a bit higher on one draw, but you’re afebrile and stable, so we’ll continue observation and ulcer treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about that lactate number they mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One lactate value was elevated, but another was normal earlier. Given your stable exam and vitals, we’re not seeing signs of poor blood flow to the gut. We’ll keep monitoring and repeat labs if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgery planned. This looks most consistent with ulcer-related pain, and we’re treating it medically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is still there but not as sharp. The burning is a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’re continuing the IV pantoprazole. Today we’re also adding sucralfate, which coats the ulcer area and helps it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is sucralfate like an antacid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Different—pantoprazole reduces acid production. Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over irritated lining. Together they often help symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink anything besides water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, water by mouth only. Your nutrition will come through the G-tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m scared to go home and have it flare again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have a clear plan: continue acid suppression at home and take sucralfate four times a day. And we’ll review warning signs that should bring you back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Midday check-in: how’s the pain after starting sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s noticeably better. Still sore, but I’m not curled up anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Are you tolerating the tube feeds without nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Same rate. And I’ve been sipping water okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the feeds running and continue the IV medication today. If you keep improving, we can switch you back to your home regimen by discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what I should avoid so I don’t make the ulcer worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—avoid all NSAIDs and aspirin, and also avoid alcohol and tobacco. Those can worsen ulcers and delay healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t smoke or drink. I just want this to stop happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s exhausting. The revisional G-tube surgery you have scheduled should help address the tube-related issues. For the ulcer symptoms, staying consistent with the PPI and sucralfate is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You look more comfortable today. How’s the RUQ/epigastric pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I still feel tender, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ve been stable—no fever, blood pressure and heart rate have been good, and you’re tolerating tube feeds and water. We’re planning discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home on? I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home medications, and specifically for this episode: lansoprazole 30 mg twice daily and sucralfate 1 gram four times daily. For pain: acetaminophen as needed, and a small supply of oxycodone liquid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about running out again and ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe it with no refills, but we’ll also emphasize using it only when needed and leaning on the ulcer treatment to prevent the pain from escalating. If pain is not controlled despite the plan, call your surgeon rather than waiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my tube feeds at home—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At discharge: water by mouth only, and NutriHep at 50 mL per hour continuously through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leaking? When should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor the site for increased redness, worsening pain, or drainage that’s foul-smelling or unusual in color. If you see that, or you develop fever over 101.5, severe abdominal pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe nausea/vomiting, bloating, or you can’t tolerate feeds or water—call your surgeon or come to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also take meds for anxiety and depression—those stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and lorazepam as prescribed, and zolpidem at night if needed. If anxiety spikes because of pain, let us know—sometimes adjusting the medical plan helps more than adding sedating meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, any last questions about the diagnosis or why we treated it this way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to be clear—since the ultrasound was normal, you’re confident it wasn’t my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. The ultrasound showed no stones and no signs of gallbladder inflammation. Your improvement with IV acid suppression and sucralfate also supports ulcer irritation as the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m nervous but relieved it’s better. I’ll stick to the meds and the tube feed plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right approach. We’ll discharge you home now, and you’ll follow up with your surgeon as planned for the upcoming G-tube revision. Please don’t hesitate to call if symptoms return or worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I want to check in before we head to the operating room. You’re here for the ongoing pain around your G-tube site, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s been awful since it got pulled. It never really settled down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’ve been dealing with that. The plan today is to remove the current tube and place a new gastrostomy tube in a better position—an open replacement—so it’s not constantly tugging and irritating the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re not doing any bypass revision today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We discussed the bigger revisional options, but today we’re focusing on re-siting the G-tube only, as you preferred.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hypoglycemia—will I still be able to do my continuous feeds after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Right after surgery you’ll be NPO at first, then we’ll restart continuous tube feeds through the new tube and work back up to your home rate as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about pain control. The site pain is already bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Immediately after surgery we’ll use a PCA pump so you can control doses safely, and then we’ll transition to pain medication given through the G-tube once things are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. Please don’t give me those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs. We’ll use other options like acetaminophen and opioid medication as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What should I watch for after surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll review everything again, but key things are fever, worsening abdominal pain, redness or foul drainage from the incision, severe nausea or vomiting, or trouble with the tube. We’ll keep a close eye while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the OR and in recovery now. The open G-tube replacement is done, and there were no problems during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts. I feel sore all over my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected right after an open procedure. Your PCA is set up—use it when you need it, and we’ll keep checking your comfort and breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the new tube working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s in place and functioning. The dressing is clean and dry right now. We’ll keep you NPO for the moment and let things settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Evening check-in. How’s your pain with the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than earlier, but I’m still pretty uncomfortable when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Movement will be sore at first. We’ll also have you do incentive spirometry—deep breathing—to keep your lungs clear, and we’ll help you get up to walk as soon as it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Walking already? I just had surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Short, assisted walks. It lowers the risk of complications like blood clots and helps your bowels wake up. You’ll also have compression boots and we’re giving preventive heparin shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about infection. I’ve had MRSA before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re screening you during this admission, and we’re watching the incision closely. Right now you’re afebrile and the site looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight was stable. Any nausea or new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Just sore. When can I start my feeds? I’m scared my sugar will drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to restart continuous tube feeds on post-op day 2. Today we’ll keep you NPO and continue monitoring. If you feel shaky or symptomatic, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least drink something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, just small sips of water as allowed by the team. We’ll advance carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start a low rate of enteral nutrition through the new G-tube today and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt when the feeds start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You may feel some fullness, but it shouldn’t cause sharp pain. If you get worsening abdominal pain, bloating, or nausea, we’ll slow down or pause and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube feels different. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—new tube, new position, and the incision is fresh. What we want is that the pain gradually improves and there’s no spreading redness, pus-like drainage, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my labs okay? And the MRSA test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRSA screen came back negative—no MRSA isolated. Clinically you’re doing well and you’ve stayed afebrile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with the feeds so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So far okay. No vomiting. Pain is still there but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we want. Tonight we’ll keep the rate steady and continue to encourage walking and breathing exercises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Today we’ll increase your tube feeds toward your home rate if you continue tolerating them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My home rate is 65 mL an hour. Are we going back to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the goal—ramp up gradually to 65 mL/hr continuous, as long as your belly exam stays reassuring and you feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I switch off the PCA? It makes me feel foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can transition off the PCA today and move to hydromorphone tablets given through the G-tube as needed, plus scheduled liquid acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement. I’m worried I’ll get backed up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after surgery and with opioid pain meds. We’ll start a stool softener—Colace—twice daily, and we can add a laxative like bisacodyl if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your incision looks clean and dry. Any drainage or increasing redness that you’ve noticed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks okay. It’s just tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tenderness is expected. Keep using the abdominal support when you move, and let us know if pain suddenly worsens or becomes sharp and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re now at your home tube feed rate and tolerating it well. How’s your pain on the oral/G-tube meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better than yesterday. I can walk to the bathroom without help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re ambulating independently, your vitals are stable, and you’ve remained afebrile. We’re starting to plan for discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, water by mouth only. No other oral intake. Continue your continuous tube feeds through the new G-tube at 65 mL/hr.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I take my regular pills at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your home medications, but you must crush all pills and administer them through the G-tube, as you’ve done before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about managing the dressing. I don’t want it to open up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging home nursing visits to help with daily dressing changes. You can shower, but no tub baths or swimming until cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s review activity restrictions: no heavy lifting for 6 weeks, and avoid abdominal exercises. Walking is encouraged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Do not drive or operate machinery while you’re taking hydromorphone. It can make you drowsy and slow your reaction time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—today is discharge day if everything stays on track. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, or worsening belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the usual soreness. I’m nervous about going home though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. The good news is you’re stable, walking on your own, urinating without assistance, tolerating water by mouth and your tube feeds, and your incision looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly should make me call you or go to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or return right away for fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain or pain not relieved by meds, severe nausea/vomiting, severe bloating, inability to take water or run feeds, or foul-smelling or colorful drainage, redness, or swelling around the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And constipation—what do I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take Colace twice daily as needed, and you’ll also have bisacodyl available if constipation persists. Staying mobile helps too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before you leave: you’ll continue tube feeds at 65 mL/hr continuous, water by mouth only, crush and give your home meds through the tube, avoid NSAIDs, and follow the lifting and wound-care instructions. Home nursing will help with daily dressing changes. Do you feel comfortable with the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m relieved the tube pain is finally different, and I understand what to watch for. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me where the pain is and how long it’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s mostly on the right side, and also up in the middle and kind of low, like suprapubic. It’s been about four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How severe was it at its worst, and is anything making it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was really bad at first. It gets better if I just lie still. Moving makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting? Any change from your usual nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I always have some nausea and I take Zofran in the morning. It’s not really worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. With your Roux-en-Y history and the G-tube, we want to make sure there’s no blockage or other complication. For now we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—and give IV fluids. We’ll also pause your tube feeds temporarily while we evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stopping the tube feeds worries me. I get low blood sugar if I don’t have them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important point. We’ll monitor your blood sugar closely while feeds are off, and we’ll restart feeds as soon as it’s safe. The goal is to avoid worsening pain or nausea while we check what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you thinking it’s an obstruction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s on the list of possibilities given your anatomy after bypass, but it’s not the only possibility. We’re going to use labs and imaging to look for signs of obstruction or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What tests are you ordering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check bloodwork—things like blood counts, electrolytes, kidney and liver tests, and lipase. And we’re planning a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for any blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT be through my tube or by mouth? I can’t tolerate much by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can do it without oral contrast. The CT uses IV contrast, and we’ll coordinate the best approach given your tube and your tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My incision still needs packing too. It’s been a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue daily wound care here—packing and dressing changes—and we’ll check the area each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for pain? It’s not as bad as earlier, but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll treat your pain and nausea while we work this up. We’ll avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do my labs show anything scary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far, your labs look reassuring—no big signs of infection, and your kidney function and electrolytes look okay. We’ll keep trending them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I get the CT results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As soon as radiology finalizes the read, I’ll come back and go over it with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have your CT results. The scan shows your Roux-en-Y anatomy and the G-tube in the excluded part of the stomach, and importantly there’s no evidence of small bowel obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no dilated bowel loops and no obstruction seen. The scan also notes your midline incision with packing material, and there isn’t fat stranding around it on CT, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Abdominal pain can still happen even without an obstruction—sometimes from irritation, inflammation that doesn’t show clearly on imaging, or sensitivity around prior surgical sites. The good news is we don’t see an emergency surgical blockage. Our plan is supportive care: rest the gut briefly, control pain and nausea, and then restart feeds slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start my tube feeds tonight? I’m worried about hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart gradually rather than jump to your full home rate. Tonight we’ll keep you on IV fluids and monitor sugars, and we’ll begin a slow feed advancement as your symptoms allow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was your pain overnight? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is better if I don’t move much. Nausea is about the same as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Since the CT didn’t show obstruction and you’re stable, we’ll start tube feeds at a low rate and increase stepwise toward your baseline as long as pain and nausea stay controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the goal rate again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your baseline is 60 mL per hour. We’ll work up to that gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The dressing change hurts. Is the wound infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s uncomfortable. Right now, we’re doing daily packing and dressing changes. The imaging didn’t show concerning changes around the incision, and you don’t have fever or lab signs suggesting infection. We’ll keep checking it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the enteral nutrition infusion today. Let us know right away if the feeds worsen your pain, cause bloating, or increase nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. If I feel crampy, should I stop it myself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t adjust it on your own—call the nurse. We can pause or slow it safely and assess you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tolerating the feeds so far. Still some pain, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll continue to advance the rate slowly. We’ll also keep your nausea controlled with your usual regimen as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in: how are you feeling with the tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The nausea is not worse. Pain is there but not like when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep advancing toward 60 mL/hr. If you stay stable at goal, we can start planning for discharge with home services for wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to drink water by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can allow small sips as tolerated, but the main nutrition will remain through the tube feeds. If anything increases nausea or pain, we’ll scale back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the pain will come back once I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled on a safe home plan, and we’ll give you clear return precautions—like fever, worsening severe pain, vomiting, bloating, or drainage changes from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medicines will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue rifaximin. We’re also planning lansoprazole twice daily and sucralfate for stomach protection, plus docusate to prevent constipation. For pain, hydromorphone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the stomach medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history after bypass and prior ulcer issues, we want to reduce irritation and protect the lining. Lansoprazole reduces acid, and sucralfate coats and protects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m at a higher feed rate now and it’s okay. When do I hit my normal 60?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you continue tolerating it overnight, we should be able to reach 60 mL/hr by tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re at goal tube feeds—60 mL/hr—and your pain and nausea are controlled. That’s what we needed to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge today with home services to help with wound packing and dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for with the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or come back if you get fever over 101.5, redness or swelling around the incision, foul-smelling or colorful drainage, or if the pain suddenly worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I can’t tolerate the feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop severe nausea or vomiting, abdominal bloating, or you can’t keep feeds running, you should call your surgeon’s office right away or return to the emergency department—especially given your risk of hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you review the pain medicine? I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hydromorphone is only as needed for pain, every 4 hours if required. Use the lowest amount that controls your pain. It can cause constipation, so take the docusate, and avoid driving or alcohol while using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—just confirming I shouldn’t take anything like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Stick to the plan we’re prescribing and call if you’re unsure about any over-the-counter medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: your discharge diagnosis is PO intolerance with tube feed adjustment. You came in with abdominal pain and nausea, we ruled out obstruction on CT, rested your gut briefly, then advanced tube feeds back to goal while continuing daily wound care. Do you have any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that makes sense. I’m relieved the CT didn’t show a blockage. I’ll follow the instructions and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I hear you came in feeling dizzy and nauseated. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For about a week I’ve been getting lightheaded when I stand up. Tonight it got worse, and I felt really nauseated and kept dry heaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any actual vomiting? Any blood? And are you able to keep liquids down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting, just wretching. I can sip water. No blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any belly pain, bloating, or trouble passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m passing gas. My belly doesn’t hurt like last time. The only pain is at my incision when I’m retching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any fevers, chills, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I did feel my heart racing earlier, like palpitations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked an EKG—your rhythm looks normal, no concerning changes. We’ll keep an eye on it. How have your tube feeds and oral intake been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been struggling to take much by mouth. I’m mostly on the G-tube feeds, but even then I feel like I’m not getting enough in. I feel dried out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with dehydration. We started IV fluids in the ED—have you noticed any improvement in the dizziness since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little. I’m still scared to stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll recheck your blood pressure and symptoms when you sit and stand, but we’ll do it safely. I also want to ask about your blood sugars—any low readings at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I get hypoglycemic a lot since the bypass, especially when I try to rely on eating instead of the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll monitor your glucose here and make sure you’re not dropping low while you’re not eating much. Your initial labs look reassuring—no elevated white count, kidney function looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you don’t think it’s an obstruction again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now you’re passing gas, your belly exam is soft and not tender, and you’re tolerating liquids. That makes obstruction less likely. If anything changes—worsening pain, vomiting, bloating—we’d reassess quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had diarrhea yesterday, which is weird for me. I’m usually constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for mentioning that. A day of non-bloody diarrhea can contribute to dehydration. We’ll keep replacing fluids and electrolytes and see if it settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart rate is always low. Is that part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pulse is on the low side, but your blood pressure and oxygen level are stable, and the EKG is normal. Dehydration can make you feel lightheaded even if the heart rhythm is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to examine your incision and the open area in the midline wound. Any redness, drainage, or new pain there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No redness. It’s just sore when I retch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam it looks like healthy red granulation tissue and no surrounding redness—good sign. We’ll keep your usual wound care going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to stay in the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the presyncope, nausea, and your history with limited intake, we’d like to admit you for observation overnight—continue IV fluids, monitor glucose, and make sure you can tolerate water without symptoms returning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want this to keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely reasonable. Before discharge we’ll talk through a plan to prevent dehydration—how much fluid you can take by mouth, how to use your tube feeds, and what warning signs mean you should call or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still nauseated. Can I have something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s use ondansetron as needed. It’s on your home list too. We’ll also keep your stomach-protecting meds like lansoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling now after fluids overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Less dizzy. I slept a little. Still a bit queasy but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your morning labs look stable—electrolytes and kidney numbers are okay. We’ll have you sip water and see how you do sitting and standing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood sugar? I’m worried it’ll crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been checking it. It’s been in a safe range here. We’ll keep monitoring while you’re increasing fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When I stood up just now, I didn’t get that blacking-out feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we want to see. Your vitals are stable, and you’re tolerating water. If this continues, we can plan for discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think the nausea is from the bypass? Or bacterial overgrowth like they said last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to pin to one cause in a short stay, but dehydration itself can worsen nausea. You’re already on rifaximin, which is used when bacterial overgrowth is suspected, and we’ll keep that the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s my heart when I feel palpitations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The EKG was reassuring, and you haven’t had chest pain or shortness of breath. Dehydration and low intake can make your heart feel like it’s fluttering. If it becomes persistent, painful, or you pass out, that’s an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any more diarrhea? Any new abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more diarrhea. No new pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll transition off IV fluids as long as you keep drinking. The goal is to make sure you can maintain hydration at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I go home, what should I do if I start feeling dizzy again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, sit or lie down right away to avoid falling. Try small frequent sips of fluid. If you can’t keep fluids down, if you’re having repeated wretching or vomiting, or if you feel like you might pass out, you should call us or come to the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my tube? Could it be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube site looks okay, and you’re not having signs that suggest a tube complication right now. The bigger issue seems to be not getting enough fluids in overall. We’ll make sure you have a clear plan for hydration with your tube feeds and oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How did you do overnight—any dizziness when you got up to the bathroom?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I felt steady. I drank water without gagging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ve been afebrile and stable, and your symptoms have resolved with fluids. From our standpoint, you’re ready for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the diagnosis is just dehydration?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—dehydration causing lightheadedness and nausea. We didn’t find signs of infection or a surgical emergency during observation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep all my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll continue lansoprazole and rifaximin, and your usual medications for mood and anxiety. For nausea, you can use ondansetron as needed. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of psych meds—could they be making me dizzy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some medications can contribute to lightheadedness, but in your case the timing and improvement with IV fluids strongly point to dehydration. If dizziness returns despite good hydration, bring it up with your prescribing doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see my surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have you follow up with Dr. ___ in clinic as scheduled. The appointment details will be in your discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: return right away for fever, worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath, or concerning wound changes. Otherwise, keep up with hydration and your tube-feeding plan, and we’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I understand you’ve had a week of dry heaving and epigastric pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same thing as last week. I keep dry heaving and my upper stomach burns. I’m scared something is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Any actual vomiting, blood, black stools, or fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fever. Mostly just retching and pain right here in the middle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are your G-tube feeds going—are you able to tolerate them? And are you taking your medications through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can do the tube feeds. I’ve been putting my meds through it too. I just feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea recently? And are you able to drink anything by mouth at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really drinking much. No diarrhea right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your Roux-en-Y history and prior ulcer at the gastrojejunal connection, we take this seriously. The good news is your vital signs look stable and you don’t look toxic. We’re going to give IV fluids and nausea and pain medicine, and check labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another CT scan? Last time they said it wasn’t obstructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, based on your exam and how stable you are, we’ll start with labs and symptom control. If anything suggests obstruction or you worsen, we’d escalate. Your prior CT showed no obstruction, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to miss something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep a close eye on you. Also, I see you’re allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—so we’ll avoid those for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can’t take them. They told me it could make ulcers worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll use other options. We’ll also continue your acid suppression—your lansoprazole—and we may add a stomach-coating medicine to help with irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this gastritis? Or is my ulcer back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your symptoms and the initial workup so far, this looks most consistent with gastritis or irritation in the upper stomach area. With your history, an ulcer is always on the list, but you’re not showing signs of bleeding, and your labs will help us assess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried because I get shaky sometimes after bypass. Could this be low sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
