conversation_lines.text: You’ve had post-bypass hypoglycemia before, so we’ll keep an eye on your glucose while you’re here, especially since you haven’t been taking much by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs are back: white blood cell count is normal, kidney function and electrolytes look okay, and your lactate is normal. Lipase is normal too, which argues against pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing scary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing pointing to an emergency like infection or pancreatitis. That supports treating this as gastritis/irritation and dehydration from poor intake and retching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is still there, but the nausea is a little better after the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re going to admit you to the surgical ward for observation, continue IV fluids, keep your PPI going, and give nausea and pain meds as needed. We’ll also give vitamins—thiamine, folate, and a multivitamin—in your fluids since intake has been limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—after bariatric surgery, and especially when intake is poor, vitamin deficiencies can happen. Thiamine is important to protect your nerves and brain when you’ve had prolonged nausea or poor nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in. How are you feeling now—any dry heaving overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept a little. No vomiting. The burning is less, but it comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your urine test was normal and pregnancy test was negative. We also checked B12 and folate—B12 is in a good range and folate is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I restart my tube feeds? I’m afraid it’ll trigger the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your G-tube feeds carefully. The plan is protein formula at full strength, running continuously at 55 mL per hour, and we’ll see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds through the tube are okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your home medications, including lansoprazole and rifaximin, and use ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see your tube feeds have started. Any cramping, worsening nausea, or increased pain since the infusion began?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s actually okay so far. I’m surprised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep the rate steady and monitor. If you feel fullness, worsening pain, or start retching again, tell the nurse right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why does this keep happening? I feel like I’m back here every week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your surgical anatomy and history of a gastrojejunal ulcer, the upper GI tract can be sensitive. Dehydration and irritation can set off nausea and pain. The goal is to keep acid controlled and protect the lining, and make sure you’re getting consistent nutrition and fluids through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything new you’re adding for protection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning to add sucralfate—Carafate—four times a day. It coats irritated areas and can help with gastritis symptoms and ulcer-related irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take that through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can administer it through the G-tube. We’ll also space it from other medications when possible so it doesn’t interfere with absorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Evening update: you’ve stayed afebrile and your blood pressure and heart rate have been stable. How’s your pain now on a 0 to 10 scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a 3 now. Earlier it was a 7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. We’ll keep using nausea medicine as needed and pain medicine if you need it, but we’ll aim for the lowest effective dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like strong pain meds. Will I have to take them at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you need them. We can prescribe a small amount of oxycodone for breakthrough pain, but the main treatment is the PPI and sucralfate, plus staying hydrated and keeping feeds going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Any dry heaving overnight? Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No dry heaving. I feel much better. I’m just tired and want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. You’ve tolerated the G-tube feeds at 55 mL/hour and your symptoms have resolved with fluids, vitamins, PPI, and pain control. If you continue like this, we can discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the diagnosis then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re calling this gastritis—irritation/inflammation of the stomach lining—causing the epigastric pain and dry heaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need antibiotics? I’m on rifaximin already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new antibiotics are needed from this admission. We’ll continue your rifaximin as you were taking it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s go over your discharge medications. You’ll continue lansoprazole 30 mg twice a day, and start sucralfate 1 gram four times a day. You’ll also have ondansetron as needed for nausea, and oxycodone 5 mg, 1 to 2 tablets every 4 hours as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs—so no ibuprofen, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no NSAIDs or aspirin. Those can worsen gastritis and ulcers and you have an allergy listed as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for worsening or persistent abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or inability to tolerate tube feeds, fever, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, dizziness or fainting, or any concern that you’re getting dehydrated again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: discharge home today. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in clinic as scheduled. Keep your tube feeds running as instructed, take the PPI and sucralfate consistently, and use the nausea and pain meds only as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel better knowing the labs were normal and it’s not an obstruction. I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I understand you were sent in from clinic for epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting when you try to take anything by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Even sips make me gag and throw up. It feels like last week all over again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this again. We’ll focus on getting you rehydrated and controlling the nausea and pain. Are you able to tolerate your tube feeds through the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube feeds are okay. It’s just anything by mouth that sets it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ll continue your tube feeds and give IV fluids tonight since you’ve been losing fluids from vomiting and not drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think it’s an obstruction? I’m scared something is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what we know so far, obstruction is less likely—your prior CT showed no evidence of obstruction. Right now your symptoms fit more with irritation or inflammation in the upper stomach area, like gastritis, or issues around the connection from your bypass. We’ll keep a close eye on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It burns right here in the middle. And I’m so nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start anti-nausea medication and keep your acid suppression going—your lansoprazole twice a day. We’ll also check labs to make sure your electrolytes and kidney function look okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I still take my meds through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your home medications through the G-tube as you’ve been doing, including your nausea medicine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. Please don’t give me those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—thank you for reminding me. We’ll avoid NSAIDs and aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: we’ve started IV fluids. How’s your pain right now on a 0 to 10 scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 7. It comes in waves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We can use your prescribed hydromorphone as needed for pain, and ondansetron for nausea. Our goal is to get you comfortable without over-sedating you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also really anxious. I keep thinking something is wrong with the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll keep you updated step by step. We’ll also continue your lorazepam as prescribed, and we can talk through what we’re seeing as results come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork is back. White blood cell count is normal, and your electrolytes and kidney function look reassuring. That supports dehydration and irritation rather than a severe infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much if the labs are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can be significant even when labs are normal—especially with gastritis or irritation near the gastrojejunal connection after bypass. Labs help us rule out some dangerous causes, but they don’t measure irritation directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do a scope now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not tonight. Given you’re stable and your labs are okay, the plan is supportive care in the hospital and then GI will arrange an outpatient upper endoscopy to look for causes like inflammation or ulcer changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Outpatient? I’m worried I’ll just come right back again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The reason outpatient is reasonable is that you’re tolerating tube feeds, we can get you hydrated and controlled here, and the endoscopy can be scheduled soon. If anything changes—worsening pain, inability to tolerate tube feeds, fevers—we’d escalate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. Still nauseated, but less. The IV fluids helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep the IV fluids going this morning and continue your tube feeds. We’ll also keep using ondansetron as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try drinking again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try very small sips later today if your nausea stays controlled, but we don’t want to push it and trigger vomiting. The tube feeds will cover your nutrition for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly incision area—where it opened a bit—still has packing. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. On exam you have a small midline wound dehiscence that’s being packed, with some serous fluid at the base. We’ll keep it clean and packed as directed and monitor for signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t look infected, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it doesn’t look infected—no concerning redness or pus noted, and your white count is normal. We’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI is planning to see you today. The goal is to set up an outpatient upper endoscopy for next week to evaluate the ongoing epigastric pain and nausea after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly will the scope show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It lets them look directly at the lining of the upper GI tract and the connection from your bypass. It can show inflammation, gastritis, or ulcer changes, and help guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s typically done with sedation so you’re comfortable and don’t feel it. GI will go over the details when they schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing this afternoon—any dry heaving or vomiting with the meds on board?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I still get that sour reflux feeling sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your reflux and gastritis regimen—lansoprazole twice daily. We’re also planning to add sucralfate, which coats and protects the lining and can help with gastritis-type pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is sucralfate safe with my tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can be given through the tube. We’ll give you instructions on timing because it can interfere with absorption of some medications if taken at the same time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m feeling better, does that mean it’s definitely gastritis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It points in that direction, but it doesn’t prove the exact cause. Improvement with fluids and antiemetics supports dehydration and irritation. The endoscopy is what will help clarify what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You look more comfortable today. How’s the epigastric pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better—maybe a 2 or 3. I’m still nervous about going home though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The good news is you’re back to your baseline—tolerating your tube feeds, nausea controlled with medication, and you’re hydrated. That’s why we’re planning discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do if I can’t keep anything down again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your ondansetron as prescribed, keep using the tube feeds and fluids through the tube as you’ve been doing, and avoid forcing oral intake. If you can’t tolerate tube feeds, have persistent vomiting, worsening abdominal pain, or feel faint, you should call us or come back in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my discharge meds changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly the same as what you came in on. The main addition is sucralfate four times a day. You’ll continue lansoprazole twice daily, ondansetron as needed, your tube feeding formula, and your other home medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have hydromorphone available as needed for pain, as before. Use the smallest amount you need, and let us know if pain is escalating rather than improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI’s plan is to arrange the outpatient upper endoscopy. You should expect scheduling for likely next week, and you’ll also follow up with Dr. ___ in the outpatient weight loss surgery clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want answers. I’m tired of being in and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The endoscopy is the next best step to get more definitive information. In the meantime, the focus is preventing dehydration and protecting your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re alert, walking independently, and your symptoms have improved. Continue tube feeds, take sucralfate and lansoprazole as directed, and follow up with surgery clinic and GI for the endoscopy. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that covers it. Thank you for explaining everything. I’ll call GI and the clinic as soon as I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you were directly admitted for epigastric abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s that same burning pain up high again. I get nauseated and I throw up if I try to take anything by mouth. I’m scared the ulcer is back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your history after the Roux-en-Y and the prior gastrojejunal ulcer. Any fevers, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No chest pain. Just the stomach pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are your tube feeds going at home—were you able to tolerate them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube feeds have been okay. I’ve been putting my meds through the tube too. It’s just anything by mouth that sets me off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. For tonight, we’ll keep you nothing by mouth to rest your stomach, continue tube feeds, give IV fluids, and start an IV proton pump inhibitor to reduce acid. We’ll also treat pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do a scope right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily tonight. First we’ll stabilize symptoms and check labs. If you don’t improve or there are concerning signs, we’d escalate. Given you’ve had similar episodes, we’ll monitor closely and coordinate next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried because I overdid it on vacation—walking a lot, not resting. Could that have triggered this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Overexertion and changes in routine can worsen nausea and abdominal discomfort, especially with your altered anatomy and prior ulcer history. It doesn’t prove an ulcer, but it can contribute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll draw blood work now—blood counts, electrolytes, kidney function, and pancreatic and liver enzymes—to make sure there’s no dehydration or other issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to end up back here again and again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal this admission is symptom control and making sure you can safely continue nutrition through the G-tube, then set you up with a plan to prevent flares as much as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is getting worse. Can I have something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s give ondansetron for nausea. For pain, we can use IV morphine as needed while we get things under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morphine makes me sleepy. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sleepiness is common. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and monitor your breathing and alertness. We’ll also work toward switching to oral pain medicine through the tube when you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs are back and overall reassuring: white blood cell count is normal, kidney function and electrolytes look okay, and lipase is normal. That supports treating this as a flare of upper abdominal pain and nausea rather than something like pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it could still be an ulcer though, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it could. Labs don’t rule an ulcer in or out. That’s why we’re treating with a strong acid-suppressing medicine and watching your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take NSAIDs anyway. I’m allergic. I haven’t taken any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know—and we’ll avoid NSAIDs and aspirin here as well. Those can worsen ulcers even without an allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting? How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting since the nausea medicine. Pain is still there but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll continue IV fluids and the IV PPI today. We’ll keep you NPO by mouth and continue tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least sip water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to fully rest your stomach since even small sips have been triggering vomiting. We’ll reassess as symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube site looks okay, but I’m always worried it’s going to get infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked it this morning—no redness, swelling, or drainage. Keep the area clean and dry. If you notice foul-smelling drainage or increasing redness, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to review your home meds to make sure we continue them appropriately—fluoxetine and aripiprazole for mood, atorvastatin, iron, multivitamin, and your lansoprazole. You’ve also been on rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Please don’t stop my psych meds—I get really anxious if they’re missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll continue them, and we can give them through the G-tube if you’re not taking anything by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain comes in waves. Is that normal with this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. With irritation at the upper stomach or the connection after bypass, symptoms can fluctuate. The key is whether the overall trend is improving and whether you can tolerate tube feeds without worsening nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are you feeling today compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than day one. Still tender, but I’m not throwing up. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the same plan today—IV PPI, IV fluids as needed, nausea meds as needed, and pain control. We’ll also start thinking about transitioning off IV pain meds as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home still not eating by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, yes. If your symptoms are controlled and you’re meeting nutrition through the tube, it can be safest to stay NPO by mouth for a bit. We’ll give you clear instructions for tube feeds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about my liver—someone told me I have fatty liver. Is that causing this pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fatty liver is something we track over time, but it usually doesn’t cause sudden severe epigastric pain with vomiting like you had. Right now, your symptoms fit better with irritation or ulcer-type pain after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your nausea this afternoon? Any need for ondansetron?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used it once. It helped. I’m scared to move around too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Gentle walking is okay and can help prevent complications like blood clots, but don’t push yourself. We’ll aim for moderate activity as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’re going to continue your tube feeding regimen and make sure you’re tolerating it well. Nutrition will also check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed the feed rate is different than at home. Why did it change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sometimes adjust the rate in the hospital to match tolerance and hydration needs. Before discharge, we’ll set a clear home plan—right now we’re targeting a continuous rate that you tolerate without worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is lower today. Do I still need IV morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re improving, we can reduce it and switch to pain medicine you can take through the tube or by mouth when appropriate. The goal is to control pain without making you overly sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home and having this come back overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We won’t discharge you until symptoms are clearly improving and you’re stable on a plan you can do at home—tube feeds, nausea medicine as needed, and a pain plan with clear return precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any vomiting today? Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Just mild nausea. Pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re on hospital day 4, and it looks like you’ve had significant improvement—less pain, no vomiting, and you’re tolerating tube feeds. How do you feel about going home later today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved, but nervous. What exactly will I do at home—still nothing by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The discharge plan is nothing by mouth for now, and continue tube feeds continuously at 50 cc per hour. That gives your upper GI tract time to settle while you still get nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your home medications: lansoprazole twice daily, rifaximin, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, atorvastatin, iron, multivitamin, bisacodyl, mupirocin ointment, and zolpidem at night. You’ll also have ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any new medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—an oxycodone prescription for breakthrough pain. It can cause drowsiness, so no driving or operating machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like taking opioids. What if I can manage without it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. It’s prescribed as needed, not scheduled. If your pain is controlled without it, you don’t have to take it. But it’s there if pain spikes and you need something stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call your surgeon if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain—especially if not relieved by medication—severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to tolerate tube feeds, or any concerning drainage or redness around the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I exercise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You may resume moderate exercise at your discretion—listen to your body and avoid overexertion, especially given this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave, any last questions about the tube feed rate, medications, or follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—tube feeds at 50 an hour continuously, nothing by mouth, and keep taking the lansoprazole twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And use ondansetron for nausea as needed, and oxycodone only if pain breaks through. We’ll send you home ambulatory and stable, and you’ll follow up with your surgical team as arranged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I hear you were just discharged and your upper abdominal pain got worse again. Can you tell me what’s been happening since you got home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It came back fast. It’s like a tight band across the top of my belly and it goes into my left side. It’s worse than last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fevers, or trouble keeping your tube feeds down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. I’ve been nauseated and I feel really bloated. I’m scared to take anything by mouth. Tube feeds have been going but I feel full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you taking your ulcer medicines—your proton pump inhibitor and sucralfate—like you were told?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I didn’t miss them. That’s why I don’t get why it hurts so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Given your history of Roux-en-Y bypass and prior gastrojejunal ulcer, we take this seriously. We’ll check labs, give IV fluids, treat pain and nausea, and we’ll likely get a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for anything new like a collection or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another endoscopy? I just had one recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you recently had an upper endoscopy, we’re not planning to repeat it right away unless something changes. We’ll start with monitoring and imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure always runs low. Is that a problem tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep a close eye on it. Right now you’re awake, talking, and your oxygen looks good. We’ll give fluids and monitor your vitals frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain, we can start with IV medication and then transition to oral options as you improve. For nausea we’ll use ondansetron as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. Please don’t give me those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin. We’ll use other options like acetaminophen and opioid medication if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site has a little yellow drainage. Is that infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I looked at it—there’s a small amount of serous yellow drainage but the site looks clean and dry overall. We’ll keep it covered and watch for redness, increasing pain, or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork is reassuring—your white blood cell count is normal, kidney function and electrolytes look okay, and your liver and pancreas-related labs don’t suggest pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so bad if the labs are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can still be significant even when labs are normal—especially with ulcer-type pain, irritation, or constipation and gas. That’s why the CT scan and how you respond to treatment are important pieces.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so bloated. It’s making the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bloating can definitely amplify upper abdominal pain. We’ll keep your tube feeds going but adjust the formula while you’re here to something easier to tolerate, and we’ll also address constipation if that’s contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after the IV pain medicine and nausea medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine helped, but I still feel swollen and uncomfortable. I haven’t really had a bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That may be a big part of it. We can give bowel medications, and if needed we can use an enema to get things moving. We’ll also keep you walking in the hall as you’re able.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What tube feed are you giving me? It tastes different when it refluxes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we switched you to Vivonex, which is a formula many people tolerate well when their stomach is sensitive. We’ll keep an eye on bloating and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your nutrition through the feeding tube today. Let us know if the fullness gets worse or if you have new vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the CT contrast. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function looks good, which is the main safety check. We’ll also make sure you’re well hydrated. The CT helps us rule out things like a fluid collection or deeper infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT abdomen and pelvis is back. The good news: there’s no fluid collection and no intra-abdominal phlegmon. It also shows interval healing of your upper midline incision with scarring and stranding similar to before—nothing new or worrisome there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is leaking or infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no signs of a collection or an abscess on the scan. That supports continuing conservative treatment: ulcer protection meds, symptom control, and addressing the bloating and constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel like my belly is stretched tight. Can we do something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given you haven’t had a good bowel movement, we can give a Fleet enema tonight. It often helps relieve bloating and pain when stool is backing things up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a huge bowel movement after the enema. The pressure is way better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep bowel meds available as needed so you don’t get backed up again—especially since opioids can worsen constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in: how’s your pain now compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still sore in the upper belly, but not that band-like pain. I’m less nauseated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Since you’re improving, we’d like to transition you off IV morphine to oral pain meds—oral hydromorphone if needed—and acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the oral stuff be enough? I don’t want to be miserable again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it stepwise and reassess. The goal is safe pain control that you can continue at home, while minimizing constipation and side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my regular meds for anxiety and depression while I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’re continuing your home regimen, including fluoxetine and aripiprazole, and clonazepam as needed for anxiety. If you feel more anxious in the hospital, tell us so we can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried this is just going to keep happening. Is it definitely an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t say ‘definitely’ from this admission alone, but your symptoms and history fit ulcer-type or irritation-type pain, and the CT didn’t show a surgical complication like an abscess. Since you recently had an endoscopy, we’re focusing on medical therapy—PPI and sucralfate—and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you tolerating the Vivonex tube feeds today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pretty well. Still some fullness, but I’m not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your urine output has been adequate and your vitals have stayed stable and you’ve been afebrile, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you look comfortable. Any new nausea, vomiting, or worsening pain overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is manageable. I’m just tired and I want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. If you continue to tolerate tube feeds, walk around, and your pain stays controlled on oral meds, we can plan discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do at home if the bloating comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your bowel regimen as prescribed—bisacodyl as needed—and keep moving and hydrated. If you get severe pain again, can’t keep down fluids or meds, or you see blood or black stools or vomit, you should call us or come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking sucralfate and the PPI even if I feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue sucralfate four times a day and your lansoprazole daily. Those protect the lining and help ulcers heal and prevent flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have ondansetron to take as needed for nausea. If you’re vomiting and can’t keep down fluids or medications, that’s a reason to seek care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, we’ll review the discharge plan: you’re going home, continuing tube feeds, continuing your home medications, and avoiding NSAIDs/aspirin. You can walk as tolerated, rest, and avoid heavy lifting until you follow up with your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I understand. I’m relieved the CT didn’t show anything scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well this stay—pain improved after treating constipation and switching to oral meds, and you’re tolerating tube feeds. If anything changes—fever, worsening pain, dehydration, blood in vomit or stool—call or come in. We’ll arrange follow-up with the surgery team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you today. I understand you came back with worsening upper abdominal pain. Can you tell me what it feels like right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a burning pain in the middle and it spreads over to the right side. It’s been getting worse since I left the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills? Any vomiting blood or black, tarry stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No blood. I’ve been nauseated and dry heaving, and I barely want to eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are your tube feeds going at home? Any trouble running them or new intolerance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The feeds have been okay. But I’ve noticed some leaking around the G-tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. On exam your belly is soft, but tender in the epigastric area. Your vitals look stable. We’re going to focus on pain control and hydration, and we’ll make sure there’s no new surgical problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s that ulcer again, or a stitch that’s stuck. It feels like something is wrong in there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern given your history of a gastrojejunal anastomotic ulcer. We’ll keep you on your ulcer medicines—lansoprazole and sucralfate—and we’ll check labs and imaging that were done in the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve only been taking Tylenol at home. It’s not touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We can use stronger pain medicine here while we evaluate. We’ll also try to avoid anything you’re allergic to—no NSAIDs or aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back with initial results. Your white blood cell count is normal, and your lactate is normal, which is reassuring. Your lipase is normal, so this doesn’t look like pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes with your surgical anatomy, pain can flare without a clear emergency finding. Our differential includes ulcer irritation, gastritis, or irritation around the G-tube. The CT scan from overnight didn’t show an abscess or any acute intra-abdominal abnormality.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The CT was normal? Then what are we supposed to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even with a reassuring CT, we still treat what we can: hydration, nausea control, and a pain plan that’s safe. We’ll also have the surgical team follow along since you’ve had multiple recent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so dry. My mouth is sticky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that too—your mucous membranes looked tacky. We’re giving IV fluids now, and we’re going to adjust your free water flushes through the G-tube to help prevent dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do flushes at home, but maybe not enough. How much should I be doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we’re planning to increase them to 100 milliliters every four hours. We’ll see how you feel and make sure your electrolytes stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is still there. I’m scared to run feeds when I feel like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can use ondansetron as needed for nausea. If you’re tolerating tube feeds without worsening symptoms, we’ll continue them, but we can slow down temporarily if needed while we get you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain after fluids and the first doses of pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better, but it keeps coming back. I don’t want to be on opioids forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good goal. We’re going to use the lowest effective dose and also add a non-opioid option for chronic pain. We’re starting gabapentin 300 milligrams three times a day to help with nerve-type pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin—will that make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially at first. We’ll watch for dizziness or sedation. If it’s too much, tell us and we can adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about that alkaline phosphatase number? Someone mentioned it was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your alkaline phosphatase was mildly elevated at 143, but your other liver tests—AST, ALT, bilirubin—were normal, and the CT didn’t show bile duct dilation or gallbladder issues. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it doesn’t explain an emergency today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before I go, I want to check in on your mood too. You’re on fluoxetine and aripiprazole—are you feeling more anxious or down with all these admissions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m exhausted and scared it’s never going to stop. But I’m taking my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll continue your home medications here and make sure you have support and follow-up. Let us know if you feel unsafe or overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or new diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I had one loose stool yesterday but nothing since. The pain is still there but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your exam is still soft without guarding, and your vitals are stable. We’ll keep focusing on hydration and a steady pain regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can someone look at the tube site? The leaking makes me nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. On our exam there’s no redness or drainage suggesting infection, but we’ll have nursing keep an eye on the site and dressing. If the leaking worsens or you see skin breakdown, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to continue your nutrition through the G-tube today. The goal is to keep you nourished while we manage symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want it to make the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you notice increased pain, bloating, or nausea during feeds, let us know and we can adjust the rate and flushes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helps, but I’m worried about constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real side effect. We’ll keep bisacodyl available as needed, and we’ll encourage fluids through your flush plan to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling on the gabapentin so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little sleepy, but manageable. The pain feels less constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s what we’re hoping for—more baseline control so you need less opioid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You look more comfortable today. How’s the pain now, 0 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a 3 or 4. It was an 8 when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. Your labs this morning are stable—blood counts and kidney function look good, and your electrolytes like magnesium and phosphorus are in a good range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I think so, as long as you’re tolerating your tube feeds and flushes, and your pain is controlled on an oral plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly is the plan at home? I don’t want to bounce back again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Key pieces: continue lansoprazole and sucralfate for ulcer protection; use ondansetron as needed for nausea; continue gabapentin 300 mg three times a day; and use oxycodone liquid 5 mg every six hours as needed for breakthrough pain, not on a fixed schedule unless you truly need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the water flushes—say it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Increase free water flushes to 100 milliliters every four hours. That’s to prevent dehydration, which can worsen how you feel and can amplify pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m still leaking around the tube, is it safe to flush that much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s minor leakage without redness, swelling, or significant pain at the site, it’s usually okay, but monitor it closely. If leakage becomes heavy, the skin breaks down, or you can’t run feeds/flushes, you should call your care team or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you know what caused this flare? It’s frustrating to hear ‘unclear.’

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The CT and labs didn’t show an acute complication like an abscess, obstruction, or pancreatitis. Given your history, irritation at the anastomosis or stomach lining, or pain related to the tube/surgical changes, are possibilities. Our job this admission was to rule out dangerous causes and get symptoms controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Someone mentioned pain clinic. Is that really necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I think it will help. They can work with you on longer-term strategies—medication adjustments like gabapentin titration if needed, and non-medication approaches—so you’re not relying on opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my code status. I was DNR before. What’s written now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: During this admission, you were documented as DNR but okay with intubation. If you want to revisit that, we can clarify it before you leave and make sure it matches your wishes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your abdomen is minimally tender now, you’re walking independently, and you’re tolerating your tube regimen. We’ll discharge you home today with the medication list and the flush schedule, plus return precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. If the pain spikes again or I can’t keep feeds down, I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—come back for severe worsening pain, fever, vomiting blood, black stools, inability to tolerate tube feeds/flushes, or signs of infection around the tube site. Otherwise, follow up as arranged, including pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you’re here for abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been about a week. My whole belly feels crampy and swollen, like I’m distended. It’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—nausea and loose stools, several times a day. I threw up once since I got to the ER, just clear stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the stool? Any fevers or chills at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fevers that I noticed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you have a gastrostomy tube. Any issues with it recently—leakage, pain at the site, or trouble with feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Five days ago it was leaking, and they changed the tube. The site looks okay now, but the pain kept getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been getting large residuals when you check the tube, or trouble flushing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No big residuals. It flushes fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: What have you taken for pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just Tylenol. I can’t take NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—no NSAIDs or aspirin because of ulcer risk after bypass. We’re going to check labs and get imaging to make sure there’s no obstruction or internal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s another blockage. It feels like everything is stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. With your Roux-en-Y history, we take that seriously. We’ll start with an abdominal X-ray now, and likely a CT scan after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: While we’re waiting, we’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—and give IV fluids and nausea medicine. Is your pain constant or comes in waves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Waves. Cramping. Then it eases a little and comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a non-obstructive bowel gas pattern—no free air and no clear signs of a blockage on that test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: An X-ray can miss things, especially after bypass surgery. Given your symptoms, we still want the CT scan to look for obstruction or an internal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need surgery tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. If the CT shows a surgical problem, we’d talk about next steps right away. If it’s reassuring, we may observe you, treat symptoms, and restart tube feeds carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bloodwork so far looks reassuring—white blood cell count is normal and your lactate is normal, which makes a dangerous lack of blood flow to the bowel less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I still feel bloated though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue IV fluids overnight and keep monitoring. If you have more vomiting, worsening pain, or you feel feverish, tell the nurse right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any more vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more vomiting. Still nauseated on and off. The cramps are a little better with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to proceed with the CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast this morning to evaluate for obstruction or internal hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the contrast safe with my tube and bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll get IV contrast, and you’ll also drink oral contrast if you can tolerate it. It helps us see the bowel pathways after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CT results are back. The good news: no signs of bowel obstruction, and no CT signs of an internal hernia. Your gastrostomy tube position looks unchanged in the gastric remnant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong? But I’m still hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT rules out the big emergencies we worry about. Pain can still happen from cramping and irritation even without a blockage. Right now, since you’re stable and the imaging is reassuring, the plan is observation and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tube site—could it be infected from when it leaked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam the tube site looks normal—no redness, swelling, or drainage—and you haven’t had fevers. We’ll keep watching closely, but there’s no sign of infection at this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since your nausea is improving and the CT is reassuring, we’ll start by giving you water and then re-trial your tube feeds slowly. If symptoms worsen, we’ll pause and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous to restart feeds. What if it makes the cramping worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. We’ll start gently and monitor for pain, bloating, vomiting, and residuals. You can tell us right away if it feels like too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the water and the initial tube feed trial go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So far okay. Some mild cramps, but not like before. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll continue the feeds as tolerated and keep your nausea medication available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something stronger for pain? Tylenol isn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll use a multimodal plan and transition you to oral pain medication as you tolerate intake. We can use liquid oxycodone as needed, and we’ll continue your gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me too sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We’ll use the lowest effective dose, and we’ll watch for drowsiness. No driving or operating machinery while taking it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in. Any fevers, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just tired. The pain is much better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your vitals have been stable, and there’s been no sign of infection or bleeding. Are you tolerating tube feeds and water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No big residuals. Nausea is mostly controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep encouraging you to get up and walk, use the incentive spirometer, and we’ll continue blood clot prevention with the boots and heparin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I eat real food again? I’m on that Stage III diet, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—Stage III diet only for now. Don’t advance it on your own until your follow-up. Also avoid straws and chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal exam remains soft with only mild tenderness, and the tube site still looks fine. If things stay stable overnight, we’ll plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home? I don’t want to end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call your surgeon if you get fever over 101.5, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by your meds, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, chest pain, shortness of breath, or if you can’t keep down fluids or tolerate tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been stable and tolerating water and tube feeds. Pain controlled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I still get some cramps, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll discharge you home today. You’ll continue your home meds, and remember: crush all pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which meds am I leaving with for the stomach and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your GI protection and ulcer care: lansoprazole and sucralfate. For nausea: ondansetron as needed. For pain: liquid oxycodone as needed, plus your gabapentin. And continue your tube feeding formula as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take ibuprofen if the pain flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—avoid all NSAIDs and aspirin. They can cause bleeding and ulcers, especially after gastric bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about activity? I’m worried I’ll pull something around the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for 6 weeks. You can do moderate exercise as you feel able, but avoid abdominal exercises. Keep walking—gentle movement helps your bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you may shower. No tub baths or swimming. Call if you notice increased pain, swelling, or redness at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go—any last questions about the CT results or the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm: the CT showed no obstruction and the tube is in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no obstruction, no internal hernia seen, and the gastrostomy tube position is unchanged in the gastric remnant. If symptoms worsen at home, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. You’re here for planned gastric bypass reversal because of the ongoing low blood sugars and other bypass-related complications. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous. The hypoglycemia has been scary. I just want it to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The goal of the reversal is to reduce those post-bypass hypoglycemia episodes. We’ll review the plan, risks, and what recovery looks like, and you can ask anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need my G-tube after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right after surgery, we’ll use the G-tube for decompression—keeping it to gravity while your stomach and intestines wake up. As you recover, we clamp it and advance your diet. We’ll decide longer-term needs based on how you tolerate intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the low sugars—will they stop immediately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not always immediately, but many patients see improvement as the anatomy is restored. We’ll monitor your blood glucose closely here, and you’ll keep using your continuous glucose monitor at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried about infection. I’ve been told I’m MRSA positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for bringing that up. We take that seriously—good hand hygiene, careful wound care, and we watch closely for any signs of infection. If we need antibiotics, we choose them thoughtfully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about pain control? I don’t do well when pain gets out of control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with strong pain control right after surgery—often an epidural initially, then a patient-controlled pump, and later oral medication once you’re tolerating diet. We’ll adjust based on your comfort and safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. That’s in my chart, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s clearly listed. We will avoid NSAIDs. We’ll use acetaminophen and opioid medication as needed, plus other supportive options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have anxiety and PTSD. Hospitals can be hard for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. We’ll keep communication clear, explain what’s happening before we do things, and we can continue your home psychiatric medications as appropriate. If you feel overwhelmed, tell us early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before we head to the operating room: any new symptoms—chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, or worsening abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just the usual abdominal discomfort and nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll proceed as planned. After surgery you’ll wake up in the recovery area, then come to the ward for close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi—surgery is done. You underwent a gastric bypass reversal. There were no adverse events in the operating room. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy. Is the tube hooked up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your G-tube is to gravity for decompression. You’ll be NPO for now, and we’ll give IV fluids. We’re also monitoring your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly feels tight. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness and a tight feeling are expected after abdominal surgery. We’ll keep checking your abdomen and your incision sites. Let us know if pain suddenly worsens or you feel very bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard someone mention a line in my neck. What is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a right internal jugular triple-lumen central line for reliable access for fluids and medications. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right position and your lungs look clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared I’ll get low blood sugar overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your glucose regularly. If it drops or you have symptoms—shakiness, sweating, dizziness—tell the nurse right away. We can treat per protocol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Post-op day 1. How was the night? Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Some nausea, but no vomiting. Pain is there, but the button helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Today we’re doing an upper GI study to make sure there’s no leak or obstruction before we start advancing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that test involve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll drink contrast while radiology takes images as it moves through. It helps us confirm the new anatomy is working and there’s no leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your upper GI study looks good—no evidence of leak or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I can eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet today. We’ll still go slowly. You’ll remain NPO initially while your gut function returns, and we’ll keep the G-tube to gravity for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Post-op day 2 check-in. Any gas or bowel movement yet? How’s the bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Some gas. No bowel movement. Less bloated than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Keep walking in the hall and using the incentive spirometer—those help recovery and prevent lung issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My incision looks bruised. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some bruising and discoloration around the staples can be part of normal healing. We’ll keep checking for redness spreading, foul drainage, or increasing warmth—those would be concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Post-op day 3. Today we plan to clamp your G-tube and start advancing your diet stepwise if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does clamping it do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Instead of draining to a bag, we close it so your stomach contents move forward normally. If you get significant nausea, distension, or pain, we can unclamp it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about hypoglycemia once I start taking in calories again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring your glucose closely as we reintroduce intake. The reversal is intended to help, but we still treat any lows promptly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do with the diet advancement so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than I expected. Small amounts are okay. Nausea comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep you on a staged plan and use ondansetron as needed. We’ll also keep tracking your intake and output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I switch from the pump to pills for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As you tolerate the Stage III diet reliably, we transition to oral pain medication. The plan is oral hydromorphone as needed, plus acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m afraid of constipation from opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real concern. We’ll use stool softeners and laxatives as needed—like Colace and bisacodyl—and encourage walking and fluids as allowed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals have been stable, and you’ve been afebrile. No signs of infection or bleeding. How’s your energy today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but I can walk more. The breathing exercises are annoying but I’m doing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Annoying but effective. Early ambulation and incentive spirometry reduce complications. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my regular meds now? Some of my pills are big.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can resume your home medications, but you must crush all pills for now. We’ll also have you on pantoprazole twice daily to reduce reflux and protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why pantoprazole if my reflux was ‘resolved’ before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After surgery, the stomach and connection sites can be more sensitive. Pantoprazole decreases acid and helps healing during this early recovery period.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting to plan for discharge. You’re tolerating the Stage III diet, walking independently, and your pain is controlled on oral medication. Any concerns about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll miss signs of something going wrong. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or come to the ER for fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by meds, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or any foul-smelling or colored drainage, redness, or swelling around incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll be removed at your follow-up appointment. You can shower, but no tub baths or swimming. If there’s clear drainage, cover with clean dry gauze.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I handle low blood sugar at home if it happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your continuous glucose monitor. If you’re low or symptomatic—dizzy, fast heartbeat, weak, vision changes—take a glucose gel packet or quick sugar like juice. If symptoms are severe or you’re not recovering, call us and go to the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final day check: you’re alert, walking, urinating without help, and keeping down the Stage III diet. Pain okay on oral meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Still sore, but manageable. I’m ready to sleep in my own bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. A few key discharge points: stay on Stage III diet until your follow-up—don’t self-advance. No straws or chewing gum. Crush all pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why no straws or gum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can increase swallowed air and contribute to bloating and discomfort while your GI tract is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What pain meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen as needed and oral hydromorphone as needed. Hydromorphone can make you drowsy—no driving or operating machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ondansetron (Zofran) as needed. If nausea becomes severe or you can’t keep liquids down, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking my vitamins?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—start a chewable complete multivitamin with minerals. No gummy vitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember being told never to take NSAIDs. Still true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still true—no NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen, and no aspirin unless a doctor specifically instructs you. They can cause ulcers and bleeding in your digestive system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about activity? I don’t want to mess up the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for 6 weeks. You can do moderate exercise as you feel able, but avoid abdominal exercises. Walking is encouraged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I see redness around the staples, how much is too much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A little irritation can happen, but call if redness spreads, the area becomes increasingly warm or painful, or there’s foul-smelling or colored drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
