conversation_lines.text: All set—your discharge paperwork and prescriptions are in. You’re going home today. We’ll see you at follow-up for staple removal and to reassess diet progression and glucose control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m hopeful this will finally help the hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. I hear you’ve had a lot of nausea and haven’t been able to keep much down. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. For the last two days, every time I try to drink or eat I get nauseous. I’m barely getting anything in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been vomiting? If so, how many times and what did it look like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up once yesterday and twice this morning. It was greenish, like bile. No blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, or sick contacts? And how’s your belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or chills. My stomach is just mildly sore. I’ve only taken Tylenol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about bowel movements—any diarrhea, black stools, or blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been loose since surgery, but this morning was the first formed one. No blood, not black.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any dizziness when you stand up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially today. I feel lightheaded when I get up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with dehydration. Your vitals look okay right now, and your fingerstick blood sugar is 88, which is fine. On exam your abdomen is soft and not tender, and your G-tube site looks clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried something is wrong with the reversal. Could it be a blockage or a leak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your exam and that you’re not having severe belly pain or fevers, a leak is less likely. Right now this looks most consistent with nausea leading to poor intake and dehydration. We’ll check labs and focus on IV fluids and nausea control, and we’ll keep a close eye on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The Zofran at home didn’t help at all. I kept taking it and still threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We can give anti-nausea meds here and adjust the plan. We’ll start IV fluids now, and we’ll keep Zofran available. If it’s not enough, we can add another medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat anything? I’m scared to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start gently. You were on a bariatric Stage 3 diet, but we’ll tailor it to what you can tolerate. For now, small sips of water and clear liquids as tolerated, and we’ll reassess after fluids and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also feel like the protein shakes make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Some people do better temporarily with softer, simpler foods. If shakes are triggering nausea, we can shift toward a mechanical soft approach once you’re ready—things like broth and smooth cereals—while still trying to get protein in where you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back with your initial labs. Your white blood cell count is normal, and your kidney function and electrolytes look okay, which is reassuring. Your hemoglobin is a bit low but stable compared to prior values.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing in the labs suggests infection, and you don’t have a fever. We’ll keep monitoring, but right now this looks like dehydration from not being able to take in enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still nauseous even sitting here. Will the fluids actually help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They often do—dehydration itself can worsen nausea and dizziness. The other key is getting the right anti-nausea regimen so you can start drinking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after the IV fluids and medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little less dizzy. The nausea comes in waves, but I haven’t thrown up since earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Tonight, keep it to small frequent sips—don’t force large amounts. We’ll continue fluids overnight and reassess in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any vomiting overnight? And were you able to drink anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I sipped water and some broth. I’m still afraid to try the shakes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Since you’re linking nausea to the protein shakes, we can advance you to a mechanical soft diet rather than pushing shakes right now—broth, cream of wheat, and other soft options—while we work on protein in other tolerable forms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it okay that I’m not getting much protein? I don’t want to mess up healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Protein is important, but the first step is keeping you hydrated and stopping the vomiting. We’ll have you meet with the team for diet education so you can choose soft foods that are easier on your stomach and still help with protein goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea is better with broth, but I’m still having loose stools sometimes. Should I worry about an infection like C. diff again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, it’s reasonable to check stool studies when symptoms suggest infection. We sent stool testing, and so far the cultures we have are negative for common bacteria, and the ova and parasite exam didn’t show parasites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The C. diff PCR test was cancelled, so we don’t have that result from this set. The good news is you’re not having fevers, your white count is normal, and your stools are improving—formed this morning—so infection is less likely. If symptoms worsen, we’d reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any nausea with the mechanical soft foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cream of wheat went down fine. Water is okay. I’m nervous but it’s better than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want—slow and steady. We’ll keep encouraging small frequent intake and keep anti-nausea meds available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my regular pills? I remember being told to crush them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your home medications, but crush all pills for now. That helps them pass and absorb better after your bariatric surgery changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can’t take ibuprofen, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no NSAIDs and no aspirin because they can cause ulcers and bleeding in your digestive tract, especially after bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain? Are you needing the oxycodone liquid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is mild. Mostly I’m just uncomfortable. I haven’t needed much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep pain control simple and avoid anything that irritates the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—your labs today look stable: electrolytes and kidney function are good, and your blood counts are steady. Clinically you look much better hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel less dizzy. I’m still scared the nausea will come back when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common worry. To help, we’re adding a second anti-nausea medication called prochlorperazine—Compazine. You can alternate it with Zofran as needed, rather than relying on just one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I alternate them? I don’t want to take too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Zofran as prescribed, and if nausea breaks through, you can take Compazine as needed. Don’t take extra doses beyond the instructions on the labels. If you’re needing them constantly or can’t keep liquids down, call us or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What diet am I supposed to be on now? Stage 3 or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on Stage 4—soft mechanical diet—until your follow-up appointment. Don’t self-advance the diet yet. Also avoid drinking through a straw and avoid chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why no straw or gum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can increase swallowed air, which can worsen bloating and discomfort and sometimes nausea. It’s a small thing, but it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special for my incisions or the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower, but no tub baths or swimming. If you notice clear drainage, cover it with clean, dry gauze. Call if there’s increasing redness, swelling, pain, or drainage that looks or smells concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I okay to go back to normal activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Walk and do light activity, but no heavy lifting for 6 weeks and no abdominal exercises. You can resume moderate exercise as you feel able, as long as it doesn’t strain your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, here are the reasons to call or return: fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe belly pain, vomiting that won’t stop, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or any concerning incision drainage. You’re stable, tolerating soft foods and liquids, walking independently, and your pain is controlled—so we’ll discharge you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you came in with worsening upper abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me where the pain is and when it started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s mostly in the middle and kind of up high. It started two days ago and got worse yesterday. Today I felt nauseous and threw up once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Was the vomit bright red, or did it look like coffee grounds or dark material?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was dark, but I don’t think it was blood. It just scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Any fever or chills? And have you been able to eat or drink since the pain started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. I haven’t eaten because I’m afraid it’ll make it worse. Sips of water only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about bowel movements—any blood or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a normal bowel movement this morning. No blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of gastric bypass and the reversal, we want to be cautious. Tonight we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—give IV fluids, and use your G-tube to drain to gravity to take pressure off your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube will just drain into a bag? Will that help the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it will drain into a bag. For many people it relieves nausea and cramping because it decompresses the stomach. We’ll also give IV pain medicine and anti-nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried Tylenol and Zofran at home and it didn’t touch it. I’m worried something is leaking inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. We’re going to get a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for any leak, collection, or inflammation around the surgical connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the CT dangerous with my tube and staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safe. The contrast helps us see if anything is escaping where it shouldn’t. We’ll monitor you closely during and after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night with the G-tube to gravity and the IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is a little better when it’s draining. The pain is still there but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your vital signs have been stable. We’ll proceed with the CT scan today to better understand what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I at least have ice chips? My mouth is so dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now we need strict NPO until the CT is done and we review it. We can give you mouth swabs and keep your IV fluids running so you don’t get dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I reviewed your CT scan. It shows a lot of inflammatory change near the gastrogastric anastomosis—the connection from your reversal. There’s no clear contrast leak and no fluid collection, but the radiologist notes a subtle leak can’t be completely excluded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… it might be leaking but you can’t see it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—there’s no definite leak on the scan, which is reassuring. But because the inflammation is more than we’d expect, we’re going to treat you cautiously: keep you NPO, continue decompression with the G-tube, and start antibiotics—ciprofloxacin and metronidazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics even if you don’t know it’s an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. In this situation, antibiotics can help if there’s a small contained issue or bacterial inflammation around the surgical area. We’ll also watch your symptoms and exam closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning—pain, nausea, and how much is draining from the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Less nausea when it’s draining. The pain is still there but more like soreness. The bag has been filling some.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep the tube to gravity today and continue IV fluids and antibiotics. If you keep improving, we can try clamping the tube tomorrow to see if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious. Last time I was here it got better, but I’m scared it’ll keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. With your surgical history, these episodes are frightening. Our goal is to get you through this safely, then have a clear plan for diet progression and tube care so you feel more in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable and your abdominal exam is improving. Today we’d like to clamp the G-tube and see if your stomach tolerates it without worsening pain or nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start feeling sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel increasing nausea, bloating, or pain, tell us right away. We can unclamp it and put it back to gravity. This is a reversible trial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been clamped most of the day. I’m a little uncomfortable but not like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. If you stay stable overnight, tomorrow we can start a careful diet advancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Since you tolerated the clamp trial, we’d like to start you on a bariatric stage 4 diet today—soft foods—very small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on stage 3 before this happened. Why stage 4 now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stage 4 is still gentle but a bit more advanced. We’ll see how your stomach handles it. If you get cramping or nausea, we’ll step back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried the food and now I’m getting crampy pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling us quickly. We’ll back down to a bariatric stage 2 diet, which is more liquid-based and easier to tolerate, and we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean something is wrong again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. After inflammation near the anastomosis, the stomach can be sensitive. The fact that you’re not vomiting and your exam is stable is reassuring. We just need to go slower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube is leaking around the site. My shirt got wet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry—that’s uncomfortable. We’ll examine it now. If the tube itself is damaged or not sealing well, we may need to exchange it under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is exchanging it surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s typically done by Interventional Radiology using fluoroscopy. It’s not an open surgery. They use local numbing medicine and usually moderate sedation to keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Radiology reviewed the tube and agrees it should be exchanged today because it’s leaking and we want to confirm safe positioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about sedation. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sleepy but breathing on your own. They’ll monitor your heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen the whole time. If you’re uncomfortable, they can adjust medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the procedure. The team exchanged your gastrostomy tube successfully for a new 18 French MIC tube, and they confirmed it’s in the stomach and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy. Did anything go wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No complications were reported. There was a hole in the old tube, which explains the leaking. The new tube is secured and should seal better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO overnight after the exchange to let everything settle, then we’ll restart diet tomorrow if you’re feeling okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain this morning and how does the tube site look—any leaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The dressing is dry. Pain is more like mild soreness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Today we’ll advance you to bariatric stage 5. We’ll go slowly and see how you tolerate it. We’ll also transition your pain control to oral medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m keeping the food down. Still a little nauseous but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected as you ramp back up. You can use ondansetron as needed. Keep portions small and frequent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to keep the tube forever? I’m not even on 24-hour feeds anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That decision will be made with your surgeon in clinic based on your nutrition and symptoms. Right now, it’s also been helpful for decompression during this flare, so we want it functioning well while you recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you’re walking, urinating normally, and your pain is controlled on oral meds. Your abdominal pain has significantly improved. If you continue to tolerate stage 5 today, we can discharge you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What am I going home on? I’m worried the pain will come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home medications. For this episode, you’ll complete a 10-day course of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. For symptoms, you’ll have acetaminophen and a small supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain, plus docusate to prevent constipation, and ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—none of these are those, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no NSAIDs or aspirin. Stick with acetaminophen for baseline pain, and only use oxycodone if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call right away for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, worsening abdominal pain, vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, signs of dehydration like dizziness or fast heartbeat, or any blood or black material in vomit or stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube—what if it leaks again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you notice new leaking, increasing redness, swelling, severe pain at the site, or the tube seems displaced, call us. Keep the site clean and dry and follow the dressing instructions. We’ll also arrange follow-up with your surgeon, Dr. ___, in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. I understand you were admitted because you can’t tolerate eating or drinking much. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s this burning pain in the middle of my upper belly, and it goes up into my chest like my esophagus. I’m nauseated all the time. I can only do water and shakes—no solid food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How long has this been happening, and have you been vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two days. I didn’t vomit until I got here—then I threw up once and it looked kind of red-tinged brown. Not like a lot of blood, but it scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you came in. Any black stools, fevers, chills, or trouble passing gas or having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or chills. I’m still having bowel movements and passing gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history—Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, the reversal, and prior gastrojejunal ulcer—your symptoms could fit irritation or ulcer-type pain, but we also want to make sure there’s no narrowing, blockage, or leak. We’ll start with labs and an upper GI contrast study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this going to mean surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Right now our first step is to evaluate and support you—fluids, nausea control, and using your G-tube for nutrition if you can tolerate it. We’ll decide next steps based on the imaging and how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugars have been weird overnight. I even restarted my tube feeds at home and it didn’t fix it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Because of your post-gastric surgery hypoglycemia history, we’ll monitor your fingerstick blood sugars closely. While you’re not taking much in, we’ll use dextrose-containing IV fluids to keep things stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also worried about the burning in my chest—could it be my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pattern you describe sounds more like reflux or irritation along the esophagus, especially with the nausea and upper abdominal pain. We’ll keep an eye on your vital signs and symptoms, and if anything suggests a heart issue we’d evaluate that right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight, we’ll keep you on clear liquids as tolerated, give IV fluids, and use anti-nausea medication. Are you currently taking pantoprazole and sucralfate at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take both. I can’t take NSAIDs or aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect—avoiding NSAIDs is important for ulcers. We’ll continue your acid suppression and protectant medications here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any more vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more vomiting. Still nauseated, and the burning pain is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do the upper GI study this morning. It’s a contrast X-ray where you swallow contrast and we watch it pass through. It helps us look for a leak, stricture, or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? And what if I throw up during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shouldn’t be painful, but the contrast can be unpleasant. If you feel nauseated, tell the radiology team—they can pause. We’ll also give anti-nausea medication beforehand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your upper GI study is back: no evidence of leak, stricture, or obstruction. There was mild reflux noted, which fits with the burning sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong? Because I feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s no dangerous blockage or leak seen on that test, which is reassuring. But you can still have significant symptoms from ulcer irritation, reflux, or slow stomach emptying after your surgeries. Our goal now is to get your nutrition and nausea under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean tube feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll re-trial tube feeds through your G-tube, starting at a low rate and increasing slowly. We’ll keep the dextrose IV fluids while we ramp up so your blood sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started Vivonex through the G-tube at a low rate. How are you feeling with it running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At 30 it’s okay, but when they tried to go higher I got really nauseated and crampy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful feedback. If you can’t tolerate higher rates, we can switch to a more concentrated formula so you get the calories at a lower volume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want to be sick all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll adjust stepwise—formula, rate, and nausea meds—so it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning we’re going to change the feeding plan. We’ll trial a more concentrated formula and see if your stomach tolerates it better at a lower rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the nausea medicine going to change too? Zofran helps a little but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since ondansetron hasn’t been enough, we’ll add prochlorperazine as needed. We’ll still use what works for you, but we want better control so you can tolerate feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented the feeding through the G-tube today and we’ll keep increasing carefully. Let us know right away if you feel worsening nausea, bloating, or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also anxious—every time I feel that burning I think something is tearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense given your surgical history. The upper GI didn’t show a leak or obstruction, and your exam is reassuring. We’ll keep monitoring, and we’ll treat the reflux and nausea aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight with the new formula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than before. Still some nausea, but it’s not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re aiming for a goal rate that meets your nutrition needs. If you keep tolerating, we can work toward discharge with a home tube-feeding plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on tube feeds 24 hours a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least initially, yes—continuous feeds are often easier to tolerate. Your discharge plan may also include scheduled boluses depending on what you tolerate and what’s safest for your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar—are you seeing lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far your blood sugars have been stable with the dextrose IV fluids and the gradual feed increase. We’ll keep checking regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re switching you to Jevity 1.5 at a rate that should give you more nutrition with less volume. We’ll start and then work up toward 45 mL per hour if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s different about Jevity? Is it going to upset my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s more calorie-dense, so you don’t need as much volume per hour. Many people tolerate it better when volume is the limiting factor. We’ll go slowly and treat nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The prochlorperazine helped more than the Zofran. I’m sleepy though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sleepiness can happen with prochlorperazine. We’ll use the lowest effective dose and keep it as needed. Safety-wise, call the nurse before getting up if you feel drowsy or lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re up to a higher rate on Jevity now. Any vomiting or worsening abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. The nausea comes and goes, but it’s manageable. The burning is less constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. If you continue to tolerate, we can start tapering the IV dextrose once your tube feeds are reliably at goal and your sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home and messing up the tube feeds. What if I can’t keep up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have a clear plan: the formula, the rate, and how to give the bolus flushes. Nursing will review the pump and G-tube care with you, and we’ll arrange supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re adding a medication called erythromycin. In low doses it can help stomach motility—basically help things move along—so feeds are better tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Erythromycin like an antibiotic? Am I getting an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. It is an antibiotic at higher doses, but we’re using it here for its motility effect, not because we think you have an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is up. I’m scared the nausea will come back full force.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s understandable. The plan is to keep your nausea controlled with prochlorperazine as needed, keep your acid suppression going, and keep feeds at the rate you tolerate. We’ll only discharge once you’re stable on the regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now at Jevity 1.5 at 45 mL per hour, which is our goal rate. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, better than I expected. Still baseline nausea, but I’m not retching. Pain is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to keep monitoring your blood sugars and blood pressure as we step down the IV dextrose. If those stay stable, we’ll be close to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to keep trying to eat by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, focus on hydration and what you can tolerate. The main nutrition will be through the tube feeds. We don’t want you forcing solids if it triggers pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars have remained stable on the goal tube feeds, and you’ve been hemodynamically stable. That’s what we needed to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow morning to make sure everything is set—supplies, teaching, and your medication list. I also want you comfortable with the feeding schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over the feeding schedule again? I get confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. The plan is Jevity 1.5 at 45 mL per hour continuously, plus 200 mL bolus every 6 hours as prescribed. Nursing will also review how to flush the tube and what to do if there’s clogging or leakage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call you or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call if you can’t keep down fluids or meds, if you’re vomiting repeatedly, if you see blood or black material in vomit or stool, if you have fever or shaking chills, worsening abdominal pain, chest pressure, shortness of breath, or signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning—today is discharge day. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, but okay. The feeds are running fine. I’m not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly where we want you. Your discharge diagnosis is oral intake intolerance, and we’ve gotten you to goal tube feeds with manageable nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I still being treated for an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your ulcer and reflux protection medications—pantoprazole and sucralfate—because of your history and symptoms. And we’re avoiding NSAIDs and aspirin because they can worsen ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What nausea meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have prochlorperazine as needed for nausea. Use it when nausea is limiting feeds or hydration, and be cautious about drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the erythromycin—how long do I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take erythromycin 250 mg every 6 hours as prescribed to help with motility. We’ll reassess at your follow-up visit based on how you’re tolerating feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already for depression and anxiety. Nothing here will mess with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home psychiatric medications—fluoxetine and aripiprazole—and your as-needed lorazepam. If you notice worsening mood, severe restlessness, or anything concerning, contact your outpatient prescriber as well as us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. When do I see Dr. ___ again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in clinic as scheduled. The appointment details are in your discharge paperwork. Bring your tube-feeding log—rates, nausea episodes, and any low blood sugar symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re stable, walking independently, and tolerating goal tube feeds. If anything changes—vomiting, dehydration, bleeding, fever, worsening pain—please call or come back. We’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery team doctor. I hear you’ve been having a burning pain in your upper abdomen that goes up into your chest and throat. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s like my whole esophagus is on fire. It started a few days ago and it’s getting worse. I’m scared it’s the same thing as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with that. Any vomiting, blood, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No black stools. I haven’t really eaten—just water. I didn’t vomit blood this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you kept your tube feeds running at home up until today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I kept them going. I only stopped when I left for the ER because I didn’t know if I should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll restart them here and keep a close eye on how you tolerate them. We’re going to check labs and get an abdominal X-ray to make sure there’s no blockage or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous? It feels like something is burning through me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sensation can be intense even when it’s irritation from acid or bile reflux. We’ll treat the symptoms right away while we evaluate. We’ll start an IV acid-suppressing medicine and nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—just making sure you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we have that listed and we’ll avoid them. For pain we’ll use acetaminophen and, if needed, your prescribed oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting IV pantoprazole now. We’re also adding prochlorperazine as needed for nausea, and we’ll continue your erythromycin since it helps your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last time the erythromycin helped, but why is this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your surgical history, you can be prone to reflux and irritation at the surgical connection sites. Sometimes inflammation flares up. We’ll also add a medication called cholestyramine to bind bile acids, which can contribute to burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cholestyramine—does that cause diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but more often it causes constipation or bloating. We’ll watch your bowel pattern and keep your stool softener on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a non-obstructive bowel gas pattern and no free air—so no sign of a blockage or perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is stuck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—nothing suggests an obstruction on that study. That supports reflux or inflammation as the cause of the burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The burning is still there, but the nausea is a little better. Am I allowed to eat anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on your baseline stage 3 diet—soft foods—only as tolerated, and continue tube feeds. The goal is to keep nutrition steady without worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. The burning comes in waves, especially when I lie flat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with reflux. Try to stay as upright as you can, especially after feeds or any oral intake. We can also raise the head of the bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are my labs okay? I’m worried I’m bleeding again from an ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is normal, and your kidney function and electrolytes look stable. Your hemoglobin is a bit low on one of the checks, but we’re not seeing signs of active bleeding like black stools or vomiting blood. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve asked the GI team to see you. They may recommend an upper endoscopy—an EGD—to look directly at the stomach and the surgical connections to see if there’s irritation or ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many procedures. Is an EGD risky for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally low risk. It’s done with sedation, and it lets us see if there are ulcers or inflammation and whether there’s any narrowing or angulation that could be worsening reflux. We’ll only proceed if it’s the best next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The cholestyramine tastes awful. Do I really need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not pleasant. If bile reflux is contributing, it can make a meaningful difference. Let’s try it consistently for now, and we’ll reassess based on your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI evaluated you this morning. They recommend adding ranitidine at bedtime in addition to the pantoprazole and sucralfate, and they agree with doing an EGD to better characterize what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on three acid medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They work in different ways: pantoprazole strongly suppresses acid, ranitidine adds extra suppression overnight, and sucralfate coats irritated areas to protect them while they heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the EGD shows an ulcer, does that mean surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Many small ulcers and gastritis can be treated with medication and avoiding triggers. The EGD helps us tailor therapy and make sure there’s no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning the EGD for today. You’ll need to be NPO—nothing by mouth—for a period beforehand. We’ll coordinate tube feeds around the procedure timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated and comfortable. Most people don’t remember the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious. Can I take my lorazepam?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you’ll be getting sedation, we’ll have anesthesia and GI guide what’s safe. We can help with anxiety here, but we need to avoid stacking sedating medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EGD is completed. The anatomy looks consistent with your post-surgical state. There was an angulation between the stomach body and antrum, but the scope passed easily and there was no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked—then why does it burn so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw small clean-based ulcerations with some friability at the gastro-gastric anastomosis, and redness in the antrum consistent with gastritis. Those irritated areas can cause significant burning and reflux symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Clean-based means it’s not bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—clean-based ulcers are less likely to be actively bleeding. We’ll still treat them aggressively with acid suppression and protective medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning after the EGD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The burning is still there but not as sharp. I actually ate some of the soft diet without it coming right back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Since your oral intake is improving, we’ll start stepping your tube feeds back down toward your outpatient rate, while making sure you’re still meeting nutrition goals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried if you lower the tube feeds I’ll get weak again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it gradually and only if you’re taking enough by mouth. The goal is to avoid overfilling your stomach and worsening reflux, while keeping your nutrition stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to stay upright even overnight? I can’t sleep sitting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You don’t have to sit straight up, but elevating the head of the bed and avoiding lying flat right after feeds can help. Even a wedge pillow or raising the bed can reduce reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re transitioning you from IV pantoprazole to oral pantoprazole twice a day. That higher dose is important for healing the gastritis and the small ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only taking it once a day at home. Twice a day is safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—twice daily is commonly used for more severe symptoms or ulcer healing. We’ll also keep ranitidine at bedtime and continue sucralfate four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the erythromycin? I’ve been on it a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing it because it helps with gastric dysmotility—your stomach emptying—and that can reduce reflux. We’ll have you keep taking it as prescribed unless your outpatient team changes it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain control? Are you needing much oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not much. Mostly Tylenol. I don’t want to get constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good plan. Use oxycodone only if needed, and keep taking docusate to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you’re looking much more comfortable. Are you tolerating the stage 3 diet and your tube feeds at the outpatient rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I still get some burning, but it’s manageable. I’m eating more than I was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your exam is reassuring—your abdomen is soft and not tender, and your G-tube site looks clean and dry. If things stay stable, we’ll plan discharge home with your existing tube-feed services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over exactly what meds I’m leaving with? I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Key changes: pantoprazole is now 40 mg by mouth twice daily. New: cholestyramine 4 grams twice daily and ranitidine liquid 150 mg at bedtime. Continue sucralfate four times daily, erythromycin every 6 hours, and your other home meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for chest pain or trouble breathing, vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, signs of dehydration like dizziness, any blood or black material in vomit or stool, fever over 101.5, or worsening pain—especially if it changes location or goes to your chest or back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the ulcers heal with this? I’m worried it’ll just keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ulcers we saw were small and clean-based, and your symptoms improved with the medication regimen—that’s a good sign. Healing can take time, so staying consistent with the acid suppression, sucralfate, and upright positioning is important. You already have follow-up scheduled with your surgeon, and we’ll keep that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you were sent in from clinic for severe abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It got really bad again. The pain is all over my stomach, and I feel like I’m going to throw up. I couldn’t handle it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. On a 0 to 10 scale, how bad is the pain right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like an 8. It comes in waves but it’s constant too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. I’ve been nauseous but I haven’t actually thrown up yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to treat your symptoms right away—IV pain medicine and an IV acid-suppressing medication called a proton pump inhibitor. You’re already on pantoprazole by mouth at home; we’ll give a higher-dose IV version here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this the same thing as last time? They said gastritis and ulcers before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your history and how you’re describing it, gastritis—irritation of the stomach lining—can definitely cause this kind of pain and nausea. We’ll also check labs tonight to make sure there’s no sign of infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s something with my tube again. The G-tube is still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I examined your abdomen and the tube site—right now it looks in place. Your belly is tender but soft, which is reassuring. We’ll keep a close eye on it and restart feeds carefully once your symptoms settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for the nausea too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ondansetron through the tube or by mouth is on your home list; we can give it here as needed. Let the nurse know as soon as you feel it building.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds… I don’t want to be knocked out, but I can’t take this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll start with IV pain medication to get you comfortable, then transition you to oral pain medication as soon as you can tolerate it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want this to drag on for weeks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our goal is to get you feeling better quickly and get you home safely. If the IV pantoprazole helps like it has before, that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your initial blood work is back. Your white blood cell count is normal, which is reassuring. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable for you. Kidney function and electrolytes look okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing in the labs suggests an emergency like a major infection. We’ll keep monitoring, but right now this fits best with gastritis-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The IV medicine—how fast should it work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain medicine works quickly. The IV pantoprazole helps reduce acid and irritation; many people feel improvement over hours to a day. We’ll reassess frequently tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now after the IV medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is down to like a 5. Still there, but not as sharp. Nausea is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. If you continue improving, we’ll restart your diet and tube feeds overnight into tomorrow, slowly, and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried eating will set it off again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common concern. We’ll start gently and stop if it worsens. The goal is to keep your nutrition going while we calm the stomach irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m checking in overnight. Any new symptoms—worsening pain, vomiting, dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is more like a 4 now. I’m tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll continue the high-dose IV pantoprazole and keep pain control steady. Try to rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than yesterday. I still feel sore, but I’m not doubled over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your morning labs look stable—kidney function and electrolytes are fine. We’ll continue IV pantoprazole. Today we’re also planning a PICC line placement so you can continue IV pantoprazole at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A PICC line… that’s the long IV, right? Why do I need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a longer IV that sits in a larger vein. Because you’re responding well to the IV pantoprazole and you’ve had recurrent severe symptoms, the plan is to discharge you on IV pantoprazole twice a day at home. A PICC makes that safer and more reliable than regular IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it painful to put in? And is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people feel pressure and a brief pinch, but it’s generally well tolerated. Risks include infection or a clot, but we minimize those with sterile technique and careful care instructions. We’ll confirm the tip position with a chest X-ray afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I still use my G-tube feeds with the PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The PICC is for the IV medication. Your tube feeds and diet plan can continue as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before the PICC team comes, I want to make sure we’re on the same page: we’ll keep your pain controlled, transition fully to oral pain meds, and keep the IV pantoprazole going. How is your pain right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 3. I can talk through it. I’d rather take pills than IV pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect—that’s exactly what we want. We’ll stick with oral pain medication as needed and avoid anything you’re allergic to—no NSAIDs or aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line has been placed. Next step is the chest X-ray to confirm it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My arm feels weird—tight. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness or a tight feeling can happen right after placement. If you notice increasing swelling, redness, fever, or severe pain, tell us right away. We’ll also have home services help you with line care after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back: the PICC tip is in the correct position in the distal SVC, and your lungs look clear—no pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to feel okay on oral pain meds and you’re tolerating your diet and tube feeds. The plan is discharge later today with home IV pantoprazole through the PICC, twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I have to do the IV pantoprazole at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with the medication and refills, and you’ll follow up with Dr. ___ to decide the duration and next steps based on your symptoms and response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds—sucralfate and rifaximin and all that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home regimen: sucralfate four times a day, rifaximin twice a day, and your other usual medications. The main change is pantoprazole will be IV every 12 hours instead of the oral daily dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the PICC get in the way of showering or sleeping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can sleep normally, but avoid pulling on it. For showering, you’ll need to keep the dressing dry—home services will teach you how to cover it and how to watch for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the pain comes back tonight at home, what do I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your prescribed oral pain medication as directed and your nausea medication if needed. If you have severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting, fever, bleeding, or you can’t tolerate feeds, you should call your surgeon’s office or come back to the emergency department.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge: your pain is controlled on oral meds, you’re tolerating your diet and tube feeds, and the PICC is functioning. Any last questions about the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… is this definitely gastritis? I’m worried we’re missing something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your symptoms, exam, and stable labs—and how well you improved with high-dose IV acid suppression—gastritis is the best explanation for this episode. We’ll keep close follow-up with Dr. ___, and if symptoms change or don’t stay controlled, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you came in with burning epigastric pain and also pain in your right arm where the PICC line goes in. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been four days. The stomach pain feels like that burning ulcer pain again, and my arm hurts right where the PICC is. It even hurts when I flush it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any vomiting, blood in vomit or stool, or fevers and chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. I’ve been retching and nauseated when I try to eat, but I’m not actually throwing up. No fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your tube feeds—are you able to keep those running? Any pain or nausea with the feeds through the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube feeds are fine. They don’t make the pain worse. It’s food by mouth that sets it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. On exam your belly is soft, but you’re tender in the upper abdomen and around the G-tube site, and your arm is tender at the PICC entry without redness or drainage. Because of the arm pain, we’re going to check for a clot with an ultrasound and also send blood cultures to look for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s a blood clot. Could it travel to my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re checking. If there were a clot in the arm veins, we’d treat it to prevent complications. The good news is you don’t have swelling or shortness of breath, but we’ll rely on the ultrasound to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound is back—no evidence of a deep vein thrombosis in the arm veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much when I flush it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the line itself can irritate the vein or surrounding tissue even without a clot, and flushing can trigger that pain. We also sent blood cultures to make sure there isn’t a bloodstream infection related to the line; those take time to finalize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was put on IV Protonix because the pills weren’t enough. If you take the PICC out, what happens to my stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the key question. You’ve been on IV pantoprazole through the PICC, but you’re still having the same burning pain with eating. Since the IV dosing hasn’t given the improvement we’d expect, and the PICC is causing significant pain, we’re leaning toward removing the PICC and switching you back to oral pantoprazole twice a day, along with your sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to remove it if the cultures aren’t back yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If anything, removing a painful line can reduce risk if it were to become infected. Right now you don’t have signs of infection at the site, and you’re not having fevers. We’ll still watch you and follow the culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain and nausea right now? We’d like to try a bariatric stage III diet by mouth in small amounts, while continuing your tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better since I got here. I can try, but I’m worried it’ll flare up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll go slowly—small sips and soft foods per stage III, and we’ll use your nausea medicine as needed. If you can tolerate that plus your tube feeds, that’s a good sign for going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight, were you able to tolerate the stage III diet and your tube feeds? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I still feel some burning, but it’s not as intense. My arm still hurts when anyone touches the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the persistent PICC-related pain and the fact that IV pantoprazole hasn’t been helping the way we hoped, we’re going to remove the PICC today and continue pantoprazole by mouth twice daily. We’ll keep your other home meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another line put in later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. The plan is oral pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day, and to keep using your tube feeds for nutrition as you’ve been doing. If symptoms worsen despite that, we’d reassess with your surgeon and GI team, but we don’t have a reason today to keep a PICC just for IV acid suppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Update: your blood cultures have shown no growth so far, which is reassuring. After the PICC removal, you’ll just need a small dressing on the arm site and to watch for redness, drainage, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What should I watch for with my stomach pain when I’m home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can’t keep down fluids or meds, if you have worsening pain, black or bloody stools, vomit that looks like blood or coffee grounds, fevers over 101.5, chest pain, or shortness of breath—come back or call right away. Otherwise, continue stage III bariatric diet as tolerated plus your tube feeds, stay hydrated, walk several times a day, and avoid heavy lifting until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I follow up with my surgeon, right? I just want this to stop happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you came in with worsening upper abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me what today has been like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same burning pain in the middle, but way worse this morning. Even water makes it flare. I threw up once—just watery, not bloody.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, chest pain, trouble breathing, or black or bloody stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I had a bowel movement this morning and I’m passing gas. I just feel a little bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Given your history—Roux-en-Y bypass with reversal, ulcers, tube feeds—we’re taking this seriously. In the ED your bloodwork looked reassuring: no infection signs, electrolytes okay, liver tests and lipase normal, and lactate normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much if the labs are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain can still be severe even when labs are normal, especially with chronic ulcer-type pain, reflux, and changes after multiple abdominal surgeries. We also want to rule out dangerous things like obstruction or a perforation—those can sometimes show up on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you thinking I need surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Bariatric surgery already evaluated you in the ED and they don’t think you need surgical intervention right now. Our plan is medical management: pain and nausea control, acid suppression, and careful diet advancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat? Last time they told me not to take anything by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight we’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—so we can settle things down and make sure there’s no obstruction. We’ll continue your tube feeds at your goal rate so you’re still getting nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the tube feeds will make the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Since you’ve been on continuous feeds at home, we expect you can tolerate them, but if it clearly worsens symptoms we’ll reassess. We’ll also treat nausea so you’re more comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me for pain? Tylenol doesn’t touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use a stepwise approach: acetaminophen as needed, and your liquid oxycodone as needed for breakthrough pain. We’ll also continue your pantoprazole and sucralfate to protect the stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin, so I can’t take those anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—so we’ll avoid them. We’ll also use ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is back—no free air under the diaphragm and no acute lung issues. That’s reassuring against a perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the belly X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows a nonobstructive bowel gas pattern—no signs of a small bowel obstruction, and no free air. Your G-tube is seen in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not blocked. Then why does drinking water hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With reflux or ulcer irritation, even small amounts of liquid can trigger burning pain. Also, after multiple surgeries, the stomach and intestines can have altered motility—things don’t move as smoothly, which can cause discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this just going to keep happening? I’ve been in the hospital so many times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Part of our work this admission is symptom control, but also setting a realistic plan: this may not fully resolve in a day or two. We want to stabilize you and coordinate with your bariatric and GI teams to build a regimen that improves quality of life over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any more vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more vomiting. Still nauseated on and off. Pain is a little better after meds but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your morning labs are stable—no electrolyte problems and no signs of infection. We’d like to try advancing you to clear liquids by mouth today, very slowly, while continuing tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What counts as clear liquids? And what if it burns again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sips of water, clear nutritional drinks if tolerated. If it flares, stop and let us know—this is a trial, not a test you have to push through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a few sips. It stung but I didn’t throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful information. We’ll keep it slow. We’re also thinking about bacterial overgrowth and dysmotility contributing to symptoms, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my ammonia was high before? They told me it might be overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, bacterial overgrowth can contribute to symptoms like bloating, discomfort, and sometimes lab abnormalities. It’s not the only possibility, but it’s one piece we can treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you going to do for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start a short trial of erythromycin. In low doses it can help gut motility, and sometimes that reduces nausea and pain related to slow movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that an antibiotic? I’m worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is an antibiotic, but here we’re using it mainly for its motility effect. We’ll use a limited course and watch for stomach upset. If it makes things worse, we’ll stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how are the clear liquids going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do small sips. I’m still scared to eat. I don’t want to trigger it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. Our goal isn’t to force solid food right now. We’ll keep tube feeds as your main nutrition and use oral intake as gentle practice—water and maybe an Ensure-type shake if tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My reflux feels worse when I lie down. Is there anything else besides pantoprazole and sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We can add ranitidine at night to help with nighttime acid and reflux symptoms. It works differently than pantoprazole, so the combination can help some people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interfere with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally compatible with your current regimen. We’ll keep an eye on how you feel, and you should continue taking sucralfate as prescribed since it coats the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today compared with when you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not gone, but it’s steadier. I haven’t thrown up again. I did okay with cream of wheat and a little pudding yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your exam is reassuring—your abdomen is soft and only minimally tender, and the G-tube site looks okay without redness or warmth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you know if I have H. pylori again? I’ve had ulcers before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent H. pylori blood testing. The result isn’t back yet, so it will be pending at discharge. We’ll make sure the outpatient team follows it, and we’ll also tell you how to check the result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it’s positive, what happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s positive, your doctors would prescribe a specific combination of medications to eradicate it. For now, we’re continuing strong acid suppression and lining protection, which is appropriate either way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge later today if you continue to tolerate tube feeds and small amounts by mouth and your pain stays controlled with your home regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home. What if it spikes again tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The key is having a clear plan: continue tube feeds at your goal rate, keep oral intake gentle, and use your prescribed nausea and pain meds. If you can’t keep anything down, have repeated vomiting, severe worsening pain, black or bloody stools, fever, or you feel faint—those are reasons to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you changing my tube feed formula? I use Jevity 1.2 at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
