conversation_lines.text: Nutrition recommends Jevity 1.5 at 50 mL/hour as a goal. If you’re staying on 1.2 for now, your outpatient provider who manages tube feeds can adjust and write the prescription if a change is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What new meds am I leaving with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two main additions: ranitidine 150 mg nightly for reflux, and a short course of erythromycin 250 mg three times daily. We’re also adding rifaximin 550 mg three times daily for a short course to target possible bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rifaximin is expensive, isn’t it? I can’t afford another medication I can’t fill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with your home pharmacy and it should be affordable. If there’s any issue at pickup, call the bariatric clinic right away so they can help troubleshoot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I take the erythromycin and rifaximin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re short courses—about a week. At your bariatric surgery follow-up, you’ll review whether they’re helping and decide whether to continue or stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the goal is not that I’m pain-free, just stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want you safe—no obstruction, no dehydration, no ongoing vomiting—and on a plan that gradually improves symptoms. With your surgical history, it often takes weeks to months of careful adjustments with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review: continue pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate four times daily, add ranitidine nightly, finish erythromycin and rifaximin as prescribed, keep tube feeds running, and slowly advance oral intake as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I can only do water and shakes for a while, that’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Water and Ensure-type shakes are a reasonable start. Add solids very slowly over weeks to months, only as tolerated, and keep close follow-up with bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want my life back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal, and we’ll keep working toward it with you. You’re leaving in stable condition, and you can always reach out if symptoms change or you’re worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you were just here a few days ago and you’re back with worse abdominal pain—can you tell me what changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s different this time. Before it was burning all over, but now it’s really focused right around my G-tube. It scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to come in. Any fevers or chills? Any vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No vomiting today. I had a normal bowel movement yesterday. I’m just in a lot of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still running your tube feeds at home? And are you taking anything by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been doing the feeds. I’ve only been able to do clears—Ensure and Carnation Instant Breakfast. I thought maybe I needed a night off the feeds because it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the emergency department your vital signs were stable, and the bariatric surgery team saw you. They recommended we admit you, give your stomach and abdominal wall a rest, and have GI weigh in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think the tube is infected or moved? I keep looking at it and worrying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now the skin around the tube doesn’t look infected—no spreading redness, warmth, or drainage that worries us. The tube also appears to be sitting appropriately. But we’ll keep checking it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to examine your abdomen. Tell me where it hurts most.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right there—around the tube. Even light touch hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to have you tense your abdominal muscles—like a small sit-up—while I press gently in the same spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ow—yeah, it hurts more when I tighten up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That pattern suggests the pain may be coming from the abdominal wall muscles near the tube site rather than deeper inside the abdomen. It doesn’t rule everything out, but it’s helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not like an obstruction again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray—the KUB—showed a non-obstructive bowel gas pattern and no free air, which is reassuring. It did show some gas distention in part of the stomach, which can contribute to discomfort, but no signs of a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They mentioned maybe an endoscopy. Am I going to need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bariatric team suggested we consider it depending on how you do and what GI thinks. Tonight our plan is bowel rest—hold tube feeds overnight—control pain and nausea, and reassess in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone at home didn’t touch it. I felt like I had no choice but to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll treat your pain here, but we also want a plan that works at home. We’ll continue your usual stomach-protecting medicines—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate—and your antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth, rifaximin and erythromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it okay to keep taking all of those? I’m scared something is making this worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what we’re seeing, we don’t have a clear medication culprit. We’ll keep monitoring, and if anything changes—new fever, worsening redness, vomiting—we’ll adjust quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you promise I’m not being brushed off? I feel like people think it’s just anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not being brushed off. Your pain is real, and you’ve been through a lot medically. Anxiety can amplify symptoms, but it doesn’t mean the pain isn’t real. We’ll address both the physical pain and the stress it causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For tonight: we’ll hold tube feeds, give IV fluids as needed, and use nausea medicine like ondansetron. For pain, we’ll use what’s safest and effective while we evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If we stop the feeds, will my blood sugar drop? I’ve had hypoglycemia issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re holding feeds just overnight, and we’ll keep a close eye on you. If you feel shaky, sweaty, or lightheaded, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It still hurts when I move. The site looks the same, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—still no concerning signs of infection. The tenderness is localized, and your abdomen remains soft without signs that would suggest an emergency inside the belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night with the feeds held?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t vomit. The pain is still there, but I guess it didn’t get worse overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Today we’d like to restart your tube feeds at your goal rate and see if it increases the pain. If it doesn’t, that supports that the feeds aren’t the main trigger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. What if it flares up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart while you’re here so we can watch closely. If pain spikes, we can pause and reassess. We’ll also keep you on clears by mouth as you’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you still thinking about an endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, because the imaging doesn’t show obstruction or free air and your symptoms are localized to the abdominal wall near the tube, we’re focusing on medical management. GI can help guide whether an endoscopy would add value, but it may not be necessary during this short stay if you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to talk about pain control. You’re already on gabapentin 300 mg three times a day at home. We think increasing it may help with this abdominal wall-type pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Increase it to what? And will it make me too sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to increase to 600 mg three times a day. Sleepiness can happen, especially at first. We’ll monitor you here, and if you feel too drowsy or unsteady, tell us—we can adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to be able to function at home. I’m tired of coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Along with medication changes, we also want a clear plan for who to call when pain flares—so you’re not stuck feeling the hospital is the only option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The feeds are running again. It’s uncomfortable but not worse than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep them at goal. Nutrition also reviewed your formula—here we recommend Jevity 1.5 at 50 mL per hour. I know you’ve used Jevity 1.2 at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have to switch? I don’t want a mess with supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You don’t have to change today. The recommendation is for outpatient planning—if your outpatient provider managing tube feeds thinks it’s appropriate, they can write for it. We’ll include it in your discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A social worker is going to stop by today. The goal is to support coping strategies and make sure you feel supported with the chronic pain plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I do have a therapist, but sometimes it feels like no one can help when the pain hits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want to address—what you can do in the moment, and who you can reach out to. We’ll also make sure you have a clear plan to contact your GI doctor with questions about abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today compared with when you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s closer to my usual baseline. Still sore around the tube, but I’m not panicking like I was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam the tube site has only minimal redness and it looks like it’s improving. No signs of deeper infection, and your abdomen remains soft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused it? Did I do something wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You didn’t do anything wrong. The pattern fits abdominal wall pain—sometimes the muscles and tissues around the tube get irritated and become very tender. The stomach gas distention seen on the X-ray may also have contributed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One other thing: your white blood cell count is mildly low. It was 2.3 and improved to 2.8 today, still a bit below your baseline. You don’t have signs of infection, and we don’t see a clear medication cause right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low white count sounds scary. Am I immunocompromised?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can sound alarming, but mild leukopenia like this can happen and often resolves. Because it’s low, we want you to repeat a CBC with your primary care doctor in about a week to make sure it trends back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going home today? I’m worried the pain will spike again tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning discharge today since you’re back to baseline, tolerating clears by mouth, and tolerating tube feeds at goal without worsening pain. We’ll send you home with the increased gabapentin dose and your other home medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly changes with my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main change is gabapentin: increase to 600 mg three times a day. You’ll continue pantoprazole twice a day, ranitidine daily, sucralfate four times a day, and ondansetron as needed. You’ll also continue erythromycin and rifaximin to complete the planned courses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone? I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone liquid only as prescribed for breakthrough pain. The goal is that the gabapentin increase helps reduce how often you need it. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy and ulcer history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the pain gets bad again, what should I do first?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, use your prescribed medications and your coping plan. For questions about your chronic abdominal pain and tube-feed related symptoms, contact your GI doctor—don’t wait until it’s unbearable. If you have red flags like fever, persistent vomiting, worsening redness or drainage at the tube site, or severe pain with a hard abdomen, then come to the emergency department.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still anxious, but I feel better having a plan. Will I keep seeing my therapist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—please continue with your outpatient therapist. We’re also continuing your home medications for depression and anxiety—fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and lorazepam as needed, plus zolpidem as needed for sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m ready to go home. Thank you for taking it seriously.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you’ve had worsening abdominal pain for about three days, mostly around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sharp constant pain right where the tube is. My belly also feels really full. It’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, chills, redness, drainage, or pus around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. It looks the same. Just hurts a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, blood in stool, black stools, or not passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bleeding. I’m passing gas and I’ve had bowel movements. I do get nauseated sometimes, but mostly it’s pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with tube feeds at home? Did you try holding them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t hold them. If I stop, my sugar drops fast. But when I run feeds, the pain feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your history of hypoglycemia. Our first priority is keeping your blood sugar safe while we figure out the pain. We’ll check fingerstick sugars regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared you’re going to tell me it’s all in my head again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Your pain is real. The question is what’s driving it—tube site irritation, abdominal wall pain, stomach irritation, or something else. We’ll take it step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam, I don’t see signs of infection at the tube site—no redness, swelling, or drainage. Your belly is soft, and the tenderness is mostly around the tube and left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens tonight? I can’t keep doing this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tonight we’ll rest your stomach: nothing by mouth for now, hold the tube feeds, give IV fluids with dextrose to protect your blood sugar, and treat pain and nausea. We’ll continue your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop my feeds, will my sugar crash even with the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use dextrose-containing IV fluids and check your sugars every four hours. If we see them trending down, we can adjust quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think the tube is in the wrong place or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s nothing suggesting it’s displaced—no leakage, no severe distention, and you’re still passing gas and stool. We’ll keep monitoring closely, and if anything changes we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs look reassuring—no major abnormalities that point to infection or pancreatitis. We’ll repeat labs as needed and keep an eye on hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also really anxious. Every time I’m here I feel like I’m stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll keep your home medications for anxiety and depression going, and we can also involve support services if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after we held the tube feeds and started the dextrose IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain eased up some. Still there, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful information. Your blood sugars overnight stayed in a safe range, and you didn’t have symptoms of low sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean the feeds are causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests the pain may be triggered by feeding or by the tube itself—either the stomach being stimulated or the abdominal wall around the tube. It doesn’t mean anything dangerous is happening, but it guides our plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At this point, no. We’re managing conservatively, and there’s no sign you need an operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got a chest X-ray yesterday to make sure there wasn’t an infection in the lungs contributing to symptoms. It was clear—no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to know why I keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a complicated course after bariatric surgery and reversal, and you’re balancing two hard problems: protecting your stomach lining and managing hypoglycemia. We’re going to try to reduce reliance on tube feeds if it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’d like to start a careful trial of oral intake—small amounts, spaced out—while we continue to monitor sugars. How does your pain feel this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than when I came in. I’m nervous to eat because it hurts when I try solids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start gently. The goal is to see if you can meet your needs by mouth without triggering pain or low sugars. We’ll keep nausea medicine available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my sugar drops, what will I feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Common symptoms are shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, or feeling very hungry. If you feel any of those, call right away—we’ll check a fingerstick and treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been slowly weaning the dextrose IV. Your fingerstick sugars have stayed stable, mostly in the low 100s, and you’ve been asymptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That surprises me. I thought I couldn’t go without the tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be that with the right pattern of eating—small, frequent, low-glycemic carbs with protein—you can maintain safer sugars. We want to prove that safely here before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not eating much. I don’t have an appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been tracking your intake with calorie counts, and you’re right—it’s been low. If it stays low, we’ll need a strategy to help you eat enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to talk about appetite. Since your intake has been poor, we’d like to start a medication called dronabinol—also known as Marinol—to stimulate appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with everything else I’m on? And will it make me feel weird?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start at a low dose and monitor you. Some people feel sleepy or a little off; if that happens, tell us and we can adjust. The goal is to help you take in enough calories by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do after starting Marinol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually felt hungry for the first time in a while. I ate more yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your calorie count improved significantly, and your sugars stayed stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can keep the tube off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’re encouraged. We’ll keep the tube feeds held while we confirm you can consistently meet most of your needs by mouth and keep sugars safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is still there, but it’s less intense when the feeds aren’t running. Is that what you’re seeing too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pain pattern fits with that. We’re continuing your acid suppression and sucralfate, and using pain medication as needed while trying to avoid anything you’re allergic to like NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll go home and crash again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re building a plan you can follow at home: structured eating, glucose monitoring, and close follow-up. We’ll also make sure you have clear instructions on when to seek help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A specialist team is going to meet with you about managing hypoglycemia with diet—small frequent meals, low-glycemic carbs, and protein-focused snacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you explain low-glycemic in plain terms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means choosing carbs that don’t spike your blood sugar quickly—paired with protein. The goal is to avoid big swings: no rapid highs followed by lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your intake yesterday was close to 90% of your daily calorie goal—about 1400 to 1600 calories out of an 1800 calorie target. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t think I could do that. The Marinol really helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your fingerstick sugars remain steady in the low 100s without symptoms. That’s exactly what we want to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m eating more, why do I still need the tube at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it’s a safety net. The plan is not to remove it immediately. We want sustained stability at home first, then reassess in clinic. The long-term plan is to remove it in a few months if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is the nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’ve only needed the ondansetron once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Less nausea usually makes it easier to keep up with the small frequent meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still anxious at night. I keep thinking my sugar will drop while I’m asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear is common with your history. We’ll review a home monitoring plan: checking before bed, and checking more often if you feel symptoms. We also recommend using your Dexcom continuous glucose monitor to watch trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to practice the discharge routine while you’re still here: meals and snacks spaced out, protein snacks, and glucose checks before meals and at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I’m about to drive and I’m not sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar before driving, and don’t drive if you feel symptoms. If it’s low, treat it and recheck. We’ll put that in your written instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. It’s not gone, but it’s not like when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s consistent with what we’ve seen: holding tube feeds reduced the pain, and you’ve been able to maintain nutrition by mouth with Marinol support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse said something about tube feeding again today. Are we restarting it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing a controlled reintroduction of nutrition through the tube today to make sure you can tolerate it if you ever need it as backup. We’ll watch your pain and sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’ll flare the pain back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it does, we’ll stop and reassess. The goal is to leave you with a safe plan—either oral-only if you’re stable, or a backup option if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you feel with the tube nutrition trial this afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It didn’t go great at first, but it wasn’t unbearable. I’m still better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that helps us tailor the plan. We’ll keep focusing on oral intake as the main strategy, with the tube as backup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge day if everything stays stable. You’ve been afebrile, your vitals are stable, your labs have been reassuring, and your sugars have stayed steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m happy to go home, but I’m scared the pain will come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the pain worsens, if you develop fever, redness or drainage at the tube site, persistent vomiting, or you can’t keep your sugars safe—those are reasons to call or come back. Otherwise, we’ll manage this outpatient with close follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly do I need to do for the sugar plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small frequent meals with low-glycemic carbs, spaced out through the day; snacks should be protein without carbs. Check glucose before meals and at bedtime, and more often if you have symptoms or before driving. Use your Dexcom to watch trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube—are you taking it out now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. You’ll follow up with our surgery clinic in a few weeks to re-evaluate the tube. If you keep doing well, the plan is to remove it in several months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I stay on all my stomach meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine daily, and sucralfate four times daily as prescribed. Those help protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have acetaminophen liquid as needed and your oxycodone liquid as needed, and continue gabapentin. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy and ulcer risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I can do that. I just want my life back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ve made real progress this admission—less pain off feeds, better oral intake with Marinol, and stable sugars. We’ll support you closely after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. I hear you’re back with abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was fine after I got home, eating okay, sugars were in the 100s. Then I woke up with this constant pain right at my G-tube site and it shoots to my left side. Every time I try to eat, I throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills? Any blood in the vomit or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No blood. Just nausea and vomiting and the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are your bowel movements—any constipation, diarrhea, or not passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No big change. I’m passing gas. I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam, the area is tender but I don’t see redness, swelling, or drainage around the tube. Your vitals and initial labs look reassuring so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much? I’m scared something is leaking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand the worry, especially with your prior scans and the ulcer irritation at the connection site. Tonight, we’ll treat this conservatively: nothing by mouth for now, IV fluids, and nausea and pain control while we watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m not eating, won’t my sugar crash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll check your blood sugar regularly while you’re here, and the IV fluids will help keep you hydrated. If your glucose trends low, we can adjust the fluids and treat it quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you do something for the nausea right now? I feel like I’m going to vomit again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s start with ondansetron, and we can add another medication like prochlorperazine if needed. We’ll also vent the G-tube to release any built-up air or stomach contents and see if that eases the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Venting it won’t mess it up? I’m worried it’s blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it gently and check that it’s patent. Right now it appears unobstructed, and venting is a common way to relieve nausea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is a little better after the medicine, but the pain is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll use acetaminophen first and reserve stronger liquid pain medication only if you need it. We want to control pain but also avoid worsening nausea or constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight, your labs stayed within normal limits. We also got chest and abdominal X-rays—no free air and no signs of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is wrong? Then why am I vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging rules out some dangerous causes like perforation or a clear blockage. It doesn’t always show irritation or functional issues. Given your history of ulcerations and gastritis, we’re going to keep your stomach-protective meds going—pantoprazole and sucralfate—and keep treating symptoms while we reintroduce intake slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water at least?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can start with small sips and see how you do. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down some sips, but I’m scared to eat. Last time it set everything off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll go stepwise—clear liquids first, then something bland. We’ll keep the G-tube clamped if you’re comfortable, and we can vent it again if nausea builds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the tube in the right place? It was exchanged recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on what we’ve seen and how it functions when we vent it, it appears to be in place and not blocked. If symptoms persist, we can get more detailed imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate a little and didn’t throw up, but the pain near the tube still comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress on the vomiting. For the pain, we’ll keep using non-NSAID options since you’re allergic and NSAIDs can worsen ulcers. We’ll also keep nausea meds available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How was your night? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. I’m still nauseated sometimes, but the zofran helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Today we’ll advance your diet a bit more if you’re willing, and we’ll resume your home medications. We’ll keep checking your blood sugars—so far they’ve stayed in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about going home and ending up right back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real concern. Our goal is to make sure you can keep food down, your pain and nausea are controlled with oral meds, and your sugars stay stable with your usual routine before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think this is from the ulcer area again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be irritation at the gastrogastric connection where you’ve had small clean-based ulcers and gastritis seen on endoscopy before. That’s why we’re emphasizing acid suppression with pantoprazole and coating with sucralfate. But we also want to be sure there isn’t another cause, especially since you’re having recurrent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it’s inflammation around the surgical connections, irritation from the tube site, or functional stomach emptying issues. If symptoms don’t keep improving, we’ll get a CT scan to look for abscess, obstruction, or anything acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning, you look more comfortable. How’s the pain and nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than when I came in. I still feel sore around the tube, and I’m nervous to eat full meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep meals small and frequent. The nutrition team will also check in—what matters is whether you’re meeting enough of your calorie needs by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need tube feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we’re holding tube feeds because they seemed to worsen symptoms before, and you’ve been able to take food by mouth. If you can consistently meet your needs orally and sugars stay stable, we can avoid restarting feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is really bad when the pain spikes. I keep thinking something is being missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s been so stressful. We’ll keep you updated step by step. It’s also okay to use your as-needed anxiety medication if you need it, and we’ll make sure your depression and anxiety meds are continued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had intermittent pain and nausea despite some improvement, so we’re going to get a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast today to look for any acute cause like obstruction or a collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the CT safe with my tube and all the surgery I’ve had?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The scan will help us see the anastomoses and confirm the G-tube position. You’ll drink oral contrast and also get IV contrast, and we’ll monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s going to show a leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If there were a leak or abscess, we’d act quickly. The good news is your vitals and labs have stayed stable, which makes a major leak less likely, but the CT will give us more confidence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have your CT results. It shows normal-appearing surgical connections without evidence of obstruction, and the G-tube balloon is appropriately positioned in the stomach. There’s no abscess or other abnormality to explain the nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s normal… but I still feel it. What does that mean for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we’re not seeing anything dangerous that needs surgery right now. The plan is to keep managing this conservatively—control nausea, protect the stomach lining, and focus on steady oral intake while we work on longer-term outpatient strategies for the recurrent pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If tonight goes well—no vomiting, pain controlled with oral meds, and you’re eating enough—then yes, discharge tomorrow is reasonable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’m still tender, but I’m not throwing up. Zofran is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The dietitian reviewed your intake, and it looks like you’re taking in more than 75% of what you need by mouth. Your blood sugars have also stayed in normal limits during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’re keeping the tube in place, but you can keep it clamped. If you feel bloated or nauseated, you can vent it as you were taught. We’ll continue to reassess as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sugar plan? I’m scared of hypoglycemia if I’m eating small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick with the plan you were given: small frequent low-glycemic meals, protein-based snacks, and check glucose before meals and at bedtime, and more often if you have symptoms or before driving. Keep using your Dexcom to watch trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home on for this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day to protect the stomach. You’ll have oral ondansetron for nausea as needed. For pain, acetaminophen first, and a small amount of liquid oxycodone only if pain is severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the marinol? That helped my appetite last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue dronabinol twice a day since it supports appetite and helps you meet your calorie needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I worry and come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call urgently if you can’t keep liquids down, have worsening abdominal pain that doesn’t respond to meds, fever or chills, blood in vomit or stool, black stools, or if your sugars are repeatedly low and not responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried this is going to be my life—pain, admissions, and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The CT being reassuring helps us focus on outpatient management—stomach protection, nutrition strategies, and follow-up with your surgical team and dietitian. We’ll also make sure your mental health medications continue and that you have support, because the stress of recurrent symptoms is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, can you repeat back the main plan—diet, glucose checks, and meds—so I know it’s clear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Small frequent low-glycemic meals, protein snacks, check sugars before meals and bedtime and use my Dexcom. Keep the tube clamped but vent if needed. Take pantoprazole and sucralfate, use zofran for nausea, Tylenol first for pain and only a little oxycodone if I really need it. And keep my follow-up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll discharge you home now. Please take it easy for the next few days and reach out if symptoms flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with a lot of diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, and worsening belly pain around the G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on since you left the hospital last week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was bad pain near the tube, but the oxycodone kept it under control. Then two days ago I started having nonstop diarrhea—like more than nine times a day—and I couldn’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Any fevers or chills? Anyone around you sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No sick contacts that I know of.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting—when did that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday. My surgeon told me to try Imodium, and after I took it I got really nauseated and threw up like eight times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The last time had little specks of blood. I was retching a lot. No black stools though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that detail helps. Small streaks after repeated retching can be from irritation in the throat or upper stomach, but we’ll keep a close eye on it. Right now your blood pressure and oxygen look okay, and your labs in the ER didn’t show infection or kidney trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s something wrong with the tube or my surgery again. The pain is right there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. Bariatric Surgery has already weighed in and doesn’t think this looks like a surgical complication today. Your belly exam is tender but soft, and there’s no guarding. We’ll still be cautious and check for things like obstruction if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what are you doing for me now? I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, IV fluids to treat dehydration from the diarrhea and vomiting. Second, nausea medicine through the IV. Third, pain control—starting with IV medication while you can’t tolerate pills, then switching back to your liquid oxycodone when you’re able to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—please don’t give those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin. We’ll use options that are safe with your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also going to send stool tests. Given the volume of diarrhea, we want to rule out C. difficile and check for viral causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. Could it be back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, so we’re testing. The good news is your white blood cell count is normal and you don’t have a fever, which makes severe bacterial infection less likely, but the stool test will help us be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is so dry. Am I really that dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your exam shows dry mucous membranes, and with more than nine diarrheal stools a day it adds up quickly. The IV fluids should help you feel better over the next several hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any more vomiting since you arrived?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting here. Still diarrhea though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now and slowly reintroduce liquids when your nausea is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your abdominal pain and G-tube history, we’re getting a plain abdominal X-ray to look at the bowel gas pattern and make sure there’s no obstruction or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a CT scan? I don’t want a lot of radiation again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s much less radiation than a CT. It’s a quick X-ray—helpful as a screening test when the exam is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain meds help, but I’m scared I’ll be stuck on them. I only feel okay when it’s scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to treat the acute pain while your stomach and intestines recover, then step back to the lowest amount you need. Today we’ll use IV medication only while you can’t take anything by mouth, and we’ll switch back to your home liquid oxycodone as soon as you’re tolerating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows no obstruction or ileus and no free air. The G-tube is seen in the left upper abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no evidence of blockage on the X-ray, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my stomach meds? I’m worried about my ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re continuing acid protection. While you’re not eating much, we’ll start with IV proton pump inhibitor, then switch back to your home pantoprazole by mouth when you can tolerate it, along with ranitidine and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We collected the stool sample tonight. Results will take some time, but we should have the C. diff test back soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting or more blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No more blood. Still crampy and going to the bathroom a lot, but maybe a little less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your electrolytes and kidney function look stable this morning. We’ll keep IV fluids going and recheck labs as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile test is negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stool viral panel came back positive for norovirus. That’s a common, very contagious viral gastroenteritis that causes sudden diarrhea and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—antibiotics don’t help norovirus. Treatment is supportive: fluids, nausea control, and time. Most people improve over a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did the Imodium make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can in some cases—slowing the gut during an infection can make people feel more bloated or nauseated. The key now is hydration and letting your body clear the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you haven’t vomited here, we can try sips of clear liquids and then advance to a light bariatric diet as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to eat. Every time I try at home, I get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. We’ll go slowly—small amounts, frequent sips, and we’ll give ondansetron as needed. If nausea returns, we pause and step back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube—should I vent it like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel very bloated or nauseated, venting can sometimes help, but right now your symptoms fit norovirus more than a tube problem. We’ll have nursing help you if you need to vent it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now that you’ve had some fluids and nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still sore around the G-tube, but not as sharp. I’d like to switch off the IV meds if I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. If you’re tolerating liquids, we can transition from IV morphine to your oral liquid oxycodone every 4 hours as needed, like your prior discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take dronabinol for appetite, but I think I reacted to it before. Are you giving it to me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding dronabinol during this gastroenteritis, especially since you reported a possible prior reaction. Once you’re fully recovered, you can discuss whether to restart it with your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You had a low-grade temperature overnight but you look much better. How many diarrheal episodes since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Way fewer. I’m still going, but it’s not constant. I kept down the bariatric tray last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s what we need to see: improving diarrhea and reliable oral intake. Your labs this morning look stable as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the blood specks I had at home—do I need a scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it was small volume, happened after repeated vomiting, and you’ve had no further vomiting or bleeding here, it’s most consistent with irritation from retching. We’re continuing your acid-suppressing meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate. If you have recurrent vomiting with blood, black stools, or feel faint, you should seek care right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I contagious? I don’t want my husband to get this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Norovirus is very contagious. At home, wash hands with soap and water, clean high-touch surfaces, and avoid preparing food for others until you’re fully better. If possible, use a separate bathroom for a couple of days after symptoms stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge today if you continue to tolerate food and your symptoms keep improving. Any concerns about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the pain will spike again and I’ll end up back here. And I still want this G-tube out eventually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain, we’ll send you home on the same liquid oxycodone plan you had before, plus acetaminophen as needed—no NSAIDs. For the G-tube, that decision should be made with your bariatric surgery team once your oral intake is consistently good; we’ll make sure you have follow-up arranged with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw something about protein in my urine. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urinalysis showed a small amount of protein. It can happen transiently with illness or dehydration. We recommend repeating it with your outpatient doctor once you’re recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep all my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your home medications: fluoxetine and aripiprazole for mood, lorazepam as needed for anxiety, gabapentin for neuropathy, atorvastatin for cholesterol, and zolpidem as needed for sleep. Continue pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate for stomach protection, and ondansetron as needed for nausea. We’re recommending you do not restart dronabinol until you’ve fully recovered and have discussed it with your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more item: we sent a rectal swab to screen for resistant bacteria while you were here. It came back with no VRE isolated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And diet—what am I supposed to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on Bariatric Diet Stage 5. Keep portions small, focus on what you tolerate, and prioritize hydration. If diarrhea worsens again and you can’t keep fluids down, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also want to switch to a new primary care doctor. Can you help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’ll give you the information to establish with a new PCP and instructions on how to transfer your records. It’s important for follow-up on the urine protein, your nutrition, and medication management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: your diagnosis is norovirus gastroenteritis. You improved with IV fluids, nausea control, and pain management, and you’re now eating and drinking. Do you feel ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still tired, but I’m not vomiting and the diarrhea is better. I just want to recover at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you were just discharged a few days ago and you’re back with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and trouble keeping anything down. Can you tell me what’s been happening at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It never really stopped. I’m still throwing up and having watery diarrhea. I can’t keep food or even much liquid down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit or stool? Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fevers. I’m just exhausted and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your abdominal pain compared to your usual baseline pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not worse than usual. Mostly it’s the nausea. The area around the tube is sore like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER your vital signs were stable and you didn’t have a fever. Your labs looked overall reassuring—kidney function was okay, and your blood counts were okay. One liver enzyme, AST, was mildly elevated, which can happen with dehydration or stress on the body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still the norovirus? Why is it lasting this long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading thought—ongoing viral gastroenteritis. Some people have a longer course, and with your altered GI anatomy from the bypass and reversal, your gut can be more sensitive and take longer to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another scan? I’m scared something is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bariatric surgery team reviewed your case in the ER and didn’t think imaging was needed right now because your exam and labs don’t suggest obstruction, and your symptoms match what you just had. We’ll keep checking you—if anything changes, we’ll reassess quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you going to do for the nausea? The Zofran helps but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule ondansetron (Zofran) regularly and add prochlorperazine (Compazine) as needed. We’ll also give IV fluids to treat dehydration and let your stomach rest with a clear liquid diet to start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to use my G-tube for feeds? I can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now we’re going to hold tube feeds because they can worsen diarrhea while your gut is inflamed. The goal is to hydrate you through the IV and then slowly restart oral intake as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll get weak again. I feel shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll monitor your electrolytes closely and keep an eye on your blood sugar symptoms too. Right now your labs don’t show dangerous electrolyte problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something for pain? The ER gave me Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prioritize your home regimen—gabapentin and liquid acetaminophen—and use your liquid oxycodone only if needed. Strong IV opioids can slow the gut and sometimes worsen nausea and abdominal discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate feeling like I’m being punished for asking for pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not being punished. We’re trying to balance pain control with getting your stomach and intestines to settle. We’ll check in often and adjust if you’re suffering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: we started IV fluids. We’ll recheck labs in the morning. Tonight, try small sips of clear liquids if you can—ice chips, water, broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I throw up again, do I have to start over?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. If you vomit, we’ll pause, treat the nausea, and then try again more slowly. The goal is gradual progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting? How many diarrhea episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up once. Diarrhea is still there, a few times overnight. I’m still nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Your morning labs show your potassium is in a safe range and your kidney numbers look good. We’ll keep fluids going and continue Zofran scheduled with Compazine as backup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to repeat stool tests? Last time they said norovirus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you were just diagnosed recently and your symptoms are the same, we’re not repeating stool studies right now. If you develop fever, blood in stool, or things change, we would reconsider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about C. diff? I’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. On your last admission, testing for toxigenic C. diff was negative. With no new antibiotic exposure and no new red flags, it’s less likely—but we’ll stay alert for signs that would prompt retesting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take Imodium? I just want the diarrhea to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to avoid loperamide for you because it previously made your abdominal symptoms worse. Instead we’ll focus on hydration, gentle diet, and letting the virus run its course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with clears? Any dizziness when you stand?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little dizzy earlier, but better now. I can keep down some water and broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep IV fluids for now and start adding oral nutrition supplements with meals as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site looks crusty. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I looked earlier—there’s some serosanguinous crusting around the site, but no signs of a deep infection like spreading redness, pus, or fever. We’ll keep it clean and continue your topical mupirocin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any vomiting since yesterday? How’s the diarrhea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. Diarrhea is less frequent, still watery though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your electrolytes remain stable. We can start advancing your diet from clears to soft foods today, and keep the Ensure supplements with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to eat. Every time I try, I feel sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense after what you’ve been through. We’ll go slowly—small portions, bland foods, and we’ll time anti-nausea medication before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Someone mentioned bacterial overgrowth before. Could this be that instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did consider small intestinal bacterial overgrowth because of your surgical history. But since you’re improving with supportive care, we’re not pursuing testing during this admission. If symptoms persist after discharge, your outpatient team can revisit it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain today? Are you needing much oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Less than yesterday. I took one dose. Mostly I’m using Tylenol and my gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good balance. We’ll keep minimizing opioids to help your gut recover, but you’ll have your home liquid oxycodone available if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Are you tolerating soft foods? Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate a little and kept it down. Still some nausea, but no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We can advance toward a regular diet as tolerated today, still focusing on small frequent meals and supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home? I’m worried it’ll come right back again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main discharge criteria are: you can keep down enough fluids and food to stay hydrated, nausea is controlled with oral meds, and your labs are stable. If today goes well, we’ll aim for discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need tube feeds when I’m home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We held tube feeds here because of diarrhea. If you’re meeting your needs by mouth, we’d prefer oral intake. You should follow up with bariatric surgery about whether the G-tube can be removed now that your intake is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also anxious. Being back in the hospital makes me panic at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s been so stressful. We’ll continue your home medications for anxiety and depression, including lorazepam as needed, and we can also work on a plan for sleep while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my sleeping pill tonight? I haven’t slept in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can use your zolpidem as needed tonight. We’ll also try to cluster nighttime checks so you can rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning—how are you feeling today? Any vomiting or diarrhea overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Diarrhea is much better. I’m eating a little and drinking okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood work this morning looks stable. We’re planning discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home with for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue ondansetron as needed, and we’re adding prochlorperazine tablets as another option if nausea breaks through. Use the lowest amount that keeps you comfortable and able to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you restarting my iron? It makes me sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held iron in the hospital to avoid worsening nausea. At discharge, it’s listed to continue as at home, but if it triggers nausea, discuss with your primary doctor and bariatric team—sometimes timing with food or adjusting the formulation helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need antibiotics or anything to kill the virus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—norovirus is a virus, so antibiotics don’t help. The treatment is supportive: fluids, electrolytes, and symptom control while your body clears it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back if you can’t keep fluids down, you’re getting lightheaded or faint, you have worsening abdominal pain beyond your baseline, fever, blood in vomit or stool, or signs of dehydration like very little urination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it normal that my heart rate is low? They keep saying bradycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate has been on the low side but you’ve been stable, with good blood pressure and oxygen levels. We’ll keep monitoring, and if you feel dizzy, chest pain, or shortness of breath, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my stomach ulcer history—should I keep all those meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine daily, and sucralfate four times daily as you’ve been doing for marginal ulcer protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Someone told me to stop dronabinol before. Is that still true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue to hold dronabinol, per the prior plan and bariatric surgery’s recommendation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, one more thing: a blood culture drawn during this stay has shown no growth so far, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So the plan is just keep drinking and eating slowly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—small frequent meals, keep up fluids, use nausea meds as needed, and follow up with your primary care doctor and bariatric surgery, especially about nutrition and the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m nervous, but I feel better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you came in with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The diarrhea started a few days ago, and then last night I started throwing up. The pain is right at the tube site—like it’s irritated or pulling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How many times have you vomited since last night, and are you able to keep any fluids down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bunch of times overnight. Today I can barely sip water without feeling sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit or in your stool? Any black, tarry stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. Just watery diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever that I know of.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see in your history you’ve had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with multiple G-tube procedures and a bypass reversal. When did this current pain around the tube start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It got worse after the tube was changed and the balloon was made bigger. It’s been sore since then, but now it’s really tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And tube feeds—have you been using them recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I restarted them last weekend, but I stopped them a couple nights ago because the pain got worse. The diarrhea started after I restarted the feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Right now your vitals look stable. Our plan is bowel rest for the moment, IV fluids to treat dehydration, and anti-nausea medication. We’ll also monitor your electrolytes and urine output closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think something is wrong with the tube? Like it moved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam your abdomen is soft and not distended, and the tenderness is localized at the tube site without signs of peritonitis. That’s reassuring. We’ll keep checking the site and your symptoms. If anything changes—worsening pain, fever, or new concerning signs—we’d escalate evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared because I keep ending up back here. I can’t tell what’s normal anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. With your surgical history, even common stomach bugs or feed intolerance can hit harder. Our goal is to get you comfortable, hydrated, and back to tolerating food safely—and to make sure we’re not missing anything dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me for nausea? The pills at home didn’t touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with ondansetron, and because you’re vomiting we can give it in a way that doesn’t rely on you keeping pills down. Once the nausea settles, we’ll switch back to oral as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain? It’s really sharp at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Initially we can use IV pain medicine to get you through the worst of it, then transition to oral oxycodone once you’re tolerating a diet. We’ll also avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure always runs low. Is that going to be a problem with the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, so we’ll use the lowest effective dose and keep a close eye on your blood pressure. IV fluids should also help support it while you’re not taking much by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any more vomiting? How many episodes of diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up once early, but it’s less. Diarrhea is still happening, but maybe not as constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a step in the right direction. Your labs are reassuring—kidney function looks okay, electrolytes are stable, and your lactate is normal, which suggests you’re not in shock or severe infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you don’t think it’s an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s no fever, no concerning exam findings, and no lab signs pointing strongly to infection. We’ll keep monitoring closely, but at this point supportive care is the main treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start eating? I’m starving but scared it’ll come right back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slowly. Today we’ll keep it gentle—small sips and then clear liquids if you’re not vomiting. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my reflux meds? I restarted them a couple days before I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing acid suppression here—pantoprazole—and also sucralfate to protect the lining, given your history of ulcer issues. That can help with upper GI irritation while you recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is through the roof. I feel trapped here and I keep thinking something bad is happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
