conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. We can ask Psychiatry to see you to help with anxiety management while you’re inpatient, especially given your history of depression and PTSD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to take away my lorazepam? I take it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not trying to abruptly stop it. We’ll continue your home regimen as appropriate and coordinate with Psychiatry. We’ll also be careful because sedating meds can add up with pain medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How did you do with liquids overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down broth and some water. No vomiting overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Today we can advance your diet. Our usual approach is gradual, and if you keep doing well we can move toward a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tube feeds? I’m afraid to restart them because that’s when the diarrhea started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the timing, we’re holding tube feeds for now while your gut settles. We’ll focus on oral intake as tolerated and track your symptoms. If diarrhea worsens with any change, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry came by. They mentioned a clonidine patch. What is that for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Clonidine can sometimes help with anxiety symptoms and physical hyperarousal. The concern for you is it can lower blood pressure, and you’ve had intermittent low systolic readings here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re not going to do it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not planning to send you home on it because of the low blood pressure risk. It’s something you can discuss with your outpatient psychiatrist, who knows your longer-term history and can monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your abdominal pain today, especially around the G-tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still tender, but not as intense. I can move around without it spiking as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Since you’re tolerating food better, we’ll transition away from IV pain medication and use oral oxycodone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about taking opioids. Will I get constipated or dependent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are real concerns. We’ll use the smallest amount for the shortest time, only as needed. Constipation can happen, so we’ll keep an eye on your bowel pattern—especially since you’ve also had diarrhea. The goal is to taper off as your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate some regular food at lunch. I’m nervous it’ll trigger vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. If you can keep it down without worsening pain or vomiting, that’s a good sign. Keep portions small and go slowly. Let us know right away if nausea ramps up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any vomiting in the last 24 hours? How’s the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Diarrhea is much better—still loose sometimes, but not constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re tolerating a regular diet, and your hydration looks better. We’ll keep encouraging walking and using the incentive spirometer to keep your lungs strong while you’re in bed part of the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why do I need the leg squeezers and shots? I’m not having surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even without surgery, being in the hospital and less active increases the risk of blood clots. The compression boots and the heparin shots lower that risk, along with getting up and walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure dipped again earlier. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve seen some low systolic readings in the 80s to 90s at times, but you’ve been alert and not showing signs of poor perfusion. We’ll keep monitoring, make sure you’re hydrated, and avoid adding medications that could lower it further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today looks like a good day to plan for discharge if you continue to do well. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m eating, I’m not throwing up, and the pain is manageable. I’m just worried it’ll come back when I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That worry makes sense. The key things at home are: keep up with fluids, eat small frequent meals, and use ondansetron as needed for nausea. If you start vomiting and can’t keep down fluids or meds, or you feel dehydrated—dizzy, dry mouth, fast heartbeat—come back in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the G-tube site pain? Do I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s no fever and no signs suggesting an infection during this stay. We’ll have you watch for redness spreading, pus-like drainage, worsening swelling, or fever—those would be reasons to call or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going home on the same meds I came in with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications. You’ll continue pantoprazole and sucralfate for stomach protection, ranitidine at night, and your psychiatric medications as prescribed. You’ll also have oxycodone for breakthrough pain and ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How should I take the oxycodone safely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it only as prescribed and only if you need it. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it, and avoid mixing it with anything that makes you extra sleepy. If your pain is improving, start spacing doses out and stop as soon as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special because of my MRSA history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mainly important for healthcare settings so we can use the right precautions if needed. At home, focus on good hand hygiene and keeping the tube site clean and dry. If you ever develop a skin infection, let your doctor know about the MRSA history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, I want to review return precautions: come back for chest pain, trouble breathing, fever over 101.5, vomiting that prevents fluids or meds, signs of dehydration, blood in vomit or stool, burning with urination or blood in urine, or worsening abdominal pain—especially if it changes location.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And activity—can I lift things?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy and keep walking several times a day. Avoid heavy lifting until you follow up with your surgeon. Rest, hydrate, and gradually return to normal activity as you feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m still anxious, but I feel more prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did the right thing coming in. We’ll discharge you home now that you’re tolerating a regular diet, walking independently, and your symptoms have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me where the pain is worst right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started on the right upper side, but now it’s more on the lower right. It’s sharp and it comes in waves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit or stool? Any black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. The diarrhea was brown and loose. I’ve been dry heaving more than actually throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, or anyone at home sick with similar symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No one else is sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ED your vital signs were stable and your bloodwork looked reassuring—no high white count, liver tests similar to your baseline, and your pancreas enzyme was normal. We also did a CT scan and an ultrasound of the right upper abdomen; both didn’t show gallstones, gallbladder infection, or any blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much if the scans are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the frustrating part. With your history—gastric bypass and then reversal—some people get recurrent flares of pain and nausea even when imaging doesn’t show a dangerous cause. We still take it seriously, but right now we don’t see signs of obstruction, perforation, gallbladder disease, or pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s less likely because you recently had an upper endoscopy that didn’t show a marginal ulcer and the biopsies were normal. We’ll keep you on your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole and sucralfate—and monitor for any bleeding symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, our plan is IV fluids since you’ve had trouble keeping things down, anti-nausea medication, and pain control while we watch how things evolve. We’ll also send stool studies if you’re still having diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t even take my morning meds at home. Am I going to miss them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your home meds as soon as you can tolerate them. Some we can give here in the hospital on schedule. We’ll also continue your Keppra for seizures and your psychiatric medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is still bad. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s use ondansetron as needed, and we’ll keep the IV fluids going. If you’re still vomiting, we can adjust the regimen, but we’ll start with what has worked for you before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: are you still having diarrhea this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a couple times since I got upstairs. No blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll collect a stool sample for culture. We also ordered C. diff testing, but it only works if the stool is watery—not formed—so we’ll see what we can send based on what you pass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared this is going to turn into another long admission. I can’t keep doing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to make sure there isn’t something dangerous we’re missing, then get your symptoms controlled and get you back home safely. Right now the tests are reassuring, and we’ll take it day by day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting? How’s the pain location today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight, just nausea. Pain is still mostly lower right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea since yesterday afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It slowed down a lot. I haven’t gone since late last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Sometimes these episodes start with diarrhea and then swing toward constipation, especially if we use opioid pain meds. We want to be careful because constipation can worsen pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain is real. The IV meds help the most.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you’re in pain. At the same time, IV opioids can make the gut slow down and can trap you in a cycle—more constipation, more pain, more nausea. Since your imaging doesn’t show a surgical problem, we want to shift toward safer options and use oral meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re saying no IV pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain, but we’re going to prioritize non-opioid strategies and avoid escalating IV opioids. You can’t take NSAIDs because of your ulcer history and allergy, and some other pain meds aren’t safe with your current antidepressant regimen. One option we can start is gabapentin, which can help with nerve-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin is for nerves, right? How would that help my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—sometimes after multiple abdominal surgeries, the nerves and the way the brain processes pain signals can become sensitized. Gabapentin can reduce that nerve signaling. It won’t work instantly, but over days it can help reduce the baseline pain and the flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a nerve block before and it didn’t work. Why would this be different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nerve block targets a specific area; gabapentin works more broadly on nerve signaling. It’s not guaranteed, but it’s one of the better non-opioid options we have given your medication interactions and ulcer history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your appetite today? Any ability to keep down liquids or food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can sip and I ate a little. Still nauseous though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep advancing slowly as tolerated. We’ll also keep your pantoprazole and sucralfate on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site isn’t red, but could the tube be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam the site looks healthy, and the CT showed the gastrostomy tube is appropriately positioned. So it doesn’t look like the tube is displaced or infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement now. I feel bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Constipation can definitely worsen bloating and nausea. Let’s start a bowel regimen—stool softener and stimulant laxative—and use Miralax as needed. We’ll also encourage walking and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Won’t laxatives make the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes you can get cramping as things start moving, but overall relieving the stool burden usually improves pain and nausea. We’ll go stepwise and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling on the gabapentin so far—any dizziness or sleepiness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little sleepy, but the pain is maybe slightly less constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll continue to slowly increase the dose as tolerated, aiming for better pain control without opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been days. I still haven’t gone. I’m worried something is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given no bowel movement for several days, it’s reasonable to check. We’re going to get an abdominal X-ray today to look for obstruction versus stool buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It does not show a bowel obstruction. It does show mild fecal loading—basically stool sitting in the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a big contributor right now—especially to the nausea and the pressure-type discomfort. The earlier diarrhea resolved quickly, and then the gut slowed down. Opioids can worsen that, which is why we’re trying to avoid them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like you think I’m making it up when I ask for IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s felt that way. I do not think you’re making it up. My job is to treat your pain and also avoid treatments that can prolong the problem or cause harm. With constipation on imaging, IV opioids would likely set you back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any bowel movement overnight after the bowel meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. I’m passing some gas though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Passing gas is a good sign. We’ll continue senna and docusate, and use Miralax as needed. If you still don’t go, we can add a suppository.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took a stool sample but it wasn’t watery. Does that matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—C. difficile testing requires a loose, unformed stool. If the sample is formed, the lab cancels it because the result wouldn’t be reliable. We did send stool cultures, and so far they’re negative for common bacteria like Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your course—diarrhea resolving quickly, stable vitals, and negative cultures—an ongoing bacterial infection is unlikely right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly hurts more after the laxatives. It’s like cramping and pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen as the intestines start moving again. Sometimes gas builds up too. We can add simethicone for gas pain, and keep encouraging walking, which helps move gas along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just don’t want to be miserable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The simethicone actually helped. I’m less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Let’s keep it as needed. How’s your nausea with eating today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I ate most of lunch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you look more comfortable. How’s the pain compared to admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there, but it’s not as intense. I’ve been walking the halls like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ve been increasing gabapentin gradually, and the goal is to get you on a stable dose you can continue at home. We’re also keeping acetaminophen scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going home with any opioids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Given the constipation and the lack of a surgical cause on imaging, opioids are more likely to worsen your symptoms. The discharge plan is scheduled acetaminophen, gabapentin, and a bowel regimen to keep things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain flares again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting, blood in stool or vomit, black stools, fever, or you can’t keep fluids down, you should come back. For milder flares, use the scheduled meds, keep your bowel regimen, and contact your outpatient team. We also want you to follow up with the chronic pain service to discuss other non-opioid options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They told me my ultrasound showed fatty liver. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound described an echogenic liver consistent with fatty change, which you’ve had noted before. By itself it doesn’t explain this acute pain episode. It’s something to follow with your outpatient doctors—often managed with lifestyle and monitoring labs over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge day if you feel ready. You’ve been tolerating a regular diet, walking independently, and your exam is stable. How are you feeling about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, but I do feel better than when I came in. I just don’t want to bounce back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Let’s review the plan so you feel prepared: continue pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate for stomach protection; continue your home meds including Keppra, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and atorvastatin; and new meds are scheduled acetaminophen, gabapentin three times a day, plus senna and docusate twice a day, Miralax as needed, bisacodyl as needed, and simethicone as needed for gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin is 900 three times a day? That sounds like a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is a higher dose, but we increased it gradually here and you tolerated it. The main side effects are sleepiness and dizziness—so avoid driving if you feel impaired, and let your outpatient team know if it’s too sedating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have ondansetron as needed for nausea. The best prevention is keeping constipation under control and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool tests—anything I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing further right now. The bacterial stool cultures were negative, and the C. diff test was cancelled because the sample was formed. Since your diarrhea resolved, we’re not pursuing more infectious testing unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: please schedule follow-up with the chronic pain service. They’ve seen you before and may not recommend opioids, but they can help with non-opioid strategies and adjusting gabapentin. If you develop severe pain with vomiting, fever, bleeding, or inability to eat or drink, come back to the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you came in with upper belly pain and nausea. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started about two days ago—sharp, constant pain right in the middle, like my epigastric area. I’ve been nauseous and I can barely eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, diarrhea, black or bloody stools, fevers, or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No diarrhea. No blood. No fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’ve had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in the past and later a reversal, and you’ve been hospitalized before for similar pain. Does this feel like those episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It feels like when they told me it was gastritis about a month ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Do you know if any stomach-protecting medications were stopped recently—like a proton pump inhibitor, an H2 blocker, or Carafate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. My bariatric surgeon stopped a bunch of my GI meds recently. I didn’t really understand why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. In the emergency department, your blood work looked reassuring—no signs of infection, kidney problems, or pancreatitis. The CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis didn’t show an acute problem either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much if the CT is normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A CT is good for big structural problems—like obstruction, perforation, bleeding, or inflammation of certain organs. Gastritis is irritation of the stomach lining and often won’t show up on CT. Your symptoms and the timing after stopping those meds fit gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They gave me morphine in the ER. Is that what I’ll need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want to control your pain, but we also want to avoid making your stomach and bowels worse. Opioids can worsen constipation and sometimes nausea. Our plan is to restart the stomach-protecting meds and use Tylenol on a schedule, plus your home pain meds, and treat constipation proactively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin, so I can’t take those anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—so we’ll avoid NSAIDs. We’ll use acetaminophen instead. We’ll also restart pantoprazole twice a day, ranitidine twice a day, and sucralfate four times a day to coat and protect the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Carafate is the sucralfate, right? How do I take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s usually taken four times daily. It can interfere with absorption of other meds, so we’ll try to space it out from your other pills when possible—nursing will help with the schedule while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve barely eaten. I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with this kind of pain and nausea. We’ll focus on hydration and nutrition. Bariatric surgery was consulted in the ED and didn’t think you needed any surgical intervention. We can also have nutrition talk with you about supplements that are easier to tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also get dizzy when I stand up. It’s been worse lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noticed your blood pressure runs low at times, and you’ve had orthostatic symptoms—dizziness when standing. That can happen when you’re not taking in enough fluids. We’ll give IV normal saline and recheck your vitals when you stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous? My systolic was in the 80s earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can make you feel awful and increase fall risk, but the good news is it’s often reversible with fluids and better intake. We’ll monitor closely, help you stand safely, and treat the underlying nausea so you can drink more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just scared it’s something being missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Right now, your labs and CT don’t show an emergency cause. We’ll keep reassessing your belly exam, your vitals, and your ability to eat and drink. If anything changes—worsening pain, vomiting, fever, blood in stool—we’d broaden the workup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how’s the nausea after the anti-nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The pain is still there, but I’m not as queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight we gave fluids. Any dizziness when you got up to the bathroom?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but not as bad as yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. Your abdominal X-ray showed a nonspecific, non-obstructive bowel gas pattern—so no sign of blockage. We’re going to keep the bowel regimen going to prevent constipation while your intake is low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you giving me for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use polyethylene glycol daily, docusate twice daily, and bisacodyl twice daily. Senna will be available as needed. We’ll hold them if you get loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about taking too many laxatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fair. The goal is regular, soft bowel movements—not diarrhea. Because pain meds and low intake can slow the gut, we start a stronger regimen and then back off if stools get loose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to review your home medications too. We’ll continue your fluoxetine and aripiprazole for mood, lorazepam as prescribed, and your seizure medication levetiracetam. You’re also on pyridostigmine—are you still taking that regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Neurology started it after I had a seizure in mid-month and some other symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep it as you’ve been taking it and make sure nothing we’re doing interferes. Let us know if you feel unusually weak or have new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat normally? I get full so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start with small, frequent meals and focus on what you can tolerate. Nutrition often recommends supplements like Carnation Instant Breakfast with Lactaid milk and adding protein powder packets several times a day to boost calories and protein without large volumes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds doable. Will the stomach meds work quickly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can start helping within a day, but it may take a bit longer for the lining to calm down. The key is taking them consistently, especially since symptoms started after stopping them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain this afternoon on scheduled Tylenol and the restarted stomach meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there, but it’s more of a burning now and less sharp. I can sip fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That trend is what we want. We’ll keep pushing oral fluids and use IV fluids only as needed. We’ll also keep ondansetron available if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If this is gastritis, do I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a recent EGD that didn’t show ulcerations. Given that and your stable labs and imaging, we’re treating medically first. If symptoms persist despite restarting therapy, your outpatient GI or bariatric team can decide if repeat endoscopy is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Any dizziness when standing today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much less. I still feel tired, but I’m not getting that head rush as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your repeat labs look stable, and your liver tests that were mildly elevated on arrival have improved. We also checked a morning cortisol because of the low blood pressures—your result was 12.9, which is reassuring in this context.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the low blood pressure was just dehydration?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely from poor intake due to nausea and pain. You responded to normal saline boluses, and your symptoms improved as you were able to drink more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan for going home? I don’t want to bounce back again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The plan is discharge home once you’re tolerating oral intake and your dizziness is controlled. The biggest change is staying on the stomach-protecting regimen: pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, ranitidine 150 mg twice daily, and sucralfate 1 gram four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Tylenol as needed, and continue your home gabapentin. We’re also emphasizing regular bowel movements with polyethylene glycol daily, docusate twice daily, and bisacodyl twice daily, with senna as needed—holding any of them if stools get loose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need antibiotics or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—there’s no sign of infection in your blood work, and your imaging didn’t show an infectious process. This looks like gastritis rather than an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before discharge, I want to review warning signs: come back for severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting, black or bloody stools, fever, or if you can’t keep fluids down and feel faint.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my diet at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small frequent meals, avoid anything that clearly triggers symptoms, and use the nutrition supplements to meet calories—like the instant breakfast with Lactaid milk and added protein. Keep taking your multivitamin and iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about taking ranitidine with everything else. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For you, it’s being used as an additional acid-reducing medicine alongside pantoprazole. The main practical issue is spacing sucralfate from other meds when possible. We’ll give you a clear medication list to follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your pain is improved compared to admission, you’re drinking, and your dizziness is better. We’ll discharge you home today with the medication changes we discussed and follow-up with your outpatient teams.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll restart the stomach meds and keep up with the supplements. I just hope it stays under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you came in with left upper belly pain and nausea. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been about four days. Pain on the left upper side, and it wraps around to my left flank. I feel nauseated and full really fast when I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it constant or does it come and go? And anything make it better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s kind of always there, but it’s better when I eat, which is weird. I’m not throwing up though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, blood in stool, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. No blood. No fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about diarrhea or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday I had a normal bowel movement. Today it’s been looser, but not a ton.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any burning with urination or urinary symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the emergency department your bloodwork looked reassuring—no signs of infection, and your kidney and liver tests looked okay. Your urine test didn’t show anything concerning. We also did a chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm, and it was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not like a perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—nothing on the X-ray suggests a perforation, and your exam is not showing signs of an emergency surgical abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bariatric surgery saw me in the ER. Are they doing anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They evaluated you and recommended admission to medicine for symptom control. At this point they don’t think surgery is needed tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m in a lot of pain. The morphine helped. Can I just get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to control your pain, but we also want to avoid making your stomach and bowels worse. Narcotics can slow the gut and sometimes worsen abdominal symptoms. Let’s start with a non-narcotic plan: scheduled acetaminophen, your ulcer-protecting meds, and nausea medicine as needed. We’ll reassess frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take NSAIDs anyway. Tylenol alone doesn’t always touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin given your allergy and your ulcer history. We’ll use acetaminophen on a schedule rather than only as needed, and we’ll continue your home gabapentin. We’ll also keep you on pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate to protect the stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also worried because I feel full right after I start eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for saying that. Given your surgical history, early fullness can happen for a few reasons, but your labs and exam don’t suggest an acute blockage or infection right now. We’ll focus on symptom control and make sure you can tolerate oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been in and out of the hospital for this. Is this just going to keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. With multiple abdominal surgeries, some people develop heightened nerve sensitivity—sometimes called visceral hyperalgesia—where pain signals are amplified even without a dangerous new problem. If that’s what’s happening, chronic pain specialists can help with longer-term strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think it’s nerve pain in my belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s one strong possibility, especially since your workup is reassuring and you’ve had similar episodes. We’ll still keep watching for anything that suggests a different cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on pyridostigmine for those eye symptoms. Could that be making my stomach worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. I also see you had outpatient neurology testing, including an EMG, that was negative for myasthenia gravis. Neurology had suggested tapering off pyridostigmine. Given your nausea and now some loose stools, we should stop it here and continue that taper plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will stopping it make my double vision worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your symptoms. Since the EMG was negative and you were already in the process of coming off it, stopping it is reasonable—especially if it’s contributing to GI upset. If your diplopia worsens significantly, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? How’s the pain and nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there. Maybe a little better after I ate some crackers. Nausea comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your vital signs are stable this morning. We’ll keep pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate on schedule, and acetaminophen regularly. We’ll also keep a bowel regimen so you don’t get backed up, since constipation can worsen pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not constipated right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll tailor it—keep the baseline meds you’re already on, and we can hold or adjust if stools become too loose. The goal is steady, comfortable bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had more diarrhea today. I’m worried it’s C. diff again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, that’s a reasonable concern. We’ll send a stool test for C. difficile. In the meantime, we’ll focus on hydration and watch for fever or worsening abdominal tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take something to stop the diarrhea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We usually wait until we have more information, but if you’re not having fevers and you’re otherwise stable, we can consider symptomatic treatment once we’re confident there’s no active infection. Let’s see how you do over the next several hours while the test is pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any vomiting, blood in stool, or new severe pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Just cramps and diarrhea. Pain is still mostly on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better. Still tender, but I’m eating small amounts. Diarrhea is still happening though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Your blood tests remain reassuring—no signs pointing to a new infection or a surgical emergency. Bariatric surgery also agrees there’s no role for surgery right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan if it’s not surgical?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the stomach-protecting medications, avoid medicines that can slow or upset the gut, and use a non-narcotic pain plan. For the diarrhea, once the C. diff test results are back, we can treat symptomatically if it’s negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure feels low when I stand. I’m dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We’ll check your blood pressure lying and standing and make sure you’re hydrated. Diarrhea and poor intake can drop your pressure. Let us know before you get up so we can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile PCR came back negative, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not C. diff this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—this test did not detect toxigenic C. difficile. Given that and no other signs of infection, we can treat the diarrhea symptomatically. We’ll start loperamide as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me constipated and make the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can if overused. We’ll use it only as needed—if you’re having frequent watery stools. If stools firm up, you stop it. We’ll keep your bowel regimen flexible so we’re not pushing in both directions at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How did you do overnight with the loperamide and the pain regimen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diarrhea slowed down. Pain is still there but not as sharp. I didn’t need morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your labs this morning are stable, and your exam doesn’t show guarding or rebound. I think we can plan for discharge later today if you keep tolerating food and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home without stronger pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The reason we’re avoiding narcotics is that they can worsen abdominal pain over time and slow the gut. The plan is scheduled acetaminophen, continue your home gabapentin, and keep the ulcer medications consistent. We’ll also refer you to a chronic pain service to work on longer-term options for postoperative visceral pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly will the pain clinic do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can evaluate whether this fits visceral hyperalgesia and help with non-opioid strategies—medication adjustments, nerve-targeting approaches, and coping strategies—so you’re not stuck in a cycle of ER visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pyridostigmine—so I’m stopping it completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since your outpatient EMG was negative and you were already tapering, we’re discontinuing it now, and that may also help your GI symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for severe worsening abdominal pain, inability to keep fluids down, vomiting, blood in stool, black stools, fevers or chills, or feeling faint—especially if your blood pressure is low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review your discharge medications: continue pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine twice daily, and sucralfate four times daily; continue your bowel regimen meds as directed; use ondansetron as needed for nausea; and use loperamide as needed for diarrhea. No narcotics at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I keep my seizure medicine and my psych meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue levetiracetam for seizures, and continue your fluoxetine, aripiprazole, lorazepam, and propranolol as you were taking them. Also keep your multivitamin and iron, and atorvastatin at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who sets up the pain clinic appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing the referral, and you’ll call to schedule with the chronic pain service physician listed in your paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’m still sore, but I feel safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll get your paperwork finalized. Please keep taking the ulcer medications consistently—stopping them has been associated with flares for you in the past. We’ll discharge you home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I hear you came in with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me what’s been going on since you left the hospital last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It never really stopped. The diarrhea kept going even when I wasn’t eating, and then I tried rice and threw up twice. After that the pain hit hard in the middle, like my ulcer pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Any blood in the stool or vomit? Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. No fever. Just constant watery diarrhea and this burning pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the emergency department your vital signs were stable, and your bloodwork—things like your white count, kidney function, liver tests, and lipase—looked reassuring. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They told me something about a fistula. Is that dangerous? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed contrast getting into the excluded part of the stomach, which can be consistent with a gastro-gastric fistula. The important part is: there was no obstruction and no sign of an infection or perforation on the scan. Our bariatric surgery team reviewed it and did not see an acute surgical problem tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much? It feels like something is tearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history and how many times this has happened, one possibility is that your nerves in the abdomen are extra sensitive after multiple surgeries—what we sometimes call visceral hyperalgesia. Another piece is that if you’ve missed any of your stomach-protecting medicines, the lining can get irritated and pain can flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried to take them, but with the vomiting and diarrhea I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Tonight our plan is to control nausea, give fluids if you’re dehydrated, restart your acid-suppression and sucralfate, and check stool testing to see if there’s an infection causing the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had C. diff before. Could it be that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be, especially with profuse watery diarrhea. We’re sending a C. difficile PCR test. Until we know, we’ll avoid anti-diarrhea medicines like loperamide because they can make C. diff worse if it’s present.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But Imodium is the only thing that slows it down. I’ve been taking a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. For now, let’s pause it while we test. We’ll focus on hydration and treating the cause. If the test is negative, we can reconsider symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds? They gave me morphine downstairs. I can’t do this without something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the ED you did receive a few doses of IV morphine. On the floor, we want to balance relief with safety and with your long-term plan. We’ll restart your non-opioid regimen—acetaminophen and your gabapentin—and we can use a small amount of stronger medicine if needed while we get you through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared you’re going to send me home in pain again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t rush you out. The goals are: stop the vomiting, get the diarrhea improving, make sure you can eat and drink, and have a safe pain plan with follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how’s the nausea now after the anti-nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still crampy and I’ve had two more watery stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep you on a gentle diet as tolerated and continue your pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight was rough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I barely slept. The diarrhea is nonstop and the pain is still right here in the epigastric area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. Your labs this morning still look stable—kidneys and electrolytes are okay. We’re still waiting on the stool test for C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the urine test they did? Someone said it looked infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urinalysis had some white cells, which can happen for different reasons. The key question is whether you have urinary symptoms—burning, urgency, flank pain, fever. Do you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. None of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we usually don’t treat it right away. We’ll see what the culture shows; often it’s mixed skin flora and not a true infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have an update: your C. difficile PCR came back positive. That explains the severe watery diarrhea and can worsen abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is C. diff again. How did I get it? And is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: C. diff can recur after a prior episode because the gut bacteria balance is disrupted. It can be serious if untreated, but we caught it and we’re starting treatment today: oral vancomycin every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the diarrhea fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It often starts improving over a couple of days, sometimes sooner. The full course is two weeks to reduce the chance of it coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take Imodium now? I can’t keep running to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. While you’re actively being treated for C. diff, we hold loperamide because it can trap the toxin in the colon. Once you complete treatment and symptoms are resolving, we can revisit it with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the fistula thing—does C. diff cause that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the fistula finding is related to your prior gastric bypass anatomy. On this CT it didn’t look like an emergency—no blockage, no infection. It’s something to keep in mind with your surgical and GI teams, but it’s not what we’re treating urgently today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How many stools overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still a lot, but maybe less explosive. The nausea is better. Pain is still there though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign that the vancomycin is starting to work. For pain, we’re continuing acetaminophen and gabapentin. We can use oxycodone as needed for severe pain while you’re in this acute flare, but we want to keep it limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be judged. I’m not trying to get pills—I just can’t function with this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Chronic abdominal pain after multiple surgeries is real and exhausting. Our job is to treat your infection and help you get through the flare safely, and also set you up with the chronic pain clinic so you have more tools than just opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can GI do another scope? I’m worried it’s an ulcer again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your recent endoscopy that didn’t show ulcers and the CT not showing an acute complication, GI’s recommendation is no urgent endoscopy right now. The focus is treating C. diff and staying consistent with your ulcer-prevention medicines: pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today compared with admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diarrhea is slowing down. I’m able to sip more. Pain is still a 6 or 7 though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Progress on the diarrhea is important. For pain, we’ll keep the stomach meds scheduled and use oxycodone only when the pain is severe. We’ll also keep nausea medicine available so you can keep food and meds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I missed some doses at home because I ran out and then I got sick. Could that really make it this bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—missing the acid suppression and sucralfate can make the upper stomach and connection sites more irritated, which can amplify pain. And then C. diff on top of that can worsen cramping and overall discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any vomiting since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Still loose stools but fewer. I’m eating a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. That’s what we need to see before discharge—tolerating diet and taking the vancomycin by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood pressure? I get dizzy when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With diarrhea and poor intake, blood pressure can run low. We’ll encourage fluids and slow position changes. Your labs show your kidneys are handling things okay, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to talk about the plan for going home soon. Your diarrhea is improving on vancomycin, and you’re eating and drinking more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous it’ll come right back when I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common worry. The most important thing is finishing the full two-week course of oral vancomycin exactly as prescribed. Also, don’t restart loperamide until the C. diff treatment is complete.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? Are you sending me home with nothing again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because this is an acute flare on top of chronic pain, we’ll discharge you with a short course of oxycodone for severe pain only, along with acetaminophen and your gabapentin. The goal is to bridge you to your chronic pain clinic appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment set up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have follow-up arranged with a chronic pain doctor. At that visit, they can talk through longer-term strategies—medication options and non-medication approaches like biofeedback or acupuncture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried a nerve block before and it didn’t work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that in your history. Even if one procedure didn’t help, the pain clinic can still offer other approaches and help coordinate a plan so you’re not stuck in this cycle of repeated hospital visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Someone mentioned bacteria in my urine again. Am I leaving with antibiotics for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The urine culture showed mixed flora and you don’t have urinary symptoms, so we’re not treating it. Treating when it’s not a true infection can increase the risk of C. diff coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Last check before discharge: how’s the diarrhea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still loose but not constant. I can eat a little and keep pills down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your discharge labs are stable. We’ll send you home on oral vancomycin every six hours to complete a two-week course, and continue your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate—so you don’t get that severe epigastric pain from irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over exactly what I should watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call us or seek care if you develop fever, worsening abdominal pain that’s different from your usual, inability to keep fluids down, blood in stool, or if diarrhea suddenly worsens again. And please keep your pain clinic follow-up—our goal is better long-term control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still scared, but I understand the plan. I’ll finish the vancomycin and not take Imodium until it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with vomiting, worsening diarrhea, and your usual abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on since you left the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It got worse. I’ve been having diarrhea all day, like ten times, and I couldn’t make it to the bathroom a few times. And I was throwing up, so I can’t keep my pills down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. When you vomit, is it right after you take your medications—especially the vancomycin for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve been trying to take it four times a day, but I throw up not long after. I’m scared it’s not working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very reasonable concern. If you’re vomiting soon after taking it, you may not be absorbing enough, and that can let the infection keep going. The good news is your vitals and labs here look reassuring—no fever, normal white blood cell count, and your kidneys look fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not getting really sick from it? Like sepsis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we don’t see signs of severe infection. But the symptoms are still significant, and dehydration is a risk. We’ll focus on controlling nausea so you can keep the vancomycin down and get you rehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach pain is bad too. It’s the same kind I always get, just more intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. On exam your belly is soft and there’s no guarding or signs that would push us toward emergency surgery. The surgery team also evaluated you in the ER and didn’t think you needed new imaging or an operation right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re not doing a CT scan this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at the moment, because your exam and labs don’t suggest a new blockage or perforation, and you’ve had a lot of imaging in the past. If anything changes—worsening pain, fever, blood pressure issues—we would reassess quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are you going to do for the nausea? Zofran at home didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the ER you got IV Zofran and fluids. Here we can continue anti-nausea medication and switch to an orally dissolving Zofran once you’re ready, since it’s easier to keep down. The goal is no vomiting so you can take your meds and drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the diarrhea? I’m embarrassed. I can’t control it when it hits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with that—this is common with C. diff because it causes urgency. We’ll make sure you have quick access to the bathroom and help with skin care. The main treatment is finishing the vancomycin course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I contagious? I live with family.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: C. diff can spread through spores in stool. At home, wash hands with soap and water, clean high-touch surfaces, and don’t share towels. Here we use contact precautions to protect others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My urine has been really dark. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That often means you’re dehydrated. Your kidney numbers look normal, which is reassuring, and we’ll keep giving IV fluids until you’re drinking enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said something about bacteria in my urine. Do I need antibiotics for that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed trace leukocyte esterase and a few bacteria, but you don’t have burning, urgency, or flank pain. That pattern is consistent with asymptomatic bacteriuria, and treating it with antibiotics can actually worsen C. diff, so we won’t treat it unless you develop symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about pain meds? In the ER they gave me morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did receive a couple doses in the ER. On the floor, we want to avoid escalating opioids because they can slow the gut and make bowel function worse. We’ll use scheduled non-opioid options and your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole twice a day, ranitidine, and sucralfate—plus acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried you think I’m making it up. The pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. Chronic abdominal pain after multiple surgeries can be very real and very hard to treat. Our plan is about safety and long-term control—opioids can backfire in the gut. We’ll also make sure you have follow-up with the chronic pain team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I can’t keep the vancomycin down, what happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re admitting you—to get the nausea under control so you can reliably take it. If you vomit after a dose here, tell us right away so we can adjust timing with anti-nausea meds and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in this evening: have you vomited since coming up to the floor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting since I got here. Still nauseous though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep the anti-nausea meds going and start with small sips and bland food as tolerated. Let’s also make sure you get your evening vancomycin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting, and how many bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I did go a few times, but it wasn’t like yesterday. I actually slept a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Nursing notes show the stools have been more formed. That’s encouraging and suggests the C. diff treatment is getting back on track now that you’re keeping doses down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean the infection is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Symptoms improving is a good sign, but it’s very important to complete the full vancomycin course as prescribed so it fully clears and reduces the chance of relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly still hurts. Are you sure it’s not an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, ulcers are always on our radar. Right now, your exam is benign and your labs don’t show bleeding or severe inflammation. You’re already on strong acid suppression—pantoprazole twice daily plus ranitidine and sucralfate—which is the right protective regimen. We’ll have GI follow you as an outpatient for ongoing evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat? I’m scared food will make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance slowly. Start with small, frequent, easy-to-digest meals and keep hydrated. If nausea returns, pause and let us know—we can adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about taking so many pills. What if I throw them up again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a key point. We’ll prescribe ondansetron as an orally dissolving tablet you can take every 8 hours as needed. Take it before your vancomycin dose if you’re feeling queasy. If you vomit up the vancomycin again, call your doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to stay on IV fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re drinking well today and your urine is lighter, we can stop IV fluids. We’ll reassess this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Update: your repeat assessment looks stable—no fever, and your abdominal exam remains soft without concerning findings. How’s your nausea after lunch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I ate a little and kept it down. Still some pain, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll continue the stomach-protecting meds and acetaminophen. We’re intentionally not adding more opioids because of the constipation and motility issues they can cause, especially while you’re recovering from diarrhea and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I have oxycodone at home. Are you taking it away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not changing your home prescription today. We just want you to use it only if absolutely needed for severe pain, because it can worsen gut function. The longer-term plan is to work with the pain clinic on safer strategies for chronic abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared the diarrhea will come back as soon as I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. The best protection is taking every vancomycin dose on schedule and staying hydrated. If diarrhea suddenly worsens again, or you develop fever, severe abdominal pain, or can’t keep fluids down, you should call your doctor or come back in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You look more comfortable today. Any vomiting overnight? And how are your stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I had a bowel movement and it was formed. I still feel tired though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want to see. The tiredness can be from the illness and not eating well for days. Your vital signs are stable, and you’re tolerating oral intake, so we’re planning for discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Main items: finish the full course of oral vancomycin every 6 hours as prescribed; use the ondansetron ODT every 8 hours as needed for nausea; keep taking pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine twice daily, and sucralfate four times daily for your stomach; and drink plenty of fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I throw up after taking vancomycin, do I take another dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t automatically double up. If you vomit after a dose, call your doctor right away for guidance—especially if it keeps happening—because we may need to adjust the plan. Try taking ondansetron first and spacing things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the urine bacteria thing—still no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Since you don’t have urinary symptoms, we’re not treating it. Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics helps prevent worsening C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, any last questions about follow-up? We want you to see GI and the chronic pain clinic to keep working on the abdominal pain and nausea long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… if the pain gets bad again, I’m afraid I’ll end up right back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you get severe worsening pain with fever, persistent vomiting, or you can’t stay hydrated, come in. Otherwise, the outpatient GI and pain teams are the best next step to reduce these repeat flares. Today you’re stable and safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I hear you’ve had a rough day—nausea, vomiting, and a lot of diarrhea. Can you tell me what’s been happening since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hit hard today. I’ve had like eight watery stools and I can’t keep anything down. It feels like when I had C. diff before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever or chills? Any blood in the stool or vomit? And any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, no blood. Just the same epigastric pain I always have, and the nausea is awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. In the ED your vitals looked stable and your white blood cell count wasn’t high, which is reassuring. Your bicarbonate was a bit low, which can happen with dehydration from diarrhea. We’re going to keep IV fluids going and treat the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is so dry. I feel like I need more fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give another liter and then reassess. We’ll also check electrolytes and keep an eye on your kidney function—so far your creatinine is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to test me for C. diff again? Last time it was negative and I still felt terrible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve sent a stool test for C. difficile. Because you’ve had it before, we take this seriously. While we wait, we’ll focus on hydration and symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s going to keep coming back. Why does this keep happening to me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Recurrent C. diff can happen even after appropriate treatment—some people are more prone to it. We’ll tailor the antibiotic plan if it’s positive, and we’ll also talk about ways to reduce risk going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach surgeries make everything complicated. Are you sure this isn’t something surgical?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now your exam is soft without guarding or rebound, and your vitals are stable. Nothing is pointing to an emergency surgical problem tonight. We’ll keep monitoring closely, and if anything changes—worsening pain, fever, or new findings—we’d reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I have something for the pain? It’s the same spot, right here in the upper middle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can use acetaminophen and focus on treating the infection and nausea, since that often helps the pain settle back to your baseline. We’ll avoid NSAIDs because of your allergy and ulcer history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t take NSAIDs anyway. I just don’t want to be miserable all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll schedule anti-nausea medication and keep fluids running. If you’re still uncomfortable after that, tell the nurse and we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a sip of water and it came right back up. Is that normal with C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
