conversation_lines.text: It can happen—nausea and vomiting can come with the infection and dehydration. For now we’ll keep you on IV fluids and use ondansetron to help you keep small sips down later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any more vomiting? And how many stools since midnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Less vomiting after the nausea medicine, but still watery diarrhea. I’m exhausted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Your inflammatory markers this morning—CRP and ESR—are low, which is reassuring. We’re still waiting on the stool test, but given your history and symptoms, we’re preparing to treat if it comes back positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it’s positive again, does that mean I did something wrong? I took the medicine last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—this isn’t your fault. C. diff can recur even when people take treatment correctly. Sometimes the bacteria come back before the normal gut bacteria fully recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan if it’s positive? Another short course?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because this would be a second recurrence, the plan is a vancomycin taper followed by a pulse schedule—so it starts four times a day, then gradually decreases over weeks. It’s designed to reduce the chance of another relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Weeks? That sounds like a lot. Will it make me sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people tolerate oral vancomycin well since it stays mostly in the gut. We’ll watch for side effects, and the key is taking it exactly as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test is back: it’s positive for toxigenic C. difficile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is C. diff again. I knew it. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting oral vancomycin today and planning the taper/pulse regimen for discharge. We’ll also keep you on IV fluids until you’re reliably drinking and keeping things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to be isolated? I don’t want to give it to anyone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll use contact precautions—gown and gloves for staff and visitors—and handwashing with soap and water is important. At home, clean high-touch surfaces and wash hands well, especially after the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly pain is a little worse with the cramping. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. The infection irritates the colon and can cause cramping and worsen your baseline abdominal pain. The goal is that as the diarrhea improves with treatment, the pain should settle back to your usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with the first doses of vancomycin? Any trouble keeping it down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept it down. Still nauseated, but not throwing up like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll continue ondansetron as needed and start easing you toward oral intake—small, frequent sips and bland foods as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any change in the diarrhea overnight? And are you able to drink more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still going a lot, but it’s not quite as constant. I’m drinking a little. I’m worried I’ll go home and it’ll come right back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That worry makes sense given what you’ve been through. The taper/pulse plan is specifically to lower the chance of it coming back. We’ll also make sure you have a clear schedule and follow-up with your primary doctor and GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my usual meds? I’m on a lot—gabapentin, Prozac, Abilify, Ativan, propranolol, Keppra.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—those are being continued here: levetiracetam for seizures, and your depression/anxiety medications. We’ll also keep your sleep medication available as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my stomach meds? I’m on pantoprazole twice a day, ranitidine, and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing them for now since they’re part of your baseline regimen and you have a history of ulcers. That said, we do think about whether long-term acid suppression is necessary in someone with recurrent C. diff, so we’ll ask you to discuss that with your outpatient doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take laxatives sometimes because I swing between constipation and diarrhea. Should I take them now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not while you’re having active diarrhea. We’re going to hold your bowel regimen meds—like senna, bisacodyl, and polyethylene glycol—until the diarrhea resolves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been able to keep down liquids today, and your exam looks stable. If you can tolerate food and your symptoms keep improving, we can plan for discharge tomorrow with the vancomycin taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home, but I’m nervous. What should make me come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for inability to keep fluids down, worsening severe abdominal pain, fever, blood in stool, dizziness or fainting, or if diarrhea becomes so frequent you can’t stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You look more comfortable today. How’s the nausea and diarrhea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’m still tender in the epigastric area, but it’s closer to my usual. I ate a little and kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your labs look stable, and your bicarbonate has normalized, which suggests you’re less dehydrated. I think you’re safe to go home today if you feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you go over the vancomycin schedule slowly? I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. You’ll take vancomycin 125 mg four times a day for 14 days, then 125 mg twice a day for 7 days, then 125 mg once daily for 7 days, and then 125 mg every 3 days for several additional weeks. Your PCP or GI will help confirm the exact end date and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start feeling better—can I stop early?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—please don’t stop early. Feeling better is expected, but stopping early increases the risk of relapse. If you’re having side effects or can’t keep it down, call your doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another colonoscopy? Someone mentioned microscopic colitis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something to discuss with GI. Your last colonoscopy had poor prep, and because you’ve had long-standing diarrhea even outside of C. diff episodes, repeating it may help evaluate other causes like microscopic colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything I should change at home with my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start with what you can tolerate—small, bland meals and plenty of fluids. The key is hydration. If certain foods worsen diarrhea, avoid them temporarily and advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also worried about my anxiety getting worse when I’m home dealing with this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very real. We’re continuing your home medications for anxiety and depression. If you notice worsening symptoms, please reach out to your outpatient clinicians—don’t wait until it feels unmanageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, quick review: keep taking your seizure medication levetiracetam twice daily, continue your other home meds, and hold the laxatives until diarrhea resolves. Do you have a way to pick up the vancomycin and get to follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my husband can pick up the meds and drive me. I just want to make sure I’m not contagious forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re most contagious when you have active diarrhea. As it improves, risk goes down, but good hand hygiene remains important. Clean the bathroom regularly, wash hands with soap and water, and avoid sharing towels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll discharge you home now. If symptoms worsen or you can’t stay hydrated, come back. Otherwise, follow up with your primary care doctor and gastroenterology to confirm the vancomycin taper end date and next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me what’s been going on at home since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It just didn’t get better. I’ve been taking the vancomycin like they told me, but I’m still having diarrhea a lot and I can’t keep food down. I feel dried out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How many times a day are you having diarrhea, roughly? And when was the last time you vomited?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was a lot at home—like all day. I threw up multiple times today before coming in. It’s mostly dry heaving now, but it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, blood in the stool, chest pain, shortness of breath, or burning when you pee?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No blood. No breathing issues. Peeing is just not much because I’m not drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with dehydration. In the emergency department your vital signs were stable, and your blood work didn’t show a high white count. We’re giving you IV fluids now and medication for nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s the C. diff again. Why isn’t the antibiotic working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could still be related, but there are a couple possibilities: sometimes symptoms lag behind even when the infection is improving, and sometimes vomiting makes it hard to keep the medicine down. We’re going to re-test your stool for C. diff toxin/PCR and also check for other infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do another scan? I’ve had so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A CT of your abdomen and pelvis was done tonight to make sure there’s no obstruction or severe colitis. The initial read shows no acute process—no dangerous swelling of the colon and no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With repeated vomiting and frequent diarrhea, the intestines can be very irritated, and dehydration can make pain feel worse. We’ll treat symptoms while we rule out anything dangerous. We’ll also keep your stomach-protecting medicines going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have that feeding tube history and the bypass reversal—could something be wrong with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your surgical history, we always take that seriously. The CT didn’t show a surgical complication or bowel obstruction. We’ll keep monitoring your belly exam closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something stronger for nausea? The Zofran helps a little but not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s schedule anti-nausea medication and keep it available as needed. The goal is to stop the vomiting so you can keep down fluids and your vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds? I don’t want to be judged, but it’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll treat your pain while keeping you safe. We’ll use acetaminophen and your home gabapentin, and we can use a small amount of opioid if needed, especially while you’re unable to eat and drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to stop feeling like I’m going to pass out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update: your lactate is normal, which is reassuring, and your kidney function looks okay. We’ll continue IV fluids overnight and recheck labs in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I’m not septic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—right now there’s no sign of sepsis. We’re still taking cultures and stool tests, but nothing suggests a dangerous infection in your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing told me you were able to keep down a few sips of water. How’s the nausea at this moment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. My mouth feels less dry. Still crampy though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep the fluids running and aim to transition you to drinking on your own as soon as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Any vomiting since you got to the floor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. Still diarrhea, but not as constant as at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We sent stool testing for C. diff and also cultures for bacteria and parasites. While we wait, we’re continuing your oral vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If the C. diff test comes back negative, why keep taking vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you were already on a planned taper for a recent recurrence. A negative test today suggests the infection may be clearing, but stopping abruptly can increase the risk of relapse. The plan is to continue the taper you were prescribed and have GI help decide when it’s safe to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the diarrhea could be from something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—diarrhea can persist from irritation after infection, from medications, or from other causes. The CT didn’t show anything acute, and your labs are reassuring, so we’re focusing on hydration, symptom control, and making sure there isn’t another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat? I’m afraid to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s start slowly—clear liquids first, then advance as tolerated. The key is small amounts frequently. If you feel nauseated, pause and use the antiemetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure always runs low. Are you worried about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it’s on the low side but you’re not dizzy and your heart rate is okay. Dehydration can lower it. We’re also watching your propranolol because it can push blood pressure down further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did lunch go? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept down some broth and crackers. Pain is still there but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep IV fluids for now and reassess later today—if you keep drinking, we can start turning them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will the C. diff result be back? I’m anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should result this evening. I’ll check and let you know as soon as it’s posted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff PCR came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Negative? Then why am I still having diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A negative PCR means we didn’t detect toxigenic C. diff in the sample. The diarrhea can still take time to settle as your gut recovers, and dehydration itself can make you feel awful. The good news is we’re not seeing signs of severe colitis or another acute abdominal problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can stop the vancomycin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Because you were treated for a recurrence recently, the safest plan is to continue the taper schedule you were already given and follow up with GI to decide the endpoint. Stopping suddenly can lead to symptoms flaring again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want to be on antibiotics forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. The taper is designed to gradually reduce it. GI will reassess with you at follow-up and decide if any changes are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today compared with when you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’m not throwing up. Diarrhea is still there but way less. I’m tired though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we’re seeing. Your exam is improved and you’re walking in the hallway. Your labs show some mild electrolyte changes and mild anemia compared to admission, which can happen with lots of fluids and illness—we’ll keep an eye on it, but nothing suggests bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the other stool tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far, stool cultures are negative for common bacteria like Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter, and the parasite tests don’t show ova and parasites or Giardia/Cryptosporidium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s basically just my gut being angry and me being dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading explanation given the negative infectious workup and the normal CT. The main treatment is hydration, continuing the planned vancomycin taper, and symptom control while your intestines recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure was low again this morning. Are you going to change my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Because your blood pressure has been low and you’re not having symptoms that require it urgently, we’re going to hold your propranolol for now and have you discuss restarting it with your outpatient doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous to stop it suddenly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At your dose, holding it is generally safe, especially since low blood pressure is the bigger immediate issue. If you notice palpitations, chest pain, or severe anxiety symptoms after stopping, you should call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating food and fluids today without vomiting, we can likely discharge you home later this afternoon. How does that sound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home, but I’m worried it’ll come right back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That worry makes sense given how many times you’ve been through this. The things that make us comfortable discharging are: you’re keeping down oral intake, your pain is controlled with oral meds, your vitals are stable, and the dangerous causes have been ruled out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I do if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the ondansetron as prescribed, take small sips of fluids, and if you can’t keep anything down or you feel faint, come back for care. Also come in for severe worsening abdominal pain, fever, or blood in stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get pain medicine to go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a small supply of oxycodone for moderate pain, and you can use acetaminophen for mild pain. Because opioids can worsen constipation and sometimes nausea, we want you to use the lowest amount needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I have diarrhea—why would constipation matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bowel pattern can swing as you recover, especially once diarrhea improves. We’re keeping your bowel regimen medications as ‘as needed’ only, and you should avoid taking them unless you become constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s review your vancomycin plan: continue it exactly as the taper schedule from your last discharge. GI will see you in follow-up and help decide when to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you write it down? I get confused with the taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—we’ll put the step-by-step schedule in your discharge paperwork, and the pharmacy label will match it. If anything doesn’t match what you were told previously, call us or your GI office before changing doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds—my seizure medicine and my antidepressants?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your levetiracetam for seizures and your psychiatric medications as you were taking them. We’re also continuing your stomach protection medicines—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate—since you have a history of ulcers and reflux symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’ve had no vomiting here, your diarrhea is much less frequent, and you’re tolerating oral intake. Your blood cultures haven’t grown anything so far, and the remaining stool tests are negative. We’ll discharge you home today with instructions and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m relieved the C. diff test was negative, but I’ll keep taking the vancomycin taper and call if things get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. Remember: don’t restart propranolol until you’ve discussed it with your outpatient doctor because of the low blood pressure here. We’ll include that clearly in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want a normal day without my stomach controlling everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I hear you came in with severe upper abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s this awful pain right in the middle, like burning and stabbing. I started throwing up and I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is the vomit bloody or does it look like coffee grounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not bloody. Just regular vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just nausea, pain, and I had diarrhea earlier this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How many times a day were you having diarrhea before you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bunch—several times a day. But today it’s mostly the vomiting and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’ve had Roux-en-Y bypass in the past and then a reversal, and you’ve had ulcers before. Does this pain feel like those ulcer episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Exactly like that. And it gets worse when I try to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been taking your stomach medications—pantoprazole or ranitidine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped them. I felt like I didn’t need them anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful to know. In the emergency department you had a CT scan, and it did not show a bowel obstruction or a surgical complication. Surgery also evaluated you and didn’t think you needed an operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt this much if the scan is normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A CT is good for blockages and major complications, but it can’t always show irritation of the stomach lining. Given your history and stopping acid medicines, one possibility is gastritis—irritation from acid or bile reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so nauseous I can’t swallow pills. And I need my Keppra—can I get it through the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. For now we can give levetiracetam by IV while you’re too nauseated to take pills, and we’ll switch back to oral once you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your fingerstick blood sugar was around 70 when you arrived. That’s low-normal, and with poor intake it can make you feel shaky. We’ll give IV fluids with some dextrose and monitor your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel shaky and weak. I’m scared it’s going to drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep checking it. The goal is to support you until you can eat again, because eating small amounts regularly is usually what stabilizes it best for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine helped a little in the ER. Can I keep getting that? My oxycodone at home didn’t touch this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We want to control pain, but IV opioids can worsen nausea, slow the gut, and can drop blood pressure. We’ll start with bowel rest, IV pantoprazole, and anti-nausea medicine, and we’ll reassess pain control frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want to suffer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll treat the underlying irritation and use safer pain options as much as possible—acetaminophen and, if needed, tramadol by mouth once you can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any more vomiting since you got to the floor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not since the last Zofran, but I still feel queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep Zofran available as needed and keep you NPO for now—just letting your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight was quiet. How’s the pain and nausea right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurts in the same spot. Nausea is a little better, but I’m afraid to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. GI is going to see you today. Our working thought is bile reflux or gastritis related to your post-surgical anatomy and stopping the reflux meds. We’re continuing IV pantoprazole twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they going to do an endoscopy now? I feel like that’s the only way to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll ask them directly. Sometimes, if symptoms improve with bowel rest and stronger acid suppression, they recommend deferring endoscopy to outpatient—especially if there’s no bleeding and the CT is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI evaluated you. They think this fits bile reflux gastritis. Their recommendation is bowel rest, IV PPI, then slowly advance your diet, and focus on smaller, more frequent meals to reduce reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no EGD while I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. They feel an inpatient EGD is unlikely to change what we do today, because the main treatment is exactly what we’re already doing—high-dose PPI and protecting the stomach lining. You also have an outpatient plan with your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m frustrated. This keeps happening and no one fixes it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. What we can do in the hospital is make sure there’s no emergency problem, get symptoms under control, and set you up with the right follow-up testing and long-term plan. We’ll also add sucralfate to coat the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure feels low. I’m dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is on the low side, and you’ve had low readings before. We’re giving IV fluids now. Also, opioids like morphine can worsen low blood pressure, so we’re going to stop IV morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop it, what am I supposed to take for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use acetaminophen and, once you can take pills, tramadol as needed. We’ll also keep treating the stomach irritation—often that’s what drives the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with sips of clear liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can sip a little. It still burns, but I’m not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep it slow and see if we can advance to small, bland meals tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any diarrhea since you’ve been here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, actually. I haven’t really gone much at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given that, we’re not going to send stool tests right now. You mentioned you stopped the vancomycin taper because you ran out—since you’re not having significant diarrhea in the hospital, we’re not treating C. diff during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it still be C. diff even without diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: C. diff typically causes frequent watery diarrhea. Without that, it’s less likely to be the driver of your current symptoms. We’ll keep watching, and if diarrhea returns we can reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars have been stable since you started taking in some calories. We’re going to stop the dextrose-containing IV fluids and continue checking fingersticks for a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the shaky feeling was from not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our best explanation. We didn’t see dangerously low values on blood tests, but low-normal sugars can still make you feel unwell, especially with your history after bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I switch back to my Keppra pills? The IV keeps beeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re keeping liquids down, yes—we can transition back to oral levetiracetam today and stop the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I saw you walking in the hallway earlier. How’s the nausea and pain with the small meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can eat a little at a time. If I eat too much, it feels like it comes right back up. The pain is still there, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That pattern fits bile reflux. The plan is small, frequent meals and staying on pantoprazole twice a day. We’re also continuing ranitidine and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to take all of those together?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but timing matters. Sucralfate can interfere with absorption of other meds, so we’ll give you a schedule—usually sucralfate four times a day, spaced away from other pills when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried you’re sending me home without figuring it out. I want an EGD before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear the concern. We spoke again with the GI team. They still feel an inpatient EGD won’t change the immediate treatment and that you’re better served keeping your planned outpatient endoscopy with your gastroenterologist, where they can follow results and adjust long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But what if it’s an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it is an ulcer, the first-line treatment is high-dose acid suppression and protecting the lining—exactly what we’re doing. The key is staying on the meds consistently and following up for the scope. If you develop black stools, vomiting blood, fainting, or worsening severe pain, you should come back immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain control, we’re avoiding oxycodone and other stronger narcotics here because of the low blood pressure and nausea. How is tramadol working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It helps some. Not perfect, but I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You finished breakfast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I ate a small tray. No vomiting. Still tender, but it’s like my usual pain now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your vitals look stable. We’ll discharge you today with pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine, and sucralfate, plus Zofran as needed. For pain: acetaminophen and tramadol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special with meals at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—small, frequent meals, and avoid large portions that trigger reflux. Keep taking the reflux medications even if you feel better. And keep your GI follow-up for the outpatient endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my low blood sugar episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The best prevention is regular small meals and not going long stretches without eating. If you feel shaky, check your sugar if you can and take quick carbohydrates, then follow with a small snack. Come in if you can’t keep anything down again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still upset, but I can go if the plan is solid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fair. We’ll print your medication list and the warning signs to watch for. We’ll also make sure you have the GI appointment information before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re on the medicine floor now. I want to check in after what sounds like a seizure this morning and then low blood pressure and fever in the ED. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m confused. I don’t remember anything except waking up and then being in the ER. Did I really have a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your husband reported a convulsion that lasted about three minutes. It’s common not to remember the event itself. Right now your neurologic exam looks normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did I fall? Did I hit my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: From what we were told, there was no head strike. We’ll keep monitoring you closely, and if you develop new symptoms like worsening headache, vomiting, or confusion, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said my blood pressure dropped. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but in your case it improved quickly with IV fluids. Because you also had a fever and a high white blood cell count, we’re treating this like sepsis—an infection affecting the whole body—until we prove otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where is the infection? I don’t even feel sick. No cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two possibilities we’re considering: your chest X-ray showed a left lower lobe pneumonia, and your urine test had a small amount of white cells and bacteria. Also, because you have a PICC line, we have to consider a line infection. We’ve sent blood cultures to look for bacteria in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why they started those antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You received broad antibiotics in the ED—vancomycin and another one—to cover the most likely bacteria while we wait for culture results. We’ll narrow them as soon as we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about my sugars. I usually need D5 through my PICC or I crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. We’re running dextrose-containing IV fluids right now and checking your fingerstick glucose. We’ll adjust based on your numbers and what you’re able to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach… if I eat the wrong thing I vomit. I’m scared to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slowly. We’ll keep your nausea meds available and continue your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate—like you take at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to be in the ICU?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now you’re stable on the floor—your blood pressure is holding after fluids and you’re breathing well. If anything changes, we’d escalate quickly, but at the moment ICU isn’t needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight you stayed stable. Your initial labs showed a high white count and a lactate that suggested your body was under stress from infection, but both are improving with fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it really is sepsis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating it as sepsis because you had fever, low blood pressure, and lab signs of infection. The key now is identifying the source and making sure the antibiotics are the right ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my PICC? I’ve had infections before. I’m terrified you’ll take it out and then I’ll have no way to keep my sugar up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a very real concern. If the blood cultures suggest the line is infected, removing it is often the safest way to clear the infection. We can support your glucose with peripheral IV dextrose while we sort out a longer-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have these headaches lately—throbbing, blurry vision sometimes. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Headaches can have many causes. Right now you don’t have signs of meningitis like neck stiffness, and your exam is reassuring. We’ll treat pain with acetaminophen and keep watching; if anything changes, we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to update you: your CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis didn’t show any obstruction or surgical complication. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does my belly hurt so much sometimes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan rules out emergencies like obstruction. It doesn’t always explain chronic abdominal pain, especially with your complex bariatric history. We’ll focus on controlling nausea, keeping you nourished, and using your pain medicines as safely as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m shaking a little. Can you check my sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—thank you for calling. We’ll check it now and treat quickly if it’s low. We’re also keeping you on dextrose-containing fluids tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning update: your white blood cell count has come down a lot since admission, which suggests the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do we know what the infection is yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One of your blood culture bottles grew a skin-type bacteria called coagulase-negative staph, specifically Staph epidermidis. Sometimes it’s a contaminant, but with a PICC line and your presentation, we’re taking it seriously as a possible line-associated bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think it’s from my PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s one of the leading possibilities. To help clear the infection and prevent it from coming back, we recommend removing the PICC and culturing the tip. We’ll keep antibiotics going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you remove it, how will I get my D5? I’m scared I’ll bottom out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can run dextrose through a regular IV in your arm for now, and we’ll check your sugars frequently. Also, we’re involving Endocrinology and Nutrition to reduce the need for IV dextrose by adjusting what and how you eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC has been removed. The catheter tip was sent for culture. We’ll watch the site and your vitals closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It stings a little. Does that mean the infection is gone now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Removing the line helps a lot, but we still need to complete antibiotics to fully treat any bloodstream infection. We’ll also repeat blood cultures to confirm they’re negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news: the repeat blood cultures so far show no growth, which means we’re likely clearing the bacteria from your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can stop the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Infectious Diseases recommends a full 7-day course of IV vancomycin given the concern for a central-line associated infection. We’ve stopped the extra antibiotic we were using for broad coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pneumonia they saw? I still don’t feel like I’m coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray showed a left lower lobe consolidation consistent with pneumonia. Sometimes people don’t have much cough, especially early. The antibiotics you’ve been on cover common pneumonia bacteria as well, and you’ve stayed stable on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the seizure will happen again. I’ve had several this year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case. We’re increasing your Keppra dose to 1000 mg twice a day to reduce the risk of recurrence. We’ll also arrange follow-up with your outpatient neurologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it because my sugar was low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At the time of the event, your glucose was in a normal range—so it doesn’t look like hypoglycemia triggered it this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the echocardiogram—an ultrasound of your heart. It shows normal heart pumping function and no signs of infection on the valves, which is what we were looking for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no endocarditis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no vegetations were seen. That supports that the infection is limited and responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology and Nutrition weighed in. They think your low sugars are most consistent with post-prandial hypoglycemia—blood sugar dropping after meals—which can happen after bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my bypass was reversed. Why would that still happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even after reversal, the way your gut handles food and insulin can remain altered. The pattern we’re seeing fits drops after certain foods, especially high-glycemic foods—things that turn into sugar quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what am I supposed to eat? Everything hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The plan is to move from the bariatric stage 3 diet to a diabetic, consistent-carbohydrate approach: six small meals spread through the day, focusing on protein and fats, and avoiding high-sugar foods. We’ll trial foods slowly and pair them with supplements like Glucerna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried some of the new food last night and I got horrible abdominal pain. I needed extra Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry—that sounds awful. We’ll adjust the pace of diet advancement and keep portions very small. For pain, we’ll continue your home regimen and use breakthrough hydromorphone only when needed, because it has risks like sedation and constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be judged for needing it. The pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. Our goal is to treat your pain while also keeping you safe. We’ll also make sure you have a bowel regimen to prevent constipation while you’re on opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars have stayed stable even without continuous D5 infusions, which is encouraging. We’ll keep checking after meals to see how your body responds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I won’t need a PICC again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can maintain stable sugars and meet nutrition goals by mouth, we’d prefer to avoid another central line because of infection risk. We’ll make that decision based on how you do over the next couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Update: your surveillance blood cultures remain negative, and you’ve been afebrile with stable blood pressure. You’re on track to complete the 7-day vancomycin course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did the PICC tip culture show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter tip culture did not show significant growth. Even so, given the positive blood culture and your symptoms, treating as a line-associated infection was the safest approach, and you’ve improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about going home and having another seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The Keppra dose increase is meant to reduce that risk. We’ll make sure you leave with the updated prescription and clear instructions, and we’ll emphasize neurology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition met with you and your husband. The target is about 1500 calories per day, using small meals and Glucerna supplementation. How did yesterday go with eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Small amounts still hurt, but I didn’t vomit. I managed a couple small meals and a Glucerna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. If you can keep that up for another day, it supports a safe discharge plan without IV dextrose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in a couple days. I’m worried it’ll make the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start scheduled senna and docusate. If you still don’t have a bowel movement after a few days, you can use Miralax as needed. If your stools become loose or watery, you should hold the senna and docusate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning your labs look stable, and your white count is normal. You’ve been tolerating small meals for the last 48 hours with Glucerna and no hypoglycemia. We’re planning discharge later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved, but nervous. What do I need to do at home to keep my sugars from dropping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Key points: avoid high-glycemic foods, eat small frequent meals, and check your glucose after meals as instructed. Drink fluids as tolerated. Add one Glucerna about an hour after each meal to help meet calories without spiking sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get that severe pain after eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to keep portions very small and advance slowly. You can use your prescribed pain regimen for breakthrough pain, but we want you to be cautious with hydromorphone. We’re also recommending you reconnect with your chronic pain specialist to reassess the long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’re sending me home with Narcan. Does that mean you think I’m going to overdose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. It’s a safety medication. Because opioids can cause dangerous sleepiness or slow breathing, having intranasal naloxone at home is a precaution—especially if you ever seem overly sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics—am I continuing them at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be completing the planned course here in the hospital. Your repeat blood cultures stayed negative and your heart ultrasound didn’t show valve infection, so there’s no need for prolonged IV antibiotics after discharge based on what we’ve found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need another PICC placed before I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Since your sugars have been stable without IV dextrose and you’re eating small meals, we’re discharging you without a central line to reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, two follow-ups: Neurology for seizures and Endocrinology for hypoglycemia and nutrition. Also, you’ll have outpatient lab work drawn—fasting insulin and C-peptide—with results sent to your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are those labs for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They help your endocrinologist understand how much insulin your body is making when you’re fasting, which can guide management of your hypoglycemia pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’re stable, afebrile, and your blood pressure is good. Your discharge meds include the higher Keppra dose, your stomach meds, your home pain and nausea meds, plus senna/colace and Miralax as needed. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I get fever again, or I feel faint, what should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have fever, shaking chills, worsening shortness of breath, confusion, repeated vomiting, very low blood sugars that don’t respond to your usual plan, or another seizure—call emergency services or come to the ED right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything. I’m still scared, but I feel more prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you today. I understand you came in with worsening abdominal pain. Can you tell me what feels different from your usual pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always have epigastric pain, but a few days ago it started wrapping around the right side and into my back. It’s sharper and it won’t let up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, rash, or recent injury? And how has the vomiting been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or rash. I’m still throwing up small amounts like I usually do, but it’s more frequent when the pain spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I reviewed your ED workup. Your CT scan showed the feeding tube was not in the right place—it was sitting in the abdominal wall rather than where it should be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why it hurts? Did it puncture something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan did not show a perforation, obstruction, or free air, and there wasn’t a drainable fluid collection. So we don’t see evidence it punctured bowel. But a malpositioned tube can definitely cause pain and irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took it out in the ER, right? Why do I still hurt this much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, surgery removed it without incident. Pain can persist after removal because the tract and surrounding tissue are inflamed, and you also have chronic abdominal pain and gastroparesis that can amplify symptoms. We’ll keep checking for anything dangerous, but so far the imaging and labs are reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine made me so nauseous. I don’t want more of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We can switch to a small dose of oral oxycodone instead, since morphine seemed to worsen nausea for you. We’ll also keep your nausea medicines on board—metoclopramide with meals, and ondansetron or prochlorperazine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will oxycodone make me vomit too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can in some people, but many tolerate it better than IV morphine. We’ll start low, reassess often, and pair it with anti-nausea meds. The goal is enough relief to let you sip and eat small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m dizzy when I stand up. The room spins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen when you’re dehydrated from poor intake and vomiting. Your lactate was high when you arrived, but it came down quickly with IV fluids, which supports dehydration as a big factor. We’ll continue IV fluids while you’re not able to take much by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does the high lactate mean I’m septic again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In your case, it improved to normal after fluids and your other labs and vital signs don’t suggest infection right now. So we’re not treating for sepsis at this time, but we’ll keep monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my gallbladder? This is right-sided.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. The right upper quadrant ultrasound was normal and showed no gallstones. Your liver tests and lipase were also not concerning. So gallbladder and pancreas causes look unlikely based on what we have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Main goals: control pain and nausea, keep you hydrated, monitor blood sugars since you can run low when you can’t eat, and get Nutrition involved because of the ongoing difficulty meeting needs by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars drop fast. I can feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do fingerstick checks every 6 hours while you’re here. If you’re not eating, we can run IV fluids with dextrose to prevent lows, and we’ll respond quickly if you feel symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a few sips and it came right back up. Can I just not eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, small sips and small, frequent bites are best—nothing large at once. If you can’t keep anything down, we’ll rely on IV fluids temporarily, but we want to avoid prolonged periods without nutrition if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you put the tube back in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your surgical history and the fact that the tube already migrated into the abdominal wall, replacing it here could be risky. Surgery evaluated you and didn’t think there was a safe surgical intervention to do right now at this hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what am I supposed to do? I can’t live like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know this is exhausting. One option we’re discussing is transferring you to the hospital where your primary surgeon is, so decisions about longer-term pain and nutrition strategies can be made with the team that knows your anatomy and prior operations best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how is the pain after the first doses of oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It takes the edge off more than the morphine did, and I’m less nauseous. Still hurts though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful feedback. We’ll keep it as needed for severe pain and use acetaminophen for milder pain. We’ll also keep an eye on constipation and sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure feels low. I’m lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pressures have been on the softer side at times, likely from poor intake. We’ll give another fluid bolus and recheck. Let us know if you feel faint when standing—please call before getting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight you needed some IV fluids again. Any new symptoms—fever, worsening belly swelling, blood in vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No blood. Just the same pain and nausea. I’m scared you’re missing something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. The reassuring parts are: CT didn’t show obstruction or perforation, ultrasound didn’t show gallstones, your white count is normal, and your lactate normalized with fluids. We’ll keep reassessing your exam and labs, but right now we don’t see a surgical emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about infection at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We swabbed the site; it showed mixed skin and environmental bacteria—nothing pointing to a specific dangerous infection. The area is being packed and is draining a small amount of serosanguinous fluid, which can happen as it heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower? I don’t want it to get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have nursing review wound care instructions with you. Generally we keep the dressing clean and dry and change it as directed. We’ll tailor it to how the site looks today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition is coming by today. We’re worried about malnutrition because you’re not able to take enough in consistently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard that before. Every time I eat more, I vomit. What do you want me to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The focus is on strategies that are more tolerable with gastroparesis—small frequent meals, liquids or supplements if you can tolerate them, and avoiding large high-sugar loads that can worsen your post-bypass hypoglycemia. It’s not a perfect solution, but it can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My fingerstick was low-ish earlier. I felt shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that—your lowest has been around 70. We started dextrose-containing IV fluids to support you while intake is poor, and we’ll keep checking every 6 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there any chance this is my ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible your history of marginal ulcer contributes to chronic symptoms. We’re continuing your acid suppression—omeprazole daily and ranitidine twice a day—because that’s important protection. The new right-sided wrapping pain still doesn’t have a clear structural cause on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How did you do with oral meds and a little intake yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few bites stayed down, but then I vomited again. The oxycodone helps but I don’t want to be on it long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good goal. We’ll keep it only as needed for severe pain and try to space doses out as you can. We also want to avoid escalating opioids because they can worsen gut motility and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Someone mentioned a gastric pacer before. Is that happening now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something being discussed with your outpatient surgeon for gastroparesis, but it’s not something we can start here during this admission. Another reason transfer to your surgeon’s hospital may help is to move those longer-term decisions forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about getting nutrition through an IV. I had a line infection before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your concern is very valid. Nutrition through an IV—TPN—requires a central line and carries a real infection risk. Given your history, we want to avoid that unless absolutely necessary. That’s why we’re trying to maximize what you can tolerate by mouth and discussing options with your surgical team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed some outpatient labs and you have vitamin D deficiency and iron deficiency. We started high-dose vitamin D once weekly while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that fix the fatigue? And what about the iron—do I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vitamin D repletion can help over time, but it’s not immediate. For iron, your situation fits iron deficiency; we’re not talking about a blood transfusion right now. We’ll recommend considering IV iron as an outpatient, since pills can be hard on the stomach and may not absorb well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My anxiety is through the roof. I feel like I’m stuck in a loop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s been so overwhelming. We’ll continue your home medications for anxiety, depression, and PTSD, including your as-needed lorazepam. If you want, we can also ask the team to check in about coping strategies while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I having seizures from not eating? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You haven’t had any seizures during this stay. We’re continuing your levetiracetam at your home dose, and we’re monitoring your glucose to reduce triggers like hypoglycemia. If you feel an aura or anything concerning, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re focusing on next steps. Your pain is somewhat improved with oral oxycodone, but you’re still not tolerating enough by mouth, and you’ve needed IV fluids and dextrose at times for low sugars and low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The plan is discharge to an extended care facility while we arrange transfer to the hospital where your primary surgeon is. That way you’ll have support with hydration, nutrition planning, and wound care while the transfer is coordinated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I tell them there? I don’t want to start from scratch again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a detailed summary: you came in with new right-sided wrapping abdominal pain; CT showed the feeding tube was malpositioned in the abdominal wall and it was removed; imaging and labs didn’t show obstruction, perforation, gallstones, or another acute surgical cause; you had poor intake with soft blood pressures and borderline low sugars treated with IV fluids and dextrose; and we found vitamin D and iron deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the tube site—do I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, no. The wound swab showed mixed flora and there’s no sign of a deep infection on imaging. We’ll continue local care—packing and dressing changes—and watch for redness spreading, pus, fever, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medicines am I leaving with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your home meds: levetiracetam, metoclopramide with meals, omeprazole and ranitidine, ondansetron and prochlorperazine as needed, propranolol, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, zolpidem, and lorazepam as needed. New: vitamin D once weekly. For pain: acetaminophen for mild pain and oxycodone 10 mg every 6 hours as needed for severe pain, with a plan to wean as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—just making sure that’s noted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s clearly listed, and we’re avoiding those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anything I should watch for that means I need to come back right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes: severe worsening abdominal pain with a rigid belly, persistent vomiting you can’t control, fever or chills, blood in vomit or stool, fainting, or recurrent low blood sugar symptoms that don’t improve with quick sugar. Also any worsening redness or drainage at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, any last questions about the transfer plan or your nutrition strategy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… please make sure my surgeon gets everything. I’m tired of repeating the story.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We will. We’ll send the imaging reports, lab trends, and our hospital course summary, and we’ll highlight the key issues: tube displacement and removal, ongoing pain and poor intake, intermittent low blood pressure and borderline low glucose, and the vitamin and iron deficiencies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you for explaining it in a way I can follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll proceed with discharge now and keep working on the transfer so you can be seen by your surgical team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I want to check in after your fall and passing out. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired. My stomach is burning like always, and my left knee hurts from the fall. I’m scared it’s a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to worry about. From what you and your son described—standing up, room spinning, then passing out—this could be from low blood volume and low blood pressure when you stand, especially with how little you’ve been able to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I barely get down water. Since the hiatal hernia surgery, I can’t tolerate anything. Even protein shakes make me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that in the ER—your heart rate was low at first, and you were dehydrated. We’re going to keep giving IV fluids and check orthostatic vitals—blood pressure and pulse lying, sitting, and standing—to see if they drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the slurred speech I had this morning? That freaked me out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took that seriously. The CT and the CT angiogram of your head and neck didn’t show a stroke, bleeding, or a blocked artery. Neurology also examined you and thinks a neurologic emergency is unlikely, but they’ll stay involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on the imaging, there’s no evidence of an acute stroke. We’ll still monitor you closely, especially because you’ve had dizziness and a seizure history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach pain is worse since that surgery. It’s like burning right here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Your CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis didn’t show an obstruction or anything acute, which is reassuring. Given your history of marginal ulcers and chronic nausea/vomiting, we’re going to focus on acid suppression and nausea control while we figure out nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin. Please don’t give me those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for saying that—we have it listed, and we won’t give NSAIDs. We’ll use acetaminophen and other options for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My knee—did I break it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The knee X-ray didn’t show a fracture, and there wasn’t an effusion seen. We’ll treat it with acetaminophen and a lidocaine patch and keep an eye on swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing: your head/neck scan incidentally noted a very small lung nodule—4 millimeters. It’s not causing your symptoms, but we’ll recommend follow-up imaging in about 12 months if you’re considered high risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A lung nodule? Does that mean cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most nodules that small are benign. The recommendation is just to consider a repeat CT in a year depending on risk factors. We’ll put it in your discharge plan so it doesn’t get lost.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight, did you have any more dizziness when you stood up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When I got up to the bathroom, I felt like I was going to black out again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your orthostatic vitals are still positive—your blood pressure drops when you stand. That supports dehydration and low circulating volume as the main cause. We’ll continue IV fluids and encourage small sips as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But sipping hurts. It makes the burning worse and then I throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We tried antacids and an H2 blocker, but given your symptoms we’re switching to pantoprazole twice a day, which is stronger acid suppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that different from my omeprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same class of medication, but we’re using pantoprazole at a higher, scheduled dose twice daily to calm irritation and help ulcers heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need another feeding tube? Last time it went wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not rushing into anything. First we want GI to evaluate why swallowing and intake are so hard right now. Nutrition will also see you today to assess malnutrition risk and options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case again. They still think this episode is more consistent with syncope than a seizure, but given your history they recommend EEG monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does the EEG involve? Is it painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not painful. Sticky electrodes go on your scalp to record brain waves. We’re looking for seizure activity while you’re awake and asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EEG so far looks normal—no seizures captured and no epileptiform activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I get that spinning feeling like before a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That spinning can come from low blood pressure, inner ear issues, or less commonly neurologic causes. Because your exam raised some concern, neurology recommended an MRI of the brain to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have the MRI result: it’s normal—no stroke or mass. There’s a tiny benign-appearing cyst remnant in the right hippocampal area that isn’t an acute finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s a relief. But I still feel weak when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. The main driver still seems to be low intake and dehydration. We’ll keep working on fluids and nutrition, and we’ll have physical therapy help with safe ambulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is the nausea today? Any vomiting overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up once. The burning pain is constant. I’m afraid to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart metoclopramide to help stomach emptying, since gastroparesis has been part of your history. We held it initially because of a prolonged QT concern, but we think the benefit outweighs the risk now and we’ll monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried so many meds. What if nothing works?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
